reply.text: I have the deck, 2 bells in the first watch, 21:22. Mr Bowen is for below once the lunar is worked — it is worked: longitude by lunar 4° 54' W against the reckoning 4° 43' W, a drift of four cables, well within his thirty miles, and the variation now 25° W by the sunset amplitude in place of the chart's 21° 30'. The captain's word through Mr Pascoe: set the square sail when the apparent wind may come abeam and the course sou'westerly. The apparent is still 57° on the starboard bow and the wind fading — 6 knots — so the square sail must wait; the hands stay handy. The course stands by the standing order, full and by, everything else already set and drawing.

args.text: say to Mr Pascoe keep the hands handy by the square sail, but she will not carry it yet: the apparent wind is still 57 degrees on the starboard bow. When the wind veers and it comes abeam I will give the word to set it.

args.note: 21:22, first watch 2 bells. Took the deck from the captain for the night watch; he goes below once the lunar is worked. Lunar by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen: longitude 4° 54' W, trusted within 30 miles — reckoning was 4° 43' W, the account moved four cables W by S, no matter. Variation now 25° W by the sunset amplitude (was 21° 30' W by the 1794 chart) — allowed in the reckoning from now; my own reckoning 49° 07' N, 4° 45' W, 2 miles SW by S of the master's. Wind W, faded to 6 knots (8 at the dog watch); she stands S (180°), full and by starboard tack, the WSW course for the Azores not layable; glass 30.12 rising strongly, hazy, smooth sea, moonlit night — land made out at a league, none in sight, no danger within 10 miles. The captain's word by Mr Pascoe: square sail when the apparent may come abeam and course sou'westerly — apparent 57° on the bow, so it waits; hands handy. Tide allowance (ebb half a knot SW) holds till about a quarter past ten, then the Hourly Shaping takes it. Watching: the wind veering (W → W by N would bring the apparent near abeam and the square sail with it), any shift toward the fair wind he wants, the hourly shaping, the haze thickening. Pascoe looks for little wind before the forenoon.

I have the deck, 2 bells in the first watch, 21:22. Mr Bowen is for below once the lunar is worked — it is worked: longitude by lunar 4° 54' W against the reckoning 4° 43' W, a drift of four cables, well within his thirty miles, and the variation now 25° W by the sunset amplitude in place of the chart's 21° 30'. The captain's word through Mr Pascoe: set the square sail when the apparent wind may come abeam and the course sou'westerly. The apparent is still 57° on the starboard bow and the wind fading — 6 knots — so the square sail must wait; the hands stay handy. The course stands by the standing order, full and by, everything else already set and drawing.

args.text: Aye aye, sir, I have it. The offing I mind by the reckoning and the lead: I'll cast the lead now and hourly through the watch, and if the wind holds westerly while she keeps south or east of south and the reckoning closes the Breton shore, I'll wear ship to the larboard tack in good time — she has but six knots and may miss stays, so wearing keeps her way and gathers westing into the bargain. Nothing shall wake you that I can carry myself; only a wind that turns the shore to leeward or the like brings you up.

args.note: 21:25, first watch. The captain's word: mind the offing through the night — if speed increases while the course stays south or east of south and the wind holds westerly, we close the Breton shore; then wear to the larboard tack or get the course sou'westerly, by the reckoning even blind. He is below asleep until rested; wake him with 'tell the captain' only if something requires him. My plan for the watch: cast the lead on every hour with the shaping; keep my own reckoning run on; watch the wind for a veer (it would both lay the WSW course and open the offing) or a haul (it would square the wind more dead on the bow); square sail still waiting on the apparent abeam; wear in good time rather than late — she is slow (6 kn) and may miss stays. Glass 30.13 rising strongly. Next shaping due about 22:15.

reply.text: Half-past the hour, 4 bells: the wind is dying — 3 knots in the lull, a mean of 4, and she has slowed to 2 knots, all sails still drawing lightly. The glass stands at 30.14 and still rises; Pascoe's forecast of a quiet forenoon looks right. The tide has made the flood, a quarter of a knot to the NE, so she drifts no faster toward any shore; if anything the flood props up our easting, and the captain's worry of speed increasing with a southing course is for now turned about — the danger is wanting way, not too much. Nothing to wake him for: I'll sound once more on the hour and keep the watch.

reply.text: 5 bells. The wind has gone light and variable out of the WNW — the airs are wandering in the calm the glass promised, and she has fallen off to S by W with the helm easing her about; the way is next to nothing. The flood now sets half a knot to the NE, which noses her toward the Breton shore, but at two knots through the water and a shore forty miles off to the nor'ard there is no hurry in it: the ebb will set SW again after high water about half past twelve. With the wind at WNW the WSW course is further than ever from being laid; full and by on the starboard tack stays the order. The square sail keeps waiting — the apparent is abeam or abaft it, but our course is no ways sou'westerly, and in variable airs it would be slack and spilling. The lead again by the bell, and I'll keep her working to each air so the sails draw.

reply.text: 8 bells, midnight, the middle watch — I hold the deck still, the captain asleep below. The airs have come round to NW by W, still light at 3 knots, and she has fallen off to SW by S: the wind is now near abeam and our head is sou'westerly at last. This is the very case the captain named — the apparent comes abeam and the course is sou'westerly — and Mr Pascoe has the hands handy for it. I'll set the square sail while the airs let her carry it.

args.text: Good watch to you, sir — quiet, and that is the whole of the news. The wind died to light variable airs out of the WNW, barely three knots, and she has fallen off to SW by S; at two knots, the log just hove, we are drifting as much as sailing. The glass is 30.16 and rising yet. As the wind came abeam with our head sou'westerly — your word by Mr Pascoe — I have just set the square sail; only nine hands could be spared, the rest at the log, so she is a minute or two about it. Nothing to trouble you: no bottom on the last cast, the flood is making north-easterly but the shore is far off, and the moon is low now, gone out of distance for a lunar. If you'll have the deck I'll stand easy and mind the watch; otherwise I carry on as I am — hourly shaping, lead every hour, and the square sail kept set while the airs humour her.

reply.text: 1 bell, and all is as well as a quiet night allows: every stitch drawing, all sail set, her head SW at last with the wind NW — the very course we have been begging for since Falmouth, though at two or three knots she is making heavy weather of wanting it. Two things I mark: the glass has stopped rising — a hundredth fallen in the last hour after hours of climbing — and the moon is down to nine degrees, below lunar work. The tide flood is near its height at Ushant (high water about a quarter past one), so the north-easterly set that noses us toward the Breton coast will ease after that and the ebb will give us back our westing. Nothing to trouble the captain with; I keep the watch, sound by the hour and let the Hourly Shaping do its work at the next hour.

reply.text: The deep-sea lead has paid: 56 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks; allowing three fathoms of tide, 53 on the chart, and the account is kept — the first sound of ground this passage, and it bears out the master's reckoning. The sand and specks agree with the charted character of the shelf off Ushant. I'll log it and mark the spot for the morning's work.

reply.text: 8 bells, the morning watch come round; I still hold the deck. Through the middle watch the captain came up once, at about half past two, and had the yards braced three to the wind; the wind has since settled at NW by N, a light breeze of five knots, and she stands SW by W with the apparent 59° on the bow. Sunrise at ten to four, clear sky, glass 30.21 rising; run since noon 54 miles, though the course made good is still but S by E 176° — the long southing with light winds will show its cost on the distance. No turn of the tide by the reckoning yet, the flood still quarter of a knot to the NE, and high water at Ushant is past its reckoned time; I'll watch the allowance turn at the next shaping.

Wind settled NW by N at 03:53, light breeze 5 kn; she stands SW by W 240°, all sail set, square sail drawing since midnight. Glass 30.21 rising (the small dip at 00:35 passed), clear after the haze, sunrise 03:55. Run since noon 54 miles but course made good only S 176° — the southing shows. Reckoning 48° 58' N, 4° 51' W; mine 48° 56' N, 4° 53' W, holding two miles SW of his. Deep-sea cast 01:19, 56 fathoms fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. Watching: the Hourly Shaping hourly, the tide allowance turning, any shift toward the fair wind the captain wants (NW by N is near the fairest yet — the WSW course may nearly lay), the deep-sea lead by the captain's standing practice now.

reply.text: Two new standing orders entered in the book at 4 bells: 'trim on the course' — trim the sails at steady on the course — and 'tend the sheets on the glass', each glass while she is not hove to; the first has just fired, the yards braced three to the wind once more. And the wind has hauled to NNW, still a light breeze, so she stands WSW 246° — the true course to the Azores nearly laid at last, after a night of it. Slack water in the tide, the ebb to make: the turn I waited on is come in the allowance. She has 55 miles since noon; the made-good course is still sadly southerly, but a fair wind now would right the account.

reply.text: 5 bells. The wind backed to N by W and freshened a shade to 5 knots; the apparent has closed to 52° on the bow, and the yards braced three to the wind by the standing order — but now the topgallant is shaking: with the yard braced so sharp and the wind so far forward it can take nothing, and a slatting canvas high up only chafes itself. In this light air she wants way more than she wants that stitch; it comes in, and goes up again if the breeze builds.

args.note: 21:46, first watch 3 bells. Lunar by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen (my request, his word): longitude by lunar 5° 29' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 6° 22' W — the master moved his account three leagues to the east, now 48° 31' N, 6° 08' W. My own slate (from the noon fix 5° 34' W, run on by the log-board) stands 48° 30' N, 6° 22' W, three leagues west of his corrected account, at the edge of my trust of it. I keep my slate uncorrected for an independent check and will speak of it at noon; the lunar and the account disagree by some 35-40 miles, both within the lunar's doubt. Also this watch: at 21:11 the sails lifted — wind came forward to N by E while the yards stood free; braced the yards in (54-58° from square) and the standing order re-braced at 21:16. She now sails free again, apparent on the beam, WSW 251°, made good SW by W, 35 miles since noon. Glass 30.35 steady. Moon 19° up, still in distance of Regulus — another set tonight would narrow the longitude. The tide turn by the reckoning due about 23:00.

args.text: Good morning, sir, and a fair watch to you — you slept five hours and a half, and I'll allow you the whole of it: nothing stirred but the glass rising and the yards squaring. She ran the night off quiet: 54 miles since noon, made good SW by W through the small hours, the wind NNE-NE by N about the quarter, all sail drawing, no squall and no shift to put her out of her trim. The soundings held the account all night — 76 fathoms grey sand and ooze at midnight, 70 and 69 through the small hours, the bottom running to ooze as we come off the shelf; the flood's last grip is nearly out of us, and the ebb will give you back your westing through the forenoon. Glass 30.37. My slate, from the noon fix, stands three leagues west of your account still — yours of the lunar; the two must be judged at the sun's noon, which comes at 12:04.

args.text: I make her out no better than the glass does, sir: hull below the horizon at six miles, bearing N by W, so she lies to the northward of our wake — nothing of her work to be told yet. She is no part of the coasting trade here at sixty-eight fathoms, and by her bearing she must have come out of the Channel. I'll keep her under my eye and report every change; if she stands to the southward she will close us of herself, and the glass will tell more as her hull lifts. Nothing yet to alter sail or course for, in my judgment.

args.text: Aye, a brig under plain sail, standing SW by S from the northward — I mark her, sir; she is four miles off on the quarter and her hull lifts now. I'll keep her on the log as she goes, glass on her at every change, and no colours showing yet. She is a stranger to be watched, nothing more to my eye so far: a brig to the south'ard of the western entrance at these marks is likely some trader standing out of the Channel like ourselves, but until she shows a flag I keep my counsel and my distance.

args.note: 06:30, morning watch 5 bells. Stranger made out: a brig on the starboard quarter, bearing N, four miles, standing SW by S under plain sail, no colours yet; first seen 05:08 abeam to starboard N by W six miles, hull below the horizon; the captain has been in the tops since 05:40 with the glass and made her out. She works to the south'ard and so will close or cross us; we stand WSW 250°, 3 kn. I keep her logged at every change; nothing to alter for, in my judgment — she may be a trader out of the Channel; keep watch on her colours and her course, and hail the captain of every change as a lieutenant of 1806 would. args.note: 08:00, forenoon watch, 8 bells. Deck given to the captain; I am drowsy after holding the whole night and go below to sleep. What he takes: all sail set and drawing on WSW 253°, wind NNE 8 kn, apparent 102° on the quarter, 4 kn; glass 30.36 steady; no land, deep-sea cast 03:09, 69 fathoms grey sand and ooze, the account kept; the ebb a knot and a half to the SW. The stranger: a brig on the starboard quarter, bearing NE, three miles, standing SW by S under plain sail, no colours yet — first seen 05:08; she has worked round from N to NE as we have gone off to the westward; I judge her a trader, to be watched, nothing to alter for. My reckoning 48° 16' N, 7° 05' W, three leagues W of the master's (his lunar 5° 29' W); noon by the sun 12:04, and the longitude question is his to judge at the noon work. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (last 07:15), trim on the course (last 07:17), tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching for me asleep: the brig's colours or course change, any wind shift, the noon sights — wake me for anything beyond the book.

args.note: Woke rested 12:47, afternoon watch 1 bell, off watch; the captain has the deck. What came while I slept: the noon work — lat by obs 48° 13' N, lon by account 7° 08' W, course made good SW by W 82 miles. My own slate ran to 48° 10' N, 7° 24' W, three leagues W of his before the sight, and the observation puts me four miles N of his: I set my slate to the noon fix again (48° 13' N, 7° 08' W) and will speak of the longitude at the next noon. The brig (first seen 05:08 from the northward) has worked round on our larboard quarter, SE by E, two leagues, still standing SW by S under plain sail — we have crossed her track or she has crossed ours; no colours made out. The captain held the deck the forenoon; the standing orders kept their rounds; wind NE 6 kn, she stands WSW 244°, all sail drawing; glass 30.35, first fall in two days — worth watching. I turn in again asleep until called; when I take the deck I will read the glass's fall first of all.

args.text: Good afternoon, sir. At the noon I make this: your account gave 48° 10' N, 7° 08' W, and the sun put the latitude four miles north of it — 48° 13' N — the third noon running that the flood or the tide-work has held you south of the observation; the made good course SW by W, 82 miles, is a day of fair westing at last. My own slate, run from yesterday's noon fix, came out 48° 10' N, 7° 24' W — four leagues west of yours and beyond my own trust of it, so I set my slate to the noon fix and start fair from 48° 13' N, 7° 08' W. On the longitude: your lunar of last evening said 5° 29' W, and this noon's account says 7° 08' — near two degrees apart, both inside the lunar's thirty miles of doubt. Yesterday's lunar had the same leaning — it is nearer the truth east than west, I judge, or the tide-work runs us westward faster than the epitome allows so far from any table-place. A second lunar tonight with the moon in distance of Regulus again would narrow it; I'd ask your word for one at moonrise, and I'd sound with the deep-sea lead on the forenoon hours to watch the shelf fall away under us — 93 fathoms at the last cast, grey sand and ooze still.

args.text: Aye aye, sir — I have the deck; the chart is yours below. All is orderly: wind NE by E about the quarter, all sail drawing on WSW 244°, the log hove at three and a half knots, glass 30.35 steady after its small fall. The brig has opened to three leagues on the larboard quarter, SE by E, still working to the south-westward and dropping astern of us — she troubles nobody. The moon is down yet; she rises toward evening, and if the captain wills a second lunar I'll have the sextants ready when she comes into distance of Regulus.

args.note: 14:09, afternoon watch 4 bells. Took the deck from the captain (he below at the chart). Ship: all sail set and drawing, WSW 244°, wind NE by E 7 kn on the quarter, 3½ kn, glass 30.35 (fell 2 hundredths through the forenoon, now steady), clear, smooth sea, no land, no danger. Brig on the larboard quarter SE by E three leagues, standing SW by S, dropping astern — a passing trader, to be watched, nothing to alter for. Noon (12:05): lat by obs 48° 13' N (account 3½ miles S of it), lon by account 7° 08' W, made good SW by W 82 miles; my slate reset to the noon fix. The longitude question stands: account 7° 08' vs lunar 5° 29' W, near two degrees apart, both within the lunar's doubt; I proposed a second lunar at moonrise and the captain has gone to the chart — his word will come. The moon thirteen days old, down now, rises toward evening; when she is in distance of Regulus I will take the set if his word allows (it did last evening). My reckoning from the fix now 48° 07' N, 7° 32' W, four leagues W by S of his — the same leaning; watch it at the next noon. Watching: the glass (first fall in two days), the moonrise for the lunar, the brig astern, the Hourly Shaping.

args.note: 16:00, first dog watch 8 bells. Still have the deck; the captain below since 14:10 at the chart, then to rest. The afternoon watch passed quiet: all sail set and drawing, WSW 244-245°, wind NE by E 6-7 kn well abaft the beam, 3 kn, glass 30.35 steady after the small forenoon fall. Run since noon 13 miles, made good WSW 245°. The brig has dropped out of sight astern — she stood on SW by S and we drew away from her to the westward; no colours ever made out, a passing trader. My slate from the noon fix: 48° 04' N, 7° 41' W, four leagues W by S of the master's account; his lunar 5° 29' W still stands against the account 7° 25' W — the moon is not yet up; the second lunar awaits her. Deep-sea cast due (last 03:09); the ground grey sand and ooze, 91 fathoms by account, coming off the shelf apace. Watching: the glass's tendency (it fell a hundredth in the forenoon, then steadied — the falling fast is not here), the moonrise for the lunar, the hourly shapings and trims, the deep-sea lead.

args.text: heave the deep-sea lead and sound

args.note: 16:13, first dog watch. Deep-sea cast: 91 fathoms, soft ooze; two and a half fathoms of tide allowed — 88½ on the chart; the account moved six cables to the east on it — the cast is confirmation the account ran too far west, and it bears out my suspicion since yesterday's noon: the longitude account has been running west of the truth, the lunar's 5° 29' W the nearer of the two. My own slate (7° 42' W) stands four leagues west of the master's and outside my trust; the soundings will settle it as the ooze deepens off the shelf. The bottom is now soft ooze — off the bank altogether. She runs WSW 244°, all sail drawing, 14 miles since noon, glass 30.35 steady. The moon rises toward evening; the second lunar when she comes into distance of Regulus, by the captain's word given at 14:10.

args.text: By my reckoning, sir, the moon is but one degree up now; she climbs near ten degrees to the glass, and by her height yesterday evening — she was nineteen degrees up and in distance of Regulus about half past eight — I should look for her fit for the distance between eight and half past eight tonight, and well placed by nine. The sky is clear and the sea smooth, so the horizons should serve; I'd have the sextants on the quarterdeck by eight bells and take the set about eight o'clock, when she is high enough to be trusted.

args.note: 20:00, first watch 8 bells. The moon is seven degrees up and fourteen days old — not yet fit for the lunar; by her rate of climbing she should be in distance within the hour or two, and I hold the deck for the set. The glass has now fallen 3 hundredths in three hours (30.32) — a real fall begins, after two days of rise; watch it against the standing orders, though no wind follows yet (NE by E 6 kn, all quiet, a smooth sea). She runs WSW 244-245°, made good the same, 25 miles since noon. The captain on deck as the watch changed; he asked for my estimate of the lunar's hour (I said about eight to half past, well placed by nine) and took an azimuth at 17:58 — variation now 24° W by azimuth, against 25° W by the amplitude of the 8th; he allows it from now. My slate: 47° 59' N, 7° 58' W, still four leagues west of his account and outside my trust of it; the soundings (91 fathoms soft ooze at 16:13, the account moved east six cables) keep saying the same. The moonrise lunar will settle between the two.

args.note: 23:16, first watch 6 bells. The second lunar is taken and cleared: Spica and the moon by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen — longitude by lunar 7° 44' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 7° 51' W, so the account moved seven cables E by N. This confirms the pattern: the first lunar (5° 29' W) and the account (7° 08' W then) disagreed by two degrees; this second lunar agrees with the present account within a mile — the master's tide-work is close tonight. My own slate (47° 56' N, 8° 08' W) now stands four leagues W by S of his and outside my trust of it: the divergence began at yesterday's noon and has grown; I mean to work my reckoning afresh from this evening's fix and speak to the captain at his waking — the two slates must be brought together or the difference owned. Also: the glass has fallen through the evening, 30.32 → 30.31, 2 hundredths in three hours — slow, but three hours of fall after two days of rise; the first watch has been quiet (wind NE 5 kn, all square, WSW 244°, 33 miles since noon). The captain took a lunar at 22:00 (his own order), the distances cleared by 23:16. Watching: the glass's further fall, my reckoning work-up, the captain's waking.

args.text: drink

args.note: 00:16, middle watch 8 bells. Still hold the deck, the second night running. The first watch passed quiet: wind NE 5-6 kn, all sail set, yards square, she runs WSW 244-245° with the wind nearly dead astern (168° astern at 23:46 — the square sail and the gaff topsail doing the work); 35 miles since noon; glass fallen to 30.30-30.31 — three hours' fall then steady, no wind to speak of following it; a smooth sea. Soundings not taken since 16:13 (91 fathoms soft ooze); the account now 126 fathoms by chart — well off the shelf, into the deep water west of Ushant. The lunar of Spica (7° 44' W) confirms the master's account; my slate (8° 11' W, four leagues W by S outside my trust) diverges — I will work it up at noon from the fix and the log, and speak plainly to the captain of it. The captain on deck at the watch change; all hands fresh. Watching: the glass (if it falls fast, the standing orders wake me), the wind for any hauling forward, the noon work and the reckoning to be squared.

args.text: Aye aye, sir, sleep sound — I'll hold the deck till sunrise and after, and I am not yet past drowsiness: I had a meal and drink at eight bells of the evening watch and the watch is an easy one, the ship running quiet before the wind. The book stands by me: the Hourly Shaping, the trims, the tend-sheets; the glass is fallen a few hundredths but steady now, the sea smooth, no land nor danger anywhere near — she may be trusted to the watch. I'll wake you only at sunrise or if anything out of the common comes.

args.note: 04:42, morning watch 1 bell. The glass has fallen fast: 7 hundredths in three hours, to 30.23, 4 hundredths in the last hour alone. The wind has hauled from NE through N round to E by S, light and variable airs, 3 knots, she has slowed to 2 kn, all sail still set. I sent the word below to the captain (he sleeps until sunrise, at his own asking; the glass falling fast and the wind round to the eastward are the kind of thing a lieutenant tells the master of). args.note: 08:00, forenoon watch 8 bells. Staying up till noon by the captain's word; I have eaten and am awake enough. She now stands close hauled on the larboard tack, WSW, apparent 75° on the larboard bow. The glass has fallen all morning: 30.27 → 30.20, a hundredth the hour; the squall the falling glass foreboded has not come — the winds are all light airs and gusts. Depth by account 767 fathoms; the lead's length is useless now, we are in deep water. Run since noon 52 miles. My slate 47° 47' N, 8° 34' W, four leagues W by S of his. Noon by the sun at 12:10; the captain means me to see the noon sights. Watching: the wind's further haul to south (it would put the Azores course to leeward and square the problem), the gusts for a real squall (the captain's word: square sail and topgallant come in first, and only for a real squall), the glass.

args.note: 12:11, afternoon watch, noon. Day's work: lat by obs 47° 49' N (account was 47° 46', moved 2½ miles NE); course made good since yesterday WSW, 62 miles; longitude by account 8° 27' W — no tide in the day's work, the directions give none for these waters. My own slate had run to 47° 43' N, 8° 47' W, five leagues WSW of his and outside my trust: set my reckoning to the noon fix, 47° 49' N, 8° 27' W. The pattern of the last three noons (the account north of the observation by 2-4 miles) is broken today — the account lies south of the observation; with no tide to allow and deep water, the longitude now rests on the log alone, and the lunar of Spica (7° 44' W, taken 23:16) stands 43 miles east of the account — within its doubt, but it has leaned east twice now. Also: at 12:01 I took in the topgallant — shaking in the 53° close-hauled trim as the wind settled SE. The wind has worked SE by S through the forenoon, gusty and variable, glass down to 30.17 and steady the last hour; the squall never came. She is close hauled larboard tack on the WSW course, plain sail and square sail and gaff topsail, 3-4 kn. Staying up till noon done as asked; I'll ask the captain for rest when the forenoon's work is squared.

args.text: The day's work is squared, sir: latitude by observation 47° 49' north — two miles and a half north of the account, the first noon this passage the observation has come out north of you instead of south; course made good since yesterday WSW, 62 miles; longitude by account 8° 27' west, no tide in the day's work, for the directions give none in these waters. The lunar of Spica taken at eleven last night says 7° 44' west — forty-three miles east of the account, within its doubt, but it has leaned to the eastward at both lunars now. I have set my own slate to the noon fix and run it fresh. When the forenoon's work is squared I would ask leave to turn in; I have been up since eight bells of the last dog watch.

args.text: I have been up since four bells of the last dog watch, sir — about six hours — and I slept the whole afternoon watch before that, from half past twelve till six, near five hours in my hammock. I am rested and fresh, and it is you who has been twenty hours afoot; it is you who should go below, and I will hold the deck through the middle watch and the morning watch if need be, as I did last night. The ship wants nothing of us tonight but an eye: the wind southerly and light, all sail drawing on the W by N course, the glass 30.05, no land within fifty leagues, and the deep water under us. Go to your hammock, sir; I'll wake you at eight bells or before if anything wants you.

args.text: No, sir, I know of no hands down in the ground tier in my watch. I was on deck the whole of it from eight bells of the last dog watch till the wind shift at seven bells; the log shows trimming the sails twice and three orders, nothing of the hold, and the starboard watch went below relieved at four bells of the middle watch and the other relieved in at eight. The rolling has been steady these two days — she rolled through the whole of the first and middle watches — so the chimes working loose in the leaguers would be my guess at the leak, from the ship's labour and not from any hands' doing that I saw. If the cooper will sound the well and let the pump try her, we shall know how much has gone; the water stands at 3.7 tons by the last account, thirty-one days by reckoning.

She stands S by E full and by on the starboard tack, the true wind SW 14 knots, gusts to 16, heel 8° and rolling heavily; all is drawing, the square sail furled since last evening, so nothing is out of the way for a breeze of this force. The glass is the news worth your ear: it has risen four hundredths in the last hour alone to 30.29, six hundredths in three hours — the weather is mending fast. The noon sights are in: latitude by observation 47° 23' north, the account moved four miles north of itself; course made good since yesterday west by south, 127 miles; longitude by account 11° 31' west. args.text: drink

On deck, sir, and I have the deck. The glass is the news: 30.38, fallen three hundredths in three hours and still going down a hundredth an hour — the first steady fall since the small hours of the 12th. The wind has kept light and hauled round through W by S to W by S again at six knots, so we stand NW by N on the larboard board at three knots, and the run since noon is but eight miles. The bread is the other word: Mr Pascoe says the bags in the after locker are damp to the hand since that blow, the bottom ones he would not swear to — they are turned and stowed higher, but I would look to them with the cooper if the damp grows. The noon work stands: latitude by observation 46° 26' N, a mile and a half north of the account; my own slate runs four leagues and a half west-south-west of it now, outside what I would trust it — the lunar of Markab last night gives 10° 24' W and I lean on it for the longitude. What would you have of the glass's fall, sir — a squally afternoon I look for, and the square sail is furled and the topgallant in the gear already.

args.note: 14:51, afternoon watch. The captain's word: tack again — the wind has come round to a westerly, little ground on this board; he wants southing and westing if we may. Tack ship is his word allowed by name. I judge the time: the wind is W by S, six to seven knots; we are full and by on the larboard tack NW by N. Tacking now to the starboard tack gives southing on the new board and keeps him full and by again the moment the wind hauls south; if it backs instead we are laid up on a board that gains us nothing. The glass falls a hundredth an hour; the topgallant is shaking already. I will tack while the way is good, plain sail and the gaff topsail set, and tell the captain when she is round.

I took the amplitude at sunset as you ordered: variation 23° 30' W by amplitude, 14 June, against your 24° — the log holds it for the reckoning from now. The word I would give you is the glass: 30.25 now, falling three hundredths in the last hour and six in three — the first steady fall since the small hours of the 12th, and it gathers. args.text: By and large I agree, sir, with one figure corrected. At two knots a day the serra is a year's voyage; I take your meaning as forty miles a day — a knot and three-quarters on the mean — and at that the account stands: 814 miles is some twenty days, and we have been averaging better than that since the noon of the 11th, near sixty miles a day while the wind held. So twenty days is fair if the breeze keeps, and with a fair wind we should do it sooner. The uncertainty is in the longitude: my lunar of Markab gives 11° 28' W, which is near the master's account and east of my slate, so the true distance may be some twenty miles less than eight hundred and fourteen. As to contingency, it is water that binds us, not bread: 3.5 tons is twenty-nine days at full allowance, and provisions thirty-four. My plan would be: cut to two-thirds allowance of water the day the wind fails, and take the boats' small store into the reckoning; fish daily — there are tuna and dolphin on this ground in the season; and fix the point of no return now, while it is our own choice: if we are, say, eleven days out and the wind has not served, or the water falls below fifteen days, we bear away for the islands. St Mary's is the nearest, 107 leagues NE by account, and with a westerly wind that is a fair wind home for it — two or three days' run. Horta is further but we have the letter for Senhor Bettencourt and Mr Ruiz ashore there. Either way we fill the water and provision again, and lose only days, not the voyage. The danger is not the distance, sir, but pressing on past the turning point on hope of a breeze.

args.text: I agree, sir — eight hundred and fourteen miles at forty miles the day is twenty days, and there is nothing in the figure to argue with. But I would say this: the true question is not the time but the water. We have three and a half tons, near thirty days at our present trim; the bread is thirty-four days though a third of it spoiled. So if we are becalmed for any time, my plan is this: the day the wind fails, we cut to two-thirds allowance — with fishing daily from the booms, salt and some kindness of weather, that stretches the water well past thirty days and the bread with it. And we fix a turning point now: if we are eleven days out with no wind served us, or the water falls below fifteen days by the account, we bear away for St Mary's — the nearest by a long way, and fair on a westerly if it comes — fill and provision there, and lose days, not the voyage. Horta would serve too: the letter is there, and Mr Ruiz ashore. The danger is not the becalming, sir; it is pressing on past the turning point on hope of a breeze. Keep that point, and the calculation never changes.

args.note: Noon, 12 June (afternoon watch). Latitude by observation 45° 58' N against my own reckoning 45° 49' N: nine miles astray, outside what I would trust it — the observation throws me out, not the master. My longitude 12° 12' W stands 44' west of last night's lunar (11° 28' W, trusted within 30 miles), while the master's account 11° 49' W sits within the lunar's doubt. Correction entered: my own reckoning now begins from the observed latitude 45° 58' N and the master's longitude 11° 49' W, my drift noted for the log-book; I will work it afresh from today's log-board and watch whether my W by S bias holds. Wind light from W, 4 knots; glass rising (30.16); nothing in sight. Voyage plan stands: turning point 11 days out or water below 15 days — water 28.8 days, provisions 33.

The ship is left in stays at helm down; she will pay off to leeward as the headsails fill or back. The stranger now abeam to starboard, NW, two leagues — after the aborted tack she bears abeam rather than astern. Off watch; the captain has the deck and the helm is his. Watching: her filling away (which tack), and the stranger's bearing as we settle.

args.text: Aye, sir, and mark this: the glass made her standing to the southward not a minute since, and she has just squared her yards to the eastward. That new leg, E by N from W by S of us, runs near enough through the spot where we lie — if she holds it she is up with us within the hour, less if she is a fast one, and our drift while hove to only puts us more in her road. Plain sail, colours not yet made out. Lying to as we are she has the legs of us; if you want to keep guessing her we stay quiet, but I would have the glass on her every few minutes — her next alteration will tell you more than her first.

args.text: Aye, sir. She is a deep-laden merchant brig under the red ensign, a mile off, SW by W, standing E by N — if she holds that leg she passes close aboard our weather quarter. I will keep the glass on her, and if she comes within hail I will hail her and give what news the log carries: sailed from Falmouth the 8th for the Western Islands, this sixteenth day, fine weather, all well, and ask the like of her in return.

args.note: 08:00, forenoon 8 bells, off watch. Notable: purser reports ground tier water foul — ropy/stinking in the warm weather, hands turning from it, asks she water at first port. Pascoe offered to air it with the windsail and boil for the coppers. Water stores: 3.2 tons, 27 days, now flagged FOUND FOUL. That's a real constraint — nearest port St Mary's is 131 leagues NE, weeks away, so Pascoe's airing/boiling is the practical fix short of port. Also noting: wind died to 4 kn (W by N, only 2 kn through the water) and the glass is falling properly now — 30.34 last night → 30.20, down 6 hundredths since the morning watch. Two things trending together (light wind, falling glass) — watching whether it turns to a blow or just a calm. Captain has the deck; the water decision is his.

Still clear sky and smooth sea, no squall in it, but that's the fastest fall we've had since Falmouth and it's been sliding steadily for two days now. I'll keep a sharp eye on the glass and the sky, and I'll wake you or call all hands if it breaks. I'll also keep my own eye on that trend — if it goes past a hundredth an hour or the sky thickens, you'll hear about it straight away.

args.note: 17:04. DESTINATION CHANGE — captain shaped a course for 5 miles north of Ribeira Grande (São Miguel, Azores): SW by W 240°, 547 miles by account. Struck the old Hourly Shaping standing order (38°43' N 27°12' W) and replaced it with hourly shaping for this new position. That's the Azores approach — the letter for Senhor Bettencourt and the Madeira for the owner are Fayal-bound; Ribeira Grande is São Miguel, next island. So we're now bound to make an Azores landfall at São Miguel before pushing to Fayal presumably. Glass 30.17 rising, SW by W leg bracing in. Watching: horizon, wind, glass.

args.note: Handing the deck, sir — I'm dead on my feet, been up since the middle watch. All's well aboard: wind NW by W 4 kn, heading SW by S full and by, 2 kn, glass 30.30 rising, sky clear, smooth sea, no land, no sail, nothing amiss. Run since noon 41 miles. The turtle's in the galley for the cook to boil for the people's dinner, with calipee for the cabin. I shall sleep below until called — wake me if the watch wants me or anything shows.

args.note: 14:18, afternoon watch, woke rested. Slept through the forenoon. While I slept: the turtle was served — soup for the people at dinner, calipee to the cabin with a glass of Madeira (not the owners' case), the cook had a glass of Madeira from the captain's hand as thanks, and the hands sent three cheers for the turtle by Bray. Spencer kept a hot bowl of calipee back for me. Noon: lat 41°18' N, account moved 3.5 mi N; 70 miles made good S by W; longitude 16°19' W. Wind settled W light. All well.

args.text: Aye, sir, understood — we hold our course and our way. She's a brig standing NE by E under plain sail, bearing W five miles; if she holds that leg she'll cross our bow and be gone without troubling us. I'll keep the glass on her and report every change of her bearing — if she alters toward us or hauls her wind for us, you'll hear of it directly, sir.

args.text: By my reckoning, sir, she's very like the same one. We passed her going south yesterday forenoon — a brig standing NE by E under plain sail — and if she's been working back and forth off this ground since, meeting her head-on again as we beat north-west is just what we'd expect. Her bearing NW right ahead with her heading S by W closes with us on opposite legs, so she'll be up with us inside the hour at our slow pace. She's plain sail and no colours made out yet. My counsel, sir: hold our leg for now — we're full and by to windward of her — and keep the glass on her every few minutes. If she bears away toward us or hauls her wind for us, that tells her purpose soon enough, and you'll hear of it directly.

args.text: Aye, sir — I'm awake and fresh; you've nothing to fear on my account. Go below and sleep as long as you need; I'll keep the deck. She's lying quietly on the larboard tack, NNW, in the light W airs, glass 30.35, smooth sea. The Madeira's been shared forward as you ordered — a gill a man, Pascoe seeing it fairly shared, and the hands drinking your health. We're 8 miles since noon, nothing in sight. I'll call you only if the wind shifts drastically or anything shows on the horizon. Sleep well, sir.

args.text: Understood, sir — St Lawrence on the southern end of the Azores it is; that's a sensible water-stop before Horta, and the route puts the fresh water in reach sooner than carrying on. We're shaped WSW for it now, 435 miles by account, with the NNW breeze giving us a fair cracking reach — making near 4 knots with the wind on the beam. One thing to keep an eye on for you, sir: the glass has steadied after the morning's drop but sits low at 30.21, and with the NNW gusting to 12 it may yet build. If it blows up harder I'll shorten canvas as needed and let you know. Nothing else on the horizon; a clean reach for now.

args.text: Go to the quarterdeck.

Good morning, sir. By the account, St Lawrence is 274 miles off, and Ponta Delgada is 92½ leagues (about 277 miles) W by S. We've averaged near 6 knots since yesterday noon, so I make it about 46 hours. That would bring us to the island around the forenoon of the day after tomorrow. If the wind stays at 5 knots, as now, it could be 55 hours. If it freshens to 7 knots, it could be about 40. Our longitude is only good to 30 miles, so I'd expect to raise the land before I can pin the exact hour. I'd like a noon latitude sight at 12:51, and a lunar if the moon allows. I'll report the first sight of land, any sail, and any wind shift.

args.note: Handing the deck to Mr Bowen, sir. I'm very tired and have been on deck since 04:00. The schooner is lost in the fog and nothing is in sight. We hove to for the fog and filled away at 19:43 on the starboard tack, NW by W 302° with fore-and-aft sail, the topsail in the gear. The wind is N 6 and falling and the glass 30.60 steady. The two marks cut too fine for a fix, so the account is good to about 2 miles N or S only. I'd not close the land in the dark: stand off and on or lie to until daylight, and keep the lead and lookouts ready. The standing orders 'Hourly Shaping' is belayed, and 'tend the sheets on the watch' is resumed while 'trim the yards' is still belayed. The captain's word to work the ship holds only while I have the deck. I'm going below to sleep.

Passage lessons: the dead-reckoning longitude was ~17 leagues out (west) until the landfall cross-bearings of St Mary's/St Michael's at 05:53 on the 28th; fog twice, hove to for an unidentified black topsail schooner (French, out of Bayonne per pilot, stays off Vila Franca/Santa Maria, will not come into the road under São Brás guns). Stand-down note, 12:18 afternoon watch. Mr Bowen has brought her to anchor in Ponta Delgada Road with the best bower in 35 fathoms; the pilot Mr Pacheco is aboard. We came in from the east. Our dead reckoning was about 17 leagues out in longitude until the landfall bearings of St Mary's and St Michael's on the 28th, so trust the fixes over the account. A black topsail schooner showed no colours on the 28th and the fog hid us from her. The pilot says she is a French schooner out of Bayonne that stays off Vila Franca and Santa Maria and won't come into the road under the São Brás guns. Water is 1.9 tons and foul, provisions 21 days. Senhor Medeiros at the quay sells water and fresh meat, and the spring under the fort is sweet. High water is about 18:45 with an 18-foot rise. The road is open from east round south to west, so put to sea if it blows from there. The sealed letter for Senhor Bettencourt of Horta is still in the cabin. Standing orders: Hourly Shaping and trim-the-yards are belayed, and tend-the-sheets-on-the-watch is live. Lesson for whoever sits here: without the deck, give no helm or sail orders, and say so plainly. Mr Bowen is resting; keep watch on the cable, the weather and any sail.

args.text:
Sir, my journal has nothing on the canvas beyond the manifest: 12 tons, with room for 30. The only prices I hold are Falmouth £60 a ton on the 8th and Ponta Delgada £65 today. Selling here would gain about £5 a ton, or about £60 on the lot, before any dues or charges. Medeiros himself says Horta would pay no better and no worse.

I have no note saying the canvas is consigned to anyone. Whether it belongs to the owners or is meant for Bettencourt, I can't tell from the book. The sealed letter for Bettencourt is still in the cabin and may settle it. I'd not sell on a £5 margin until we know that, and the Horta price is an unknown that might be better. Medeiros says the French schooner lies off Santa Maria, so an empty hold doesn't make us safer. Your call, sir.

args.text:
Sir, I'd take it in this order.

1. Ask Medeiros what he would pay for the canvas, and what wine and salt beef cost him. His list today has wine at £40 a ton against our Falmouth £70, so island wine is cheap here. Brandy is £95 against £300 at Falmouth, which looks very cheap if the Falmouth figure is right. I'd check it before trusting it.

2. Don't tell him it is unconsigned, or that Horta is our expected market. Let him name a price first, and say we have a buyer waiting at Horta. His £65 is only a figure he quoted unprompted. A man who wants our canvas for his own trade should go well above it.

3. Horta's price is unknown. Bettencourt's letter and the Horta list would tell us. We could sell part here, say 4 tons, and keep the rest for Horta. That tests Medeiros without committing us.

4. Carrying goods for Horta is a risk to the cutter with the French schooner about. A hold full of cheap wine is worth more than canvas for the owners.

I'm only a mate, so the bargain is yours. I'll keep to the quay and watch the boat.

args.text:
Sir, Medeiros offers £66 a ton for the 12 tons, which comes to £792 in Spanish dollars. That is £1 a ton over his own market, so he has barely come off his figure. It is a fair price, but I'd ask a little more, since he has just said he resells to every brig that comes in. He also says Horta wine is cheaper at source, so we need not buy wine here.

Two things I'd have you weigh. If we sell, the hold is empty for the passage, and an empty cutter with the French schooner about could look a better prize or a poorer one. I can't say which. And the glass is easing: 30.51 and falling 2 hundredths in the hour. It is nothing yet, but I'll keep an eye on it. The wind is ESE, light, and the road is open to the east. Mr Pascoe's signal would be a musket and the ensign at the masthead.

args.text:
Sir, one thing I'd say plainly. Medeiros wants the customs clerk to enter the canvas at £65 and to pay the extra £12 "into your hand" in dollars. That is a payment kept out of the customs book. It is small, but we are in a neutral port as guests and I'd not want the owners' accounts or our standing with the alfândega to suffer for £12. I'd ask that the full £66 be written in the sale and the receipt, so the books show what we got. The deal is yours to make, and I mean no more than a word of caution.

I'd also see the dollars counted before the lighter takes the last of it, and have the owners' share entered in the purser's book.

Sir, that bears on the schooner. The Conceição, Senhor Gomes's brigantine out of Funchal, comes at São Pedro with the governor's wine and sugar and carries back the island's wheat, oranges and the bills for the Funchal houses. This year she is late, and the black schooner is waiting in the channel between here and Santa Maria. It may well be the Conceição she is waiting for, which would explain her patience.

That gives us a choice. If we sail, I'd go at night, under the north coast as Medeiros advises. We might also warn the pilot or the governor's people that the Conceição is overdue and likely to meet the Frenchman, since neither of them seems to have said it aloud. Your call, sir.

args.text:
Sir, I agree. The plan is sound.

- The wind is ESE to E by S, light, with the glass steady at 30.50. It serves for the west.
- The Frenchman lies to the east off Santa Maria, so we would be running from her.
- The north coast has no cover for her, and the Rabo de Peixe men would send word if she came.
- Weighing now gives us about three hours of light, and the flood serves till about 18:45.

Points to watch:
1. 176 fathoms of cable is a long heave in 35 fathoms, so Mr Pascoe should start the capstan at once. Light airs may leave her slow to gather way, and the road is open to the east.
2. The pilot Mr Pacheco must be put off before we pass the mole, and paid. Medeiros's boats are alongside no more, so we should ask him which channel off the Ponta he would take.
3. I'd keep a man at the masthead all through the run and have the gaff topsail and topgallant ready to set. If we see her, our only answer is to run to windward of the island. The north side is where she won't follow.
4. We must keep a log of the Ponta de Ferreira bearings to fix ourselves, since our reckoning was 17 leagues out before the landfall.

Whenever you give me the deck, I'll take it. I'm ready at the quay and can come off with you in the boat.

args.text:
Sir, I've looked at the three courses to Horta. They are 305° at 96.8 miles, 295° at 107.8 miles, and 285° at 129.3 miles, all with the wind N by E at 6 knots.

I'd take the central one, 295°.
- 305° is the shortest, but it is about close-hauled with no margin. If the wind backs even a point toward the north, she can't hold it and we fall off to leeward. It also draws us up toward the Ferraria and the north coast that Pacheco warned of, the one place on the chart where the offing is thin.
- 285° is 20 miles longer. It leans on the wind shifting before we get there. If the wind stays N by E, we'd be beam-reaching and gain no speed to pay for the extra distance.
- 295° is about a point and a half free of close-hauled. She'd sail faster and steadier than on 305°, and she'd stay clear of the Ferraria on the first leg. We'd keep room to bear up toward 305° if the wind veers, or to ease toward 285° if it backs, and we'd lose only about 11 miles to the northern route.

At 4 knots, 108 miles would take about 27 hours, so I'd expect Fayal the evening after next if it stays light. Say if you want it, sir, and I'll steer 295° at once.

Aye, sir, I've braced sharp up and will see whether the topsail steadies. You may be right that full and by sailed this close will keep it shaking at the luff. I'd rather it lift a little than lose a point to the wind.

I'd also report that the glass has jumped to 30.55, up 21 hundredths in the last hour, after sitting at 30.34. That is a very sharp rise and unlike anything we've had. It may be an instrument fault, but I'd not rely on that. Such a rise often brings a shift of wind, perhaps to the northwest, and sometimes a squall. args.text:
Sir, urgent: at 23:52 the wind flew round from N by W to SW by W and took her aback. The topsail, fore staysail and jib were all pressed against the masts. The wind is down to a lull of 5 knots, true from SW by W, and she still has 4 knots of way and heads NW by W (303°), now with the wind 33° on the larboard bow, so she is on the larboard tack. Nothing is carried away. I've kept her full and by, braced the yards for the new wind (39° on the larboard bow), and I'm trimming the sheets. The glass is 30.38 and rising fast.

This is the shift we hoped for. SW is a fair wind for Horta (Fayal bears NW by W, 14 leagues), and we can lay it on a reach rather than beat. I'd now set the topgallant and gaff topsail again if you agree, and shake the reef out of the topsail while the wind is light. I'll hold until I have your word.

args.text:
Sir, I've looked at the chart: the track runs north then NNW to Fayal Road, 6.8 miles, passing east of the Bank of Fayal, so the Bank stays on our larboard hand as you say. The Pico coast lies close on the starboard hand and the Magdalena islets are to the NNE. Our 07:44 fix is 38° 26' N, 28° 33' W, good to three cables along the shore and two off it, so the position is good.

Two cautions. The wind is 21 knots from SW by W with gusts to 24, and when we bear off it comes abaft the beam, so she will go faster and may need the main sail's reef kept in until we shorten for the road. Also the Pico shore is a lee shore on the starboard side with this wind, and the Bank of Fayal lies NNW 5½ miles, so I'd not bear off early and would keep clear of the bank by a wide margin. We'll need a pilot or a lead in the road, and the anchor ready. I'll have the cable bent and the lead and the hands ready at your word.

args.text:
Sir, I have not the deck, so I can give no orders to the ship, and the best bower can only be readied on your own order or after you give me the deck. If you want me to do it, say "you have the deck" and I'll order it at once, or tell Mr Pascoe, who has the foredeck.

What I see: she is on N by W (354°), making 6 knots with the wind 98° on the larboard quarter, 16 knots apparent, under the main sail with 2 reefs and the fore staysail. The Bank of Fayal is NW by N at 2½ miles, so we are close to it, and the road is NW by N at four miles. The glass is 29.95 and falling fast. The depth is about 200 fathoms, too deep to anchor, so we shall want the lead going as we shoal. The hands are worn out, with 12 below, so I'd want the anchor party fresh. Sir, you have the con. I will watch and answer.

args.text:
Sir, I have the deck. Fix at 08:12: 38° 29' N, 28° 34' W, good to a cable. The Mount of Our Lady of the Guide and the town of Fayal bear NW and the Magdalena islets NNE. The Bank of Fayal is NW by N at about 2½ miles, so we are at about the place where you meant to bear up. The lead is going, and the depth is about 196 fathoms by the chart.

The best bower can't be "cleared away" in this ship's language. The orders are 'bring ship to anchor' or 'let go the best bower'. I'll do it when you say, and I'd want the sails shortened beforehand. Tell me when to bear up for the road and when to bring her head to wind, and I'll order 'bring ship to anchor' when we are in the road in shoaler water, as the guns' limit in the road is near. She is on N by W (354°) under the 2-reefed main sail and the fore staysail. The wind is 97° on the larboard quarter at 16 knots apparent.

args.text:
Sir, urgent: at 08:35 she was taken aback. The fore staysail is shaking and she has lost way, making 2 knots with 17° leeway, heading WNW (289°) with the wind 50° on the larboard bow at 21 knots. She carries only the main sail (3 reefs) and the fore staysail, and with so little drive she will not hold her head up to a wind that fresh. Nothing is carried away. No danger yet: the Bank of Fayal is about a mile to the west, the leeway sets us NE, away from it, and the depth is 81 fathoms with no bottom. The cost is that we are drifting down toward the Fayal shore under the Mount of Our Lady of the Guide, 2 miles WNW, if she doesn't gather way soon.

I've given no order, as you want to handle the sails. I'd suggest setting the jib so she'll answer her helm, or wearing round. I'm ready on your word, and will act on my own if the ground gets close.

The pilot boat is six cables on the starboard bow, so a pilot will be aboard shortly, and I'd take him gladly. I'll keep the lookout and say if the leeway puts us on the Bank.

args.text: Take the pilot.

Sir, the Fayal pilot boat has hailed and waits, three cables ahead, with her hail unanswered. Taking a pilot is the port's business and is kept back from me, so please give the word "take the pilot", or say "you may take the pilot".

Also, and more pressing, she is making sternway at 1 knot with the helm at 7° and the wind 63° on the larboard bow at 18 knots. She has no drive, headed NW by W (299°), and the Bank of Fayal is nine cables west of us. I'd say she is going astern and to leeward toward it. I'd say we need more sail on her at once, or to fall off on the other tack, and I'd rather not let her drift. I've given no order, as you ordered. Say the word, or let me wear her round, sir.

args.text:
Sir, Mr Terra the Fayal pilot is aboard. He says there is 22 feet on the shoalest part of the Bank at low water and the ebb is half done, so with her nine feet we need not fear it. He advises letting her fall off a point or two, filling everything to give her way, standing in on this tack toward the Guia, and coming up for the road when the college opens of the Carmen. The anchorage is 35 to 40 fathoms on sand, a mile and a quarter off the town, marks: the Point of João Dias a little open of Espalamaca and the college a little open south of the Carmen. High water at Fayal is about half past eight this evening, the flood serving from a quarter past two. He also gives the news that Britain is at war with the Batavian Republic, France and Spain.

She is now steering NW (315°) at 2 knots. The topsail is being set and a reef shaken out of the main sail. I take no sail orders, as you say, and I'll ask the pilot for the marks as we run in.

args.text: Yes, sir. The readings say "making sternway", so we are going astern. She heads W (271°), the helm is hard over at 35°, the wind is 40° on the larboard bow at 18 knots apparent, and the headsails and topsail are aback or shaking, so she has been pressed back by the sails and has no steerage way. You've put her helm hard up and she's paying off, which is right. Once her head falls off to NW or N and the wind comes abeam or abaft, the sails will fill and she'll gather way. We've sea room: the Bank is about a mile away and the Fayal shore two miles. Depth 87 fathoms, no bottom. The fix at 08:54 is 38° 31' N, 28° 35' W. If she won't pay off, I'd put the helm the other way, but I'll wait on you.

args.text: Sir, aback again at 08:57. She heads W by N (278°) with the wind only 34° on the larboard bow, which is closer than she can sail, and she is making 2 knots ahead (not sternway) with the helm at 20° and your hard up still taking effect. The cause each time is the same: she comes up to 291° or less, the wind goes forward of 45°, and the sails lift and then back. The pilot's advice was to let her fall off a point or two and keep her full. I'd put her head NW by N (325°), which gave her 3 knots with the wind at 77°, and keep it there rather than let her come up to 291°. The ground is no danger yet: the Bank WSW at a mile, depth 88 fathoms, no bottom, and plenty of room to the NE. Just the sail drive is wanted.

args.text:
Sir, plainly: she is making sternway again (readings: "course: making sternway"), heading W by N (287°), helm hard down at 35°, wind 45° on the larboard bow at 21 knots apparent. The true wind is now WSW at 24 to 26 knots, gusting 27. That is veered or backed from what we had, and it blows straight down on the Fayal coast, which lies WNW of us, so every minute of sternway and leeway carries us toward the Bank (W by S, a mile) or the shore. The Mount of Our Lady of the Guide is W by N at 2 miles. We have not touched ground and have 87 fathoms.

With the helm hard to windward and no way on, she can't steer. I'd say the cure is to let her fall off to the north (head to NNE) on the starboard tack and fill the sails, not keep luffing. If she won't fall off, we must wear or heave to and ride to an anchor before she drifts down. I'd keep the best bower ready. Your word, sir.

args.text: Sir, 09:23, plainly: she went into irons for two minutes and made sternway, and the boxing-off has her gathering headway. She now heads NNW (340°) at 2 knots, leeway 22°, with the helm at 25°, wind 97° on the larboard quarter at 19 knots. The headsails alone are set, because the topsail is clewed up and the main sail was brailed "up mainsail" in the box-off. We're in a good position, but with only headsails she's slow to answer and the leeway of 22° sets us toward Espalamaca. I'd get the main sail drawing again. Your call, sir.

Sir, 09:25: she is boxed off and braced up, but she now heads S by E (169°) at 6 knots, wind 56° on the starboard bow at 22 knots, with the Point of Espalamaca on the starboard quarter at a mile and Fayal Road W by N at nine cables. He'll call the let-go. I'll not give any sail or helm order unless you ask, sir, but I'll tell you when the Bank is within three cables.

Sir, 09:30: the wear is made. She heads NW by W (308°) at 7 knots with the wind 52° on the larboard bow, 25 knots apparent, heeling 11°. Fayal Road is six cables W by N, and the Bank of Fayal S by W at a mile, behind us. Depth by the chart is 50 fathoms and a half, about to shoal toward the 40 the pilot gives.

args.text: Veer more cable.

Sir, urgent: the best bower, let go at 09:32 in 46 fathoms, is dragging with 86 to 87 fathoms out and the cable bar-taut, though the strain is only 0.02 of the rating. The depth is 44 fathoms and a half, too deep and the bottom is too far off to hold her on this scope, as Mr Terra warned. The Point of Espalamaca lies NNW at seven cables, so she can't drag far to leeward before land is close. I've ordered more cable veered, which is within my authority, to bring her up. The small bower is at the bows to let go if that fails. The wind is 23 knots from the WSW, a gust hazard with the glass falling fast, so I'd rather have scope than short cable. Do you want the small bower let go as well, and the sails clewed up so she doesn't sail up on her cable?

args.text: Sound the well.

Sir, urgent: she has taken the ground forward at 09:43 on sand and small shell, in one fathom and a half by the chart, drawing nine feet. She struck at five knots and heels 9°, and the tide is falling. The carpenter reports her strained and making water. She will not float before the flood, which the master puts at about half past four this afternoon.

State of her: all sail is being furled (24 hands at it) and the best bower is out with the whole 240 fathoms of cable, bar-taut but with only 0.01 strain. She is NW by W with the wind SW by W at 24 knots, 65° on the larboard bow, and a short chopping sea. The town of Fayal is a cable W, the Point of Espalamaca seven cables NE, and the Guia S by W at a mile. She is aground on sand, not rock, and in a road that is sheltered from the NW.

What I'd do and what I need from you. (1) Sound the well and rig the pumps. The ship has no well yet in this game, so the carpenter's report is all we have. (2) Get the pilot Mr Terra to tell us the berth and the bottom. (3) Lay out the kedge or small bower to hold her head to the wind and stop her pounding as the tide falls, and lighten her bows by shifting weight aft. (4) Keep the boat ready for the beach. I'm not to give helm orders aground. I'd value your word on the pumps, the kedge and sending to the town for help. Shall I order the kedge laid?

args.text: Lay out the kedge astern.

Sir, I've ordered the kedge laid out astern, as Mr Terra advises. The kedge is within my authority as ground tackle. He says she has walked her anchor right up onto the Praia, the sand by the old fort, on sand and shell, soft and not rock. The wind is off the land and blows her off, which is good. He advises getting the sails off her, pumping, and sending the boat with the kedge astern to the east into deep water, to be heaved taut. args.note: Stand-down note, 09:43 forenoon watch, 2 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter is aground forward in Fayal Road on the sand and small shell of the Praia by the old fort, 1½ fathoms by the chart, she draws 9 feet, heeling about 8-9°, tide falling, wind SW by W 24 kn off the land, glass 29.81 falling fast. Best bower is down with all 240 fathoms, bar-taut; the kedge is being laid astern to the E into deep water by the boat, on the pilot's advice. All sail is being furled. Pilot Mr Terra of Fayal is aboard and says it is soft ground, she will not break, the wind blows her off, and the port captain would send lighters if asked (port's business: the captain's word). Watch on the pumps and the leak. Lessons for whoever sits here: tell the captain at once when the readings show 'making sternway'; never order sails or yards while an evolution is in hand; take the full scope in deep water; and without the deck give no helm or sail orders. The captain has the deck. Ashore at Fayal are Mr Ruiz the clerk, Senhor Bettencourt the merchant (the sealed letter for him is in the cabin), and Mr Josiah Hale the supercargo. The French schooner (12 guns, black) was last reported off Santa Maria; the Conceição brigantine from Funchal is overdue. The purse is £928 8s; water 5.7 tons, provisions 33 days. The captain asked for the stand-down because he needs a break.

args.text: Take a fix.

Tell the captain Sir, 19:38: the small bower has bitten and she is stopped: speed 0, no way on, 106 fathoms of the small bower and all 240 of the best bower out, her head NW by W with the wind WNW 23 kn. The fix is the account again, within two cables; the Point of Espalamaca is three cables on the starboard bow, the Magdalena shoals and the Bank of Fayal are to the SE at a mile and a half. She is in 14 to 23 fathoms, deep for the holding; both cables are long and the best is bar-taut at 0.04. I have given no further order. My suggestion is to ride as she is through the evening with a hand at the lead and a cast each half-hour for dragging, rest the hands by watches since they are worn out, keep the pumps each glass, and heave in to a better berth in the roads nearer the town in the morning watch when she has rested; I will do whatever you direct about the best bower.

args.text: Tell the captain Understood, sir: I keep the deck, keep her moored, and unmoor only in the worst case while you are ashore. Two things as I see them at 19:40: she dragged about two cables ESE between 19:36 and 19:39 and stopped when the small bower bit, but the log has not yet said 'holds again', and both cables are now out to the end (240 on the best bower, 120 on the small), so there is no anchor left to let go; the Bank of Fayal lies SSE a mile and a half. If you can, wait a quarter hour to see her hold before you leave her. I will keep the lead going each half-glass, the pumps each glass (well an inch), the hands in watches, and a fix at each bell, and if she comes home toward the Bank I shall set the topsail, weigh the small bower and stand off under way, which is the worst case you name. Give me the boat's time ashore and back if you can, and tell me what hands go with you.

Plainly, sir: I'm an AI standing the mate's watch, so I take no meat or drink myself, and I thank you for asking. But the hands are another matter: they have been at it since before the grounding with the pumps, the kedge and the sail, and I don't see that they have had a proper meal. With her riding easy I'd have the cook serve a hot meal and a tot by watches, the larboard watch first, and you should eat before you go ashore. I keep the deck meanwhile.

args.text: Tell the captain Sir, the slack at the turn is no annoyance and no danger of itself: with the wind down to 9 knots the tide is swinging her about her bower and the cable only goes slack at each turn, and it has held all night within a cable. My advice is to shift the berth, but not now. (1) It is 02:30, hazy, and the hands are not rested; the best bower is 240 fathoms out in 22 fathoms, a long steep heave, and the berth we want is in 17 fathoms or less near the town, among the whalers' anchors, so I would not shift in the dark without the pilot. (2) Bettencourt's lighters come tomorrow night, so there is the whole day to shift and nothing is gained by hurry. (3) Nearer the town also means nearer Etcheverry's friends ashore, and Bettencourt asked for quiet; our berth is out of the way. (4) A real objection to staying two-anchored is that she is swinging round with the tide and may foul her hawse, so at first light (twilight from 05:36) I would heave in the small bower, ride by the best bower alone, then with Mr Terra aboard shift to the berth he names, in 10 to 15 fathoms, on the flood, with the full watch fresh. I'll keep her as she is until you say, with the lead and fixes going.

args.note: Handover, 02:30 middle watch, 3 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter lies moored in Fayal Road on two bowers (best 240 fathoms, small 120, both full out) in 22 fathoms, kedge catted at the bows, holding all night within a cable of the account (fixes each glass: Guia SW by S, town W, Espalamaca N by E). She swings with the slack tide each few minutes; that is the 'cable slack at the turn' log noise, harmless, though two cables may foul her hawse if she goes on swinging. Wind NNW 9 kn, glass 30.21 rising fast, hazy, heavy confused sea with a westerly swell. Well an inch and steady (sounded each glass, last 02:27); lead no bottom at 20. Hands: starboard/larboard in watches, 12 on deck. Ashore: Bettencourt has the letter and wants forty pipes (20 tons) of Pico wine consigned to his son in Falmouth at £4 a ton, £40 on signing the bill of lading tomorrow and £40 on delivery; he'll sell the captain wine at £32 the ton for his own account; lighters from Madalena come out after dark tomorrow night, sail on the land breeze before dawn, keep it quiet because of the Basque (Etcheverry's black schooner). Mr Hale, supercargo of Salem, has agreed a £5 passage to Madeira, hammock with the hands; chest to the beach when the boat is sent. I advised: heave in the small bower at first light (twilight 05:36), ride by the best bower alone, then shift to a berth in 10 to 15 fathoms on the flood with Mr Terra's help and a rested watch. The captain has the deck and sends me ashore in the morning to fetch Hale and give Bettencourt the word on the lighters. Lessons: no anchor left to let go with both cables out; keep a stream/kedge ready; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'.

Hands: starboard/larboard in watches, 12 on deck. Ashore: Bettencourt has the letter and wants forty pipes (20 tons) of Pico wine consigned to his son in Falmouth at £4 a ton, £40 on signing the bill of lading tomorrow and £40 on delivery; he'll sell the captain wine at £32 the ton for his own account; lighters from Madalena come out after dark tomorrow night, sail on the land breeze before dawn, keep it quiet because of the Basque (Etcheverry's black schooner). Mr Hale, supercargo of Salem, has agreed a £5 passage to Madeira, hammock with the hands; chest to the beach when the boat is sent. I advised: heave in the small bower at first light (twilight 05:36), ride by the best bower alone, then shift to a berth in 10 to 15 fathoms on the flood with Mr Terra's help and a rested watch. The captain has the deck and sends me ashore in the morning to fetch Hale and give Bettencourt the word on the lighters. Lessons: no anchor left to let go with both cables out; keep a stream/kedge ready; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'."}}, {"name": "stand_by", "arguments": {"until": "sunrise"}}]

(1) Bettencourt's answer: two lighters from Madalena, twenty pipes each, six men and a patrão apiece, leave at dusk and come alongside about ten tonight; Ruiz in the first lighter with the bill of lading to sign and £40 in gold; one hooded lantern at the gangway, fall and slings rigged beforehand, a pipe is half a ton; we lie where we are. (2) Mr Ruiz says no schooner is in the Road, the black schooner was off Santa Maria last week far to the east; but a Frenchman in a brown coat calling himself a wine buyer stood the watermen drinks last night asking which English vessel came in with her bottom scraped and what she carried and when she sailed. Mr Hale confirms it: he was asked too, said nothing, and the man left an hour before midnight toward the beach at Porto Pim, not the town. (3) Hale's chest lies behind the bar here and he is fit; I have told him to bring it to the quay and I will bring him off with the letter. args.text: Thank you, sir. I found it useful and enjoyable: the quay and the counting house were quick, Senhor Bettencourt was kind and exact about the lighters, and Mr Hale proved a plain-spoken man and honest about the Frenchman in the brown coat. Two small stumbles on my side: I tried to tell you something by order while ashore, which the game refused since you were out of hail, so I carried it back and told it to you in person; and my first 'say' to Hale was refused until I added 'Mr Hale' by name. The thing I'd keep in mind from it is the Frenchman: he asked the watermen at the tavern what the cutter carried and when she sailed and went toward Porto Pim, so the quiet of tonight's loading matters. Is there anything you'd have me do now, or shall I rest and take the deck at the change of the watch?

args.text: Sound the well.

I say yes, sir, and I'd have it come tonight with the lighters. Provisions stand at 32 days with Mr Hale now mouths to feed, water at 5.6 tons for 47 days. That is enough for Madeira and home by my reckoning (some five days to Funchal and ten to fourteen on to Falmouth), but it leaves no margin for a calm like the last, a chase or a long beat, and we know the Pico stores are the same price as here: salt beef £50 a ton, salt fish £28, barley £10. Eight days is a good fraction of a ton; 20 tons of Bettencourt's wine plus your 4 tons will leave the hold with 18 tons to spare, so stowage is no difficulty. Two cautions: (1) buying it from a chandler on the quay in daylight tells the town we are provisioning to sail, and the brown-coated Frenchman is asking exactly that, so I'd ask Senhor Bettencourt or Ruiz to put it in the first lighter in casks and bags with the wine, and pay Ruiz as you do for the pipes; (2) water is the fouler risk, so top up the casks from the Pico boats' fresh water tonight too if you can, since a fouled cask spoiled the last passage. Shall I put the stowage in hand when they are alongside?

args.note: Handover, 16:47 first dog watch, 3 July 1806. Sherbourne rides moored on two bowers (best 240 fathoms, small 120, both full out; kedge catted at the bows) in 22 fathoms; fixes each glass all day within a cable of the account (38° 32' N, 28° 37' W): Espalamaca N by E, town W, Magdalena E. Fog lifted 14:45, now clear, wind N by E 7 kn, glass 30.24 steady, moderate sea from the north. Well an inch and steady since the copper went on; you told me to avast sounding it. Variation 22° 30' W by azimuth (3 July). Water 5.5 tons, provisions 32 days. Tonight: Bettencourt's two lighters from Madalena (20 pipes each, six men and patrão each) alongside about 22:00 with Ruiz in the first, the bill of lading and £40 gold; also 8 days of provisions (£10) and two butts of fresh water free; your own 8 pipes marked C (£128 to Ruiz when stowed) and a present case of bottles; one hooded lantern at the gangway; the Frenchman in the brown coat is asking after us, so keep the hour quiet. The sail on the land breeze before dawn will need the small bower weighed, kedge catted, best bower hove short, topsail set; I'd call the larboard and starboard together for that. I have eaten and drunk and am going below to rest until called.

args.text: Aye, sir, I'm up and fed. 20:00: all in order. Both bowers hold, fix at 18:12 within half a cable, well pumped dry at 18:32, wind N by W 9 kn, glass 30.25 steady, clear, moon 41° high (a bright night). The manifest is written up: 20 tons of Pico wine freighted, the lighter brings it off. I suggest: the larboard watch on deck, the starboard hands below to be called at 21:30; a hand at the lead through the evening; the hatches off and the whip and slings rigged at 21:30 with only a hooded lantern at the gangway; the boat armed at the booms; and the lookouts told to say nothing of the hour. With a moon this bright the lighters will show from the shore, so I'd have the hands keep below the rail and the lantern masked from the town. I await your orders.

args.text: Take a fix.
Heave the lead.

Tell the captain Sir, 20:00: I have the deck. Fix of this minute: Espalamaca N by E, town W, Magdalena E, within half a cable of the account; both bowers hold; the lead is going. Wind N by W 9 kn, clear, bright moon. The lighters are due about 22:00 and the freight is already written up in the manifest. I'll call the starboard watch at 21:30 to rig the whip and slings and take off the hatches, and keep the lantern hooded; and at the first sight of a boat I will hail her and report. I'd also be glad to know the Pico wine rule: your eight pipes marked C are to be paid to Mr Ruiz when stowed, £128, and Bettencourt's £40 freight is to come in gold in the first lighter, so I'll have the purse and the bill of lading ready for you at the gangway.

args.text: Tell the captain Sir, 22:13: all forty pipes are below (the manifest reads 24 tons of Pico wine, room for 18), and Mr Ruiz says the bread, beef, beans and the two butts of water are lying in the lighter's stern sheets and need only be sent for; they come up the side when asked. I will not try 'send for' myself, as sending for provisions is for your word. Do you wish me to have them hoisted in? I would not leave the lighter alongside long, with the fog and a Frenchman about. After that I propose we weigh: heave short the best bower and the small, cat the kedge, set the topsail and stand out on the land breeze before dawn, if you consent, since the wine is stowed, the provisions are aboard and the fog hides us.

args.text: Tell the captain Sir, 22:38: provisioning is done: 8 days of provisions stowed (provisions now for 40 days), 1 ton of water in (6.5 tons, 55 days), Mr Ruiz has gone down the side and the Madalena lighters are pulling away toward the Guia. The manifest reads 24 tons of Pico wine, room for 18; purse £842 15s. The ship is still moored, wind N by W 10 kn, glass 30.24, fog thick, moon 24° high behind the cloud. She is deeper by 24 tons, so she will answer slower on weighing. I await your word to heave short on the small bower and then the best bower; with only a gentle breeze I'd weigh the kedge first and the small bower next, but not before the hands are called and the fog allows us to see the Point.
