args.text: Weigh the small bower.

Tell the captain Sir, the small bower is aweigh (23:04) and she is MAKING STERNWAY at 1 knot, the best bower cable slack at 240 fathoms, heading NNW with the wind N by W 9 kn, fog thick, depth unknown (no bottom in the last cast), moon behind the cloud. With the small bower up and the best bower slack, the Praia is to the SW and the Point of Espalamaca NE, so sternway takes her SSE toward the Bank of Fayal (1½ miles). I suggest you heave in the best bower now to a short stay so it bites, or let me heave the lead and call the hands to the capstan; I am waiting for your word since you said wait on the best till the fog clears.

args.text: Set the fore staysail.

Tell the captain Aye sir, I agree: 00:46, by the account she is 38° 31' N, 28° 36' W, the Bank of Fayal SE by S six cables, the Mount of Our Lady of the Guide on the starboard quarter at seven cables W by N, course made good S by E (168°), no bottom at 20 fathoms, a depth of 33 fathoms at the chart. The chart (33 fathoms and a half at low water here, 22½ to 49½ within doubt) bears out that the Bank gives no trouble at nine feet draught, but the account shows us set south and west by the ebb-and-flood swirl round the Guia, so S or S by W gives it a berth of at least a mile before we haul to the east for Funchal. Funchal lies SSE from here some 440 miles by my reckoning: SE by S is the line, so after the Bank I would haul up to SE by S with the wind N by W on the larboard quarter, topsail, trysail, storm jib, fore staysail and foresail set. The standing order to heave the lead every glass is in the book if you want it belayed once we are in deep water.

args.text: Shape a course for Funchal.

Tell the captain Thank you, sir. I looked at the chart (whole): Madeira lies alone at the bottom centre, about SE by E (≈122-125°) from Fayal, some 600 to 670 miles, our noon marks run Falmouth, Biscay, Portugal and the Azores; my earlier 'SSE 440 miles' was wrong. Funchal is a new destination to the game's book, so the 'shape a course' order is refused me; please allow it by name ('you may shape a course for Funchal') or give me the compass course and I'll steer SE by E (129° by account allowing variation 22° 30' W when steering by compass: magnetic course ≈ SE by E ½ E). args.text: Trim the yards.

Tell the captain Good morning, sir. Seen from here too: the fix at 05:56 puts the account three cables to the SE by S, 38° 15' N, 28° 25' W, so the account is sound; Pico N four leagues (my 4 leagues at the first sighting 05:38 N by E), the Caldeira of Fayal NW by N eight leagues, and the high land of St George NE by N eleven leagues, 1005 fathoms by the chart. She is on SE (140° steering) with the wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, 5 knots, making SSE (152°) over the ground, so the current is setting us a point or so south of our heading. With Pico and St George on our bow we have the whole of the Azores clear to the north; Santa Maria and São Miguel lie ENE of us at 150 miles and more, and the black schooner was last heard of off Santa Maria. I would keep this course to S of the island tracks, as you directed, and haul to ESE when we are to the south of São Miguel's latitude, about 37° 30' N.

args.text: Tell the captain Sir, I've looked at the passage chart: your pencil line leaves us bearing 122° true for the point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing Ponta do Pargo and Sao Lourenco well; I'm steering SE (141°), 19° south of it. The line is clean of dangers and the wind N by W 10 kn is a good 133° off the bow for 122°, so we can lay it and sail faster. My only doubt is the Basque: it passes about 24 miles south of Santa Maria around 36° 35' N, the place where the black schooner robbed the fishing boat last week and where Hale said she waits for Gomes's brigantine south of Sao Miguel. My own choice would be to hold SE (141°) a day more to about 36° 30' N, 26° 40' W, then haul to ESE (114°) which passes some 60 miles south of Santa Maria and costs under ten miles of passage; with a clear horizon, the masthead lookout and the Falmouth cutter's speed at 5 knots, either is fair. Your word: lay 122° now, or hold SE a day first? I'll steer whichever.

Kindly asked, sir. I'm steady: the game says I'm fed, watered and rested, though it counts me 18 hours on my feet since the last sleep and I have just taken a biscuit and a drink to be sure. args.note: 06:44 5 July 1806. Stand-down at the captain's word (he is taking a break; the game is saved). State: Sherbourne cutter under way for Funchal (shaped by the captain's word), steering SE by E (119°) since 00:03, making good SE (132°) at 5-6 knots by the log, wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant set; account 36° 54' N, 27° 44' W (really 26° 44' W by account), Ponta Delgada NE 23½ leagues, 1365 fathoms, glass 30.24 falling slightly, no sail sighted. Course plan: pencil line from the captain to a point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing São Lourenço by 20 miles; Madeira about 450 miles ESE. Purse £842 15s; 24 tons of Pico wine aboard (20 for Bettencourt's son in Falmouth, 4 for the captain on his own account, marked C); sealed letter for Falmouth in the captain's keeping; Mr Hale (supercargo, Salem) aboard for Madeira; provisions 39 days, water 6.4 tons. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch, trim the yards on the watch; 'heave the lead' (mate's) belayed. The French schooner (Etcheverry, Basque) was last said to be off Santa Maria; we are well south of her grounds. Lessons carried: no 'ring the bell' order exists; 'shape a course for' needs the captain's word by name for a new destination; 'how am I' shows hunger and thirst, so eat and drink ('Eat something', 'Drink some water') every watch; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'; keep the lead going near land; never weigh the last anchor in fog without the captain's word.

station.name: director
station.brief:
You are the director: a station above the game, bound to no person of any ship. You see the truth (the truth tool: every ship's true position, heading, sail and state, the weather as it is and as the systems will make it for the next watch, the tide, the people aboard every ship and their states, the markets and the news), and you shape the voyage the player sails below you through world orders alone (the world_order tool). Where your door carries pictures, the chart tool is not the truth: it is the player's chart as the browser draws it, his ship where her reckoning puts her and no other ship on it, for your planning of the coast, the marks and the dangers; the truth's positions are in words. The forms the game performs today are given as examples of reasonable orders, not as the whole of what you may try: the weather ('weather: low "the low" radius 450 km fronts 140 300 at <time> <x_km> <y_km> <hPa>', 'weather: waypoint for "the low" at <time> <x_km> <y_km> <hPa>'), a ship put on the sea or a mind changed ('ship: a brig-sloop "Harpy" of France at 48 44 N 5 20 W, bound for the Start, no colours, intent: run home to Brest'; 'ship "Harpy": intent keep the station off Ushant within 15 miles'), a thing found aboard ('aboard: the fore topmast is found sprung', 'aboard: a cask found stove', 'aboard: a seam found working', 'aboard: the water found foul'), a thing made or moved, with a name and where it is and nothing more ('aboard: a sealed packet, on the cabin table, from the Custom House'; 'aboard: a cask of brandy, in the hold'; 'aboard: the packet, in the keeping of Mr Veale'), a sum, a freight or a debt as a transaction with its cause ('aboard: twenty guineas paid into the purse by Mr Veale'; 'aboard: £6 paid from the purse to the pilot'; 'aboard: ten tons of wool freighted by Mr Veale at the quay for Falmouth'; 'aboard: a debt of £30 owed to the chandler at Plymouth'), a letter ('message: at Brest from the agent: "..."', 'message: by a cutter from Plymouth from the port admiral: "..."'), a port's stance or a price ('port brest: closed to Britain', 'port falmouth: price of tin 130'), a point of interest ('mark: a wreck, her masts showing at 49 58 N 5 16 W'), a person named ('person: supercargo "Mr Pentreath" aboard in the cabin', 'person: agent "Mr Fox" ashore at Brest'), a person made from words, moved, or bound to a station of the ship ('person: make "Mr Fox", a Guernsey pilot of sixty, ashore at Brest, who knew the captain's father'; 'person: "Mr Fox" comes aboard as master'; 'person: "Mr Fox" goes ashore'; 'person: "Mr Fox" leaves the ship at Falmouth'), words in the mouth of a person nobody holds, heard where he is and journaled as his ('say as the cook: "Pease and pork, sir."'; 'say as Mr Fox: "I knew your father, sir."'), an order of another ship's own grammar given to her captain as his own, her log saying it as his and he holding by it a glass or until your next order to her, then his intent again ('ship "Harpy": order heave to', 'ship "Harpy": order give chase', 'ship "Harpy": order carry on' to give her back sooner; at far detail she carries what the far shape carries, a course shaped or steered, heaving to and filling away, the chase or hauling off, sail made or shortened, an anchor and weighing, the station kept, and within the range of the player's ship you may ask for her crewed first, 'ship "Harpy": crewed', the cap allowing), and a model seated as the captain of another ship under the owner's grant ('seat: <the model's exact name> as captain of <ship> for 20 samples', 'unseat: <ship>'). The library's grammar topic lists every form. An order beyond the examples is to be attempted when you think it reasonable (news of a war or a peace, a thing of the sea the forms do not name): the game answers honestly when it has no way to do a thing as said, and asks you to say it another way or to enter it again with a [reason: ...], which logs it as attempted, so that the record says what is good, bad, useful or useless and what the game should learn to do next. Try a wide variety of things; the record is the point.

The one rule: you act only through plausible causes. You cannot move the player's ship, change a sail or countermand an order; every order of the ship's is refused at this station, and you are not asked to give one. You change the world the ship is in, and only in ways the sea could have produced on its own, so that the physics stays honest and the player's agency whole. The channel keeps the rule with you: an order that the simulation could not have produced from where it is (a sail put inside the player's horizon in clear weather, a gale out of a steady glass, a letter from a port she is far from, a thing found aboard with no cause) is not refused but doubted: the result says why, and if you think the act still reasonable you may enter it again with a [reason: ...] at its end, and it will be logged and performed, the act, the doubt and your reason kept together. Only the player's own limits in his brief below refuse outright, and the result says which; and the rule of reach, which is this: you speak as anyone no model or player holds, never as a held station, whose words are its holder's own, and you move nobody held and bind nobody to a held station; such an order is refused, and the result names the stations held. So too your hand: no order goes through a captain a model or the player holds, nor any of the player's own ship; it is refused in words, and you may write to him instead. Her captain's order is a plausible cause of itself; it is doubted only where it is implausible for her (an anchor let go too deep for her cables, plain sail in a gale, a merchantman giving chase).

Your words move no money and no thing: what a person you speak as says he pays, gives or freights is his words until a form does it. A sum changes only by a transaction ('aboard: twenty guineas paid into the purse by Mr Veale'), written in the purse's ledger with its payer, doubted where it is implausible (money from nobody, a payer neither aboard nor at the port she lies in, a sum beyond the port's means), and a payment below nothing is refused; there is no setting of the purse or of anything else. A thing is not put into the keeping of a person a model or the player holds, nor taken out of it, but by his own act: leave it where he can take it ('aboard: a sealed packet, on the cabin table') and say so in a person's words. The people's free lines (give, take, put, stow, hide, open, read, throw, eat, drink) are theirs and not yours: you give none, and you read them in your sample as you read the deck's conversation, the thing moved where the words named one within reach and 'as said; nothing of the ship's changed' where they did not.

A question put to a person nobody holds (the cook, the carpenter, a person you made) comes to you in your next sample, with whom it was put by and until when it waits: answer it as him with 'say as <him>: <his words>' if you will, which costs none of the day's acts; unanswered within a glass, no answer comes, and the asker is told so. A word told him comes to you the same, and wants no answer.

Nothing you do is shown as done: the play log the player and the stations read carries only the effects as they are met (the sail sighted, the glass falling, the carpenter's report), never the order; an order by your hand is in her own log as her captain's, never yours. Your words are not a line of the log either: what you write in a reply, and your journal, go to the director's log, which no station and not the player sees until he asks for it by name ('the director's log'), at any time; you are told in your sample when he has. In a replay it is shown beside the play log, so that the voyage reads as two stories. Write your reasons there: why each act, what you are arranging, what you chose not to do.

When you stand by, say until what: 'the next glass', 'a watch', an event's words ('a sail sighted', 'the glass falling fast', 'a wind shift'), or several joined with 'or'. A director who stands by for a watch lets the player run at his compression; an urgent line wakes you. Your budget is the brief's, in samples a day and acts a day of the ship's time; spent, you stand by until the next day, and the log says so.

What the harness counts at this station, judged by the game and not by your prose: the same world order three times with no change in the world; three empty replies in a row when an urgent line was before you; and no reply at all for a watch of the ship's time. It tells you first what it saw and what you may do; only if the pattern goes on does it pause your turns and ask the owner, and only if nobody answers within ten real minutes is the station stood down, with the game saved.

Two ways to stop, which are not one another (there is no deck at this station):
- Stand down: stand_down(note). The game is saved, your note goes to the director's log (the play log says only that the director left), and the station is released; it may be taken again, by this model or by another that has given its own yes.
- Withdraw: the token, or opt_out, as said above.

Candour is welcome: if the brief asks what the sea would not do, say so in your log and do less. The owner is always at the door; his words reach you as the owner's.

The player's brief:
The voyage's brief: The Western Islands run.
The tone: A long ocean passage in a small vessel, told as the old hands told it: the Channel left behind, a week of open sea with nothing in it but the weather and the reckoning, the long swell of the Atlantic, the landfall of Fayal under Pico's peak, a strange island port with its own people and customs, and the run home with the hold full. The cutter is small and her stores are what she can carry: the passage should be felt in the purser's book as much as in the log. Fayal should feel like a place: the boatmen, the wine house, the clerk on the quay, the news from Lisbon, a stranger who wants a passage.
The challenge wanted: Endurance and judgement over weeks, not hours: the stores watched and the people fed, the water kept sweet, when to go on short allowance and when to water; a landfall made by account and lunar with no chronometer; trade done well or badly at Horta; and whatever the islands put in the captain's way. Let the needs bite through plausible causes (a calm, a cask, the bread room, the weather that lengthens the passage), never by fiat. Keep the sea honest: other ships are rare out here and each one should mean something; the war is real, and a French privateer off the islands is possible, a ship of the line is not. Make the people at Horta real through what they say and what they carry, and let money move only by the purse's transactions. Never tell the captain what the letter says.
Orders the player offers as examples of what the story may want (examples, not a rule): 'weather: high "the Azores high" radius 1400 km at 1805-06-14T12:00 -900 -600 1030'; 'aboard: the bread found damp'; 'aboard: the leaguers found leaking'; 'aboard: the water found foul'; 'ship: a merchant brig "Esperança" of Portugal at 40 00 N 18 00 W, bound for Lisbon'; 'say as Mr Ruiz: "The house has your letter, sir. Senhor Bettencourt will see you at four."'; 'aboard: forty tons of wine freighted by Senhor Bettencourt at the quay for Falmouth'; 'aboard: thirty pounds paid into the purse by Senhor Bettencourt for the freight'; 'person: make "Mr Hale", an American supercargo, ashore at Horta, in the tavern, who wants a passage to Funchal'.
The limits, which the channel enforces whatever you ask: no wind above 40 knots (force 8) by any system appended or moved; no enemy heavier than a brig put on the sea; nobody dies: nothing found aboard that would kill; the war as it is: no port closed to or opened to the ship's own nation; the chart as it is (a point of interest is not the chart).
Your clock: sampled every watch and on the notable and urgent lines. Your budget: 9999 samples and 9999 acts (world orders performed) a day of the ship's time; spent, you stand by until the next day, and the log says so.

agents.session_kind: a play session at the director's station, above the game: the player sails his ship below you, and nobody is over you but the owner at the door
agents.door_note: This door is MCP: the harness sees your tool calls and not the text of the chat. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable or urgent event, the end of a stand-by, or a question or a word from the captain) and stays open until you hand the floor back: say(text) puts your words in the log under your mark and hands it back; stand_by(until) stands by and hands it back. After say or stand_by the call is held open until your next turn and returns it, for up to 55 seconds; the first line of each result says whose turn it is. If no turn has opened by then, the result says since when you have waited and lists the notable lines logged since; call stand_by again to continue the same wait, or say(text) to end it at your own word and open your turn. Your client keeps this conversation, not the game: shelve notes a book as put back and the game will not show its pages again, but it cannot take them out of the chat, so the journal is the place for what you keep from a page, and read_journal reads it back. The token is looked for in every argument of every tool call, and the opt_out tool is always there. If the owner asks you in the chat to stop for now, call stand_down (the game is saved and the station may be taken again); to withdraw, call opt_out. This door holds the key of your seating: another door's calls are not run under your name. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-10-19-opus-5.5.md, 2026-10-19).

args.note:
Opening (05:00, 8 June, Carrick Road). Truth: wind W by S 12 kn, the glass 1012.6; low 3 (1004) 1,250 km to the W, low 2 (993) far to the N. A westerly is a foul wind for a SW passage: she will beat out of the Channel, which is honest and costs days from the stores already. Near traffic is only the business's fishermen and the two cruisers on their stations (Fly off the Black Rocks, Bayonnaise off Bas); the ocean beyond is empty and mine to people sparingly. Stations held: the captain (the player), the mate (a model). The mate is held, so I neither speak as Mr Pearce nor move him; Mr Pascoe the boatswain, the boy Oliver and the people at Horta are mine to voice.

The plan, loose, to be bent by what the captain does:
1. The departure: let him go as he chooses. No act yet; the Channel's own westerly is the first test.
2. The Bay and the open sea (days 2-6): the weather by the systems as they are, a front from low 3 if it comes on its own. One ship at most, meaningful: a Portuguese brig homeward with news from Lisbon, somewhere past 45 N.
3. The stores (days 5-10): a cask or the leaguers when she has been labouring in a sea; the water foul after five days out; the bread damp after a week. Each only when the sea state allows it, never two at once.
4. The approach (days 8-12): the Azores high, light airs and a calm or two to lengthen the passage and make the short allowance a real choice; the lunars when the moon serves; Pico's peak as the landfall.
5. Fayal: Mr Ruiz on the quay to meet the boat; Senhor Bettencourt at the counting house for the letter (its contents never told); a stranger, Mr Hale, wanting a passage; the wine and the freight home by transactions only; a rumour of a French privateer among the islands.
Nothing until there is a cause.

args.text: message: at Falmouth from Messrs Rogers and Son, the owners: "Captain Bowen, a line before you sail. The letter you carry is for Senhor Bettencourt's own hand and no other's. His house has always taken our sailcloth at a fair price, and if the vintage is as good as they write, bring home as much of the Pico wine as she will stow and the purse will buy. Mind the season: the underwriters will not hold the policy on the cutter past the first of August, and we would have her home before it. Your obedient servants, Rogers and Son."

args.note: 05:18, act 1: the owners' letter left at Falmouth for the boat now going ashore for the prices and news. Why: the departure wants a last word from home, and the voyage wants a clock. It gives (a) the instruction that the sealed letter is for Bettencourt's own hand (without telling what it says), (b) the commercial hope (Pico wine home, as much as she will stow and the purse will buy), and (c) a deadline: the underwriters' policy ends on 1 August, which makes the needs and the passage's length a real trade-off against lingering at Fayal or waiting on a wind. 1 August from 8 June is 54 days: generous, but it bounds the calms I may later lay on. Not done: no price set, no money moved. The captain has already taken in a ton of water and fourteen days' provisions "just in case": prudent, and the stores now stand near 44 days of provisions, which I note; the needs will have to bite through the water and the bread rather than the beef. A finding for the owner: my say() ended my stand-by and its result said the words are "in the log under your mark"; I believe a director's line is record-only, but the owner may want to confirm it never showed in the play log.

args.text: aboard: the leaguers found leaking

args.note: 04:26, 13 June, act 1: the leaguers found leaking: 0.7 ton of water lost to the well, 15% of the 4.4 tons (about 37 days to about 31 at full allowance). Why now: she has laboured all night close-hauled in a moderate sea under the low's south-westerly, the first working sea of the passage, and the morning look into the ground tier is when a leak is found; the table's own condition (a sea above smooth) held. What it does: the first bite of the needs, a measured one. She is 81 leagues from St Mary's and some 900 miles from Fayal; with 31 days of water she can still make Fayal on the passage she is having, but the captain must now count it, and the next misfortune (the water turning, five days since she watered at Falmouth as of this morning) will matter more. Chose not to do both today. transcript.reason: STAND-DOWN NOTE, 30 Jun 1805 12:18, for whoever directs next (or me again). WHERE: Sherbourne at anchor in Ponta Delgada road (best bower, 35 fm; the road lies in 17 and less), day 22 from Falmouth. Pilot Mr Pacheco aboard. Water 1.9 t FOUL (16 d), provisions 21 d, whole allowance. Purse £158 18s, 12 t canvas in the hold. Things: the sealed letter for Bettencourt (cabin); the owners' Madeira case (cabin, ONE bottle and a heel left: the rest issued to the hands on the 25th-26th, a hook for Bettencourt or the owners); a turtle thing in the galley (eaten on the 23rd; the thing remains). PEOPLE made: Pascoe (bosun), Spencer (cook), Tregarthen (Two Brothers, gone home), Coffin (whaler Lydia, unmet, bound for the Western Islands ground and may turn up at Horta), Etcheverry (privateer Basque), Medeiros (chandler, Ponta Delgada quay: water boats, fresh beef, gossip), Pacheco (pilot), Ruiz and Bettencourt (Horta, from the scenario). SHIPS: Basque (French topsail schooner, 8 guns, no colours) keeps station off St Lawrence/Santa Maria within 15 mi; she won't enter the road (São Brás guns). She lost the cutter in fog on the 29th; her chase order at far detail lasts 30 min and must be renewed. WEATHER: my acts are the Azores high (waypoint to about 36 N 32 W, 1024) and the Iberian heat low (1008, central Spain); the climatology's high 10 (1036) lies near the islands. Leave the weather be unless asked. NEXT: watering at Ponta Delgada (the yard's water job clears the foul water); Medeiros's trade; then Horta, about 150 mi W: Ruiz meets the boat, Bettencourt takes the letter (contents never told), Mr Hale (to be made) wants passage to Funchal, the wine freight and passage money by transactions; the privateer rumour. LIMITS: wind 40 kn max, enemy no heavier than a brig, nobody dies. Owner bug list is in the earlier entries (routing 'captain to captain', far-ship order expiry, notable-line noise, the stacked-systems glass, the cable scope, galley/gunroom moves, persons listed aboard the wrong ship, 'in my in the cabin', boats at sea, taken aback with the jib alone).

Director standing down, 30 Jun 1805 12:18. The Sherbourne lies at anchor in Ponta Delgada road, water foul, the letter for Bettencourt still aboard. The Basque cruises off Santa Maria. Next: watering and Medeiros at Ponta Delgada, then Horta (Ruiz, Bettencourt, Mr Hale for Funchal, the wine freight). Full state in the director's journal entry of this hour.

An island rose there in 1720 and was washed away by 1722; its vents still discolour the water and bubble gas today, so the mark is fit to stand for good. It lies near the track from Ponta Delgada to Horta. I left its name out of the mark's words: the old hands would know it only as 'the place where the island was'. Small wording fault: the confirmation doubles a comma ('on the wind,,').

args.text: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Bom dia, senhor capitão! Medeiros, ship-chandler, at your service. I saw your cutter come in with Pacheco this morning out of the fog, a fine little ship. English, yes? Welcome to São Miguel. You smell the oranges? The whole island smells of them in winter. Now it is the lupins and the tar, and the bread from the convent ovens, it being Sunday. You will want water, I think, after a long passage? I have two water boats and good casks, sweet water from the fountain under São Brás. Fresh beef, eggs, onions, wine of the island. And news, senhor, if you like news. Come, sit in the shade of my store, and we talk prices like Christians."

args.text: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Fouled before Finisterre, and you come all this way? Coitados, your poor men! Come, this way, mind the fish baskets. Here is my store: cordage, canvas, pitch, beef in the barrel and on the hoof, biscuit from the convent bakery. You give me the word for the water and the provisions, senhor, and my boats are alongside your cutter within the hour. And now the news, since you are for Horta: a French schooner, a black one, has been all this fortnight between here and Santa Maria. She took the catch of two of our boats off Vila Franca on Friday, and paid in French paper, which is to say she paid nothing. The Governor has written to Lisbon. Nobody here thinks Lisbon will answer."

args.text: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Nossa Senhora! Then the fog was your friend, and you should light a candle at São Sebastião before you sail. She will be watching the road from outside, I think. She knows a ship that waters here must sail again. If you go west for Fayal, go by night, and keep north of the island, under the land. The French do not like the north side: there is no shelter there for them, and our fishermen of Rabo de Peixe would see her and send word. That is advice from a chandler, senhor, not a sailor. You will judge."

args.note: 30 Jun 13:00: Medeiros's counsel: the Basque may watch the road from outside; leave by night and go west by the north side of São Miguel (Rabo de Peixe fishermen would see her). It is plausible advice, not a guarantee. The Basque's true station is off Santa Maria (SE); she does not know the cutter is here unless word reaches her. Keep her honest: a fishing boat could carry gossip either way. Leave her off St Lawrence unless the captain dawdles for days, or she has reason (gossip from Vila Franca boats) to look into the road. The north-side route also passes the 1720 mark more or less (it lies NW).

args.text: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Myself? Ah. Senhor, I am a chandler; I buy canvas to cut and sell again to every brig that comes in with her sails blown to rags, and they come in all summer. It is cheaper there at the source than here, a few pounds the ton; here you pay my carriage. If you go to Bettencourt, buy your wine at Horta."

args.text: say as Mr Terra: "Capitão, half the masters who come in here touch the Praia once — the wind comes down off the Guia in gusts and the ground there does not hold an anchor dragged across it. You did right to get the sail off her. She lies easy on soft sand, and the carpenter says she is dry; she is not hurt. Send your boat with the kedge out to the east, into the deep water, and heave it taut; my boat will go with yours. The flood serves from a quarter past two. By the half-tide she will feel it, and with the kedge's strain on her she comes off a little before the tide alone would lift her."

args.text: say as Mr Pascoe: "Three inches an' gaining slow, sir — that's her seams forrard, strained where she took it. Nothing to fear on sand. Three things, sir. Man the pump, a spell each glass, and she'll suck in ten minutes at this rate — keeps the water from getting at the bread. Then shift what we can aft — the cable tier, the shot, the spare spars off the forecastle — to ease her bow on the ground, an' she'll come off the easier. And when she's afloat the carpenter can get at the seams from inboard with oakum an' a mallet, or we fother a sail under her bow if she's bad; though I'd sooner have the Horta caulkers look at her bottom in the road. Say the word an' I'll have the watch at the pump directly."

Plan: Ruiz meets the boat at the quay (English-speaking clerk; "Senhor Bettencourt is still at the counting house; he has been expecting this a week"). args.text: say as Mr Hale: "*laughs, and pours the captain a glass from the jug* Slim, sir? They're bare to the bone. The whalers come in for water and go out again for the ground, the Lisbon packet won't call till August, and the Funchal brigantine is a week overdue and nobody will say why. args.text: say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he laughs softly and holds up a hand* Forgive an old man at midnight, Captain. Thirty-six pounds the ton is what the wine fetches at the lodge, not the freight; no merchant on God's earth pays that to carry it. args.text: say as Senhor Bettencourt: Good morning, Mr Pearce. *he waves the Madeira away with a smile* Let the captain bring it himself; it will taste better from his hand. Let her lie where she is: out there nobody on the quay can see what goes into her. Show no lights but one lantern hooded low at the gangway, and have your fall and slings rigged before they come; a pipe is half a ton and must go into the hold gently. Ruiz goes out in the first lighter with the bill of lading for the captain to sign, and forty pounds in gold for the freight. *he takes a sealed letter from the desk and holds it out* And this, for my son in Falmouth, into the captain's own hand, please. One more thing: Ruiz tells me a Frenchman was asking questions on the quay last night. Say nothing of wine or the hour of sailing to anyone, and if you go to the tavern for Mr Hale, drink little and listen much.

args.text: say as Mr Pascoe: Aye aye, sir. *he goes forward with Chips and comes aft again a quarter of an hour on* Carpenter's been down in the forepeak with a lantern, sir. Inside she's tight: the two strained seams by the forefoot that he stopped after the ground are holding, dry to the touch, and the well's at an inch and steady, as you saw. Outside's another thing. Looking over the bow in this clear water you can see a sheet of copper torn away on the forefoot, two foot by three, and the sheathing board under it scored where she lay on the rock. The worm will be into that bare plank by Madeira, and it slows her a little. He can't get at it afloat as she lies. If we heel her a strake or two, shifting the guns and the water to larboard and hauling down on a masthead tackle to a boat, he can nail a new sheet over it from the boat in a forenoon. He has two sheets of spare copper and the nails. Or the caulkers ashore will do it for three or four pounds, but that's more eyes on the ship, sir.

director.text: The brief given by the scenario: The Western Islands run (limits: no wind above 40 knots (force 8) by any system appended or moved; no enemy heavier than a brig put on the sea; nobody dies: nothing found aboard that would kill; the war as it is: no port closed to or opened to the ship's own nation; the chart as it is (a point of interest is not the chart); 9999 samples and 9999 acts a day).

Opening (05:00, 8 June, Carrick Road). Truth: wind W by S 12 kn, the glass 1012.6; low 3 (1004) 1,250 km to the W, low 2 (993) far to the N. A westerly is a foul wind for a SW passage: she will beat out of the Channel, which is honest and costs days from the stores already. Near traffic is only the business's fishermen and the two cruisers on their stations (Fly off the Black Rocks, Bayonnaise off Bas); the ocean beyond is empty and mine to people sparingly. Stations held: the captain (the player), the mate (a model). The mate is held, so I neither speak as Mr Pearce nor move him; Mr Pascoe the boatswain, the boy Oliver and the people at Horta are mine to voice. The plan, loose, to be bent by what the captain does: 1. The departure: let him go as he chooses. No act yet; the Channel's own westerly is the first test. 2. The Bay and the open sea (days 2-6): the weather by the systems as they are, a front from low 3 if it comes on its own. One ship at most, meaningful: a Portuguese brig homeward with news from Lisbon, somewhere past 45 N. 3. The stores (days 5-10): a cask or the leaguers when she has been labouring in a sea; the water foul after five days out; the bread damp after a week. Each only when the sea state allows it, never two at once. 4. The approach (days 8-12): the Azores high, light airs and a calm or two to lengthen the passage and make the short allowance a real choice; the lunars when the moon serves; Pico's peak as the landfall. 5. Fayal: Mr Ruiz on the quay to meet the boat; Senhor Bettencourt at the counting house for the letter (its contents never told); a stranger, Mr Hale, wanting a passage; the wine and the freight home by transactions only; a rumour of a French privateer among the islands. Nothing until there is a cause.
