Pearce's plan (SE to 37°30'N, then ESE ~118°) passes ~29 mi S of Santa Maria about 07-05 evening: a possible distant sighting, the Basque's own captain deciding. Leave it to the simulation; I intervene only to keep it inside the brief (schooner OK; nobody dies). The captain chose to keep south: reward caution, no contrived ambush.
Stood by until a watch.
Stood by until a watch.
Stood by until a watch.
Stood by until a watch.
Stood by until a watch.
The day's budget is renewed (1805-07-05): 9999 samples and 9999 acts.
Stood by until a watch.

06:45 (07-05). The truth: the track at 119° passes ~45-60 mi S of the Basque's station; no meeting likely. The caution is rewarded with a clean passage. Leave it so. Next interest: the landfall at Madeira (~07-08/09), Funchal: Bettencourt's son is in Falmouth, not Funchal, so Funchal is new ground: the wine sells at £110/t there (the captain's 4 t at £32 is a fine profit if he sells at Funchal rather than carry it to England at £70). Hale lands at Funchal.
Stood by until a watch.

06:45 (07-05). The captain is taking a break; Pearce stood down (the game saved). State: ~450 mi to Madeira, 119°, fair NNW wind, no threats; the Basque well north. Threads for later: the landfall and Funchal (wine £110/t there; Hale lands; Bettencourt's letter and the 20 t go on to Falmouth); the Frenchman/Porto Pim thread is dormant (the secret departure worked). Bugs for the lead are in TuningNotes "Open, for the lead".

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Director, standing down 06:45, 5 July 1806. The Sherbourne is bound from Horta for Funchal on 119°, about 450 miles to go, with a fair NNW breeze, carrying 24 tons of Pico wine (20 freighted for Bettencourt's son at Falmouth, 4 the captain's own, marked C). Mr Hale is aboard, his passage to Madeira paid. Bettencourt's sealed reply for Falmouth is in the captain's keeping. The purse stands at £842 15s; provisions 39 days, water 6.4 tons. She left Horta unseen in the fog. The Basque keeps her station off Santa Maria, well north of the track, so no meeting is expected. The Frenchman at Porto Pim is a dormant thread. Ahead: the landfall and Funchal, where wine fetches about £110 the ton and Hale lands. The brief stands: wind at most 40 kn, no enemy heavier than a brig, nobody dies, and the sealed letter's contents are never revealed. My journal holds the plans; bugs for the owner are in docs/dev/TuningNotes.md, "Open, for the lead".
Stood down by the director: its own word.

officer of the watch.text: Anchored Carrick Road, Falmouth, 05:00, morning watch 2 bells. Best bower down, 8½ fathoms where let go, veered to 43 (five times the depth). Fixed by cross bearings at 50°10' N, 5°02' W, good to a cable; account agrees within half a cable. Bearings: Trefusis Pt abeam to larboard ESE 3 cables; Trefusis Pt WNW 5 cables; Pendennis Pt SW½S a mile; Mylor Pt N by E a mile; Falmouth WSW a mile; St Anthony's Head SE½S two miles. Nearest land three cables to larboard. Tide: ebb making, a kn and a quarter to the S by W; high water Ramhead about 2 p.m. by the epitome (moon 11 days old, near springs, rise 15 ft). Dangers about: the Governor SSW 7 cables, Lugo rock SE½S 7 cables, Black Rock S 1½ miles. Deck: the captain's; sails all furled; 12 hands on deck, fresh. Glass 29.90, not yet watched an hour; fine weather, moderate sea.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

05:05, morning watch: the captain's word — checks of papers, provisions, water, hands, made and reported: water 4 tons (33.6 days), provisions 30 days for 30 men (we muster 27, so stretched), 12 tons canvas, room for 30, purse £180, all hands fresh. Nothing expended. Captain says we get under way for FAYAL if all is prepared. Deck still the captain's; sails furled, best bower down 43 fathoms, small bower and kedge at the bows. Note: Mr Ruiz and Senhor Bettencourt are ashore at Fayal (letter for Bettencourt in the master's keeping). Wind W by S 11 knots — fair on the quarter for a southern passage to Fayal. Standing by for the word.
Stood by until a word on deck.

05:11: the captain's word — the two ashore at Fayal are no men of ours, the business is private, and no names are to be spoken if an errant ear is about. Taken note of; I named them in my report, a fault of discretion — I'll speak of 'the correspondent at Fayal' only. Important cargo bound for Fayal. I confirmed stores sufficient and told him the hold allows 30 tons more and water could be topped by the boat; he will consider, morning is early. Anchor still down, 43 fathoms; wind W by S 11 knots, fair for Fayal on the port quarter if we go south. Standing by for the word to weigh.
Stood by until a word on deck.

05:13: captain demands a ton of water (£0 2s, alongside in 6 min) and 14 days provisions (£21, alongside in 42 min). Purse £180 -> £158 18s. He means to send the boat ashore for trade rumours — something cheap on the market. My part: receive and stow the stores, book them in the purser's books; have the boat ready. Ebb making in the Road, sets S by W — boat will find it on her beam to the town. Deck still the captain's. Anchor down, 43 fathoms best bower. Wind W by S 11 knots. Business private — speak no names.
Stood by until a word on deck.

05:18: boat away for the prices and news (captain's order), crew out. Water was due alongside ~05:18, provisions ~05:54 — I'll receive and stow, book in the purser's books. Notable: the Black Rock showing S, a mile — a danger. We ride at anchor so no risk; but the ebb sets S by W toward it, so when we weigh I'll recommend a berth west of it or waiting for the flood, and the lead going. Wind W by S 11 knots, glass 29.92 steady, fine. Deck still the captain's.
Stood by until a word on deck.

06:41, 5 bells morning watch: the owners' letter (Rogers and Son) read by the captain, his question — what say you of it. My answer: the season is fair — 54 days to the policy's end (1 Aug), Fayal is 8-9 days each way, so sail soon and there's a fortnight in hand. Stores ample (water 42 days, provisions 44 after this morning's casks). Wine bounded by the purse (£158 18s), not the hold (room for 30 tons more); if the canvas fetches well at Fayal the fund grows. Urged weighing on this ebb, W by W wind fair for a southing, standing west of the Black Rock and round St Anthony's Head. Discretion: no names before the hands. Provisions for 14 days stowed at 05:54, booked. Boat back alongside 06:39, hoisted in, at the booms; prices brought off (same list), quay talk: timber and coal dear at St Mary's — rumour only. Deck still the captain's.
Stood by until a word on deck.

06:43: the captain's plan for getting under way — get under way on the larboard tack, wear as she makes way, bear away S by E out of the sound. My working: loose main and topsail, heave short, cast and gather way on the larboard tack, wear (wind passes round the stern to the starboard quarter/beam) and settle S by E — a wear, not a tack, so no risk of missing stays; the ebb (a kn and a quarter, S by W) sweeps her south through it. Cautions I gave him: Trefusis land ESE two cables lies under her head mid-wear (lead going, Pascoe at the sheets); after the wear S by E passes east of the Black Rock — she draws 9 feet, lead tells the water. Stores complete: water 5 tons/42 days, provisions 44 days. Boat at the booms. Deck still the captain's; standing by for it to be given to work the evolution.
Stood by until a word on deck.

07:11, 6 bells: under way since 07:09, larboard tack, best bower catted and fished. Captain tack-ship: to come round to the starboard tack and steer S by E for the sound, Black Rock to starboard — instead of the wear he first spoke of. Helm a-lee, all hands (20 on deck). Watch points I gave him: Trefusis land right ahead 3 cables mid-tack (ebb sweeps her clear); if she misses stays, wear instead of trying twice; after paying off, S by E with Black Rock to starboard, lead going. Water 4½ fathoms at low water by chart at the position, low water about 8 a.m., then the flood makes. Pilot cutter standing out toward us under British colours — asked whether to hail her; no pilot wanted for Fayal, as I take it. Deck still the captain's.
Stood by until filled away.
Stood by until filled away.
Took the deck from the captain.

07:13 — I HAVE THE DECK. Captain's word with it: on the lead regularly, minding the land and the tideway; no pilot wanted. Ship state: larboard tack — no, starboard tack now after the tack at 07:11 (headed SW by S under way 3 kn, leeway settling from 42° to 3°). Sails: main, jib set; fore staysail ordered set by me; topsail was aback/shaking mid-tack, filling. Course to shape: S by E, Black Rock to starboard, out of the sound. Nearest land: Trefusis land 3 cables W by N (opening). Pilot cutter N a mile larboard bow, no need for her. Glass 29.91 falling a hundredth. Depth by chart at account: 8½ fathoms at low water; low water about 08:00, flood making after. My plan: lead every 10 min and every two fathoms of change after the first; watch the tideway; steer S by E when she has way on. Deck: MINE.

07:14: The tack is made, starboard tack, full and by, hands recovering. Captain keeps the conn himself out of the sound ("worry not on the conn for now, sir") — so I mind the lead, the land and the tideway, and do not steer. Standing order given: lead every ten minutes. My reckoning set: 50°10' N, 5°02' W, a cable E by N of the master's, kept beside it, to be said at noon. Course for the sound when the captain gives the word: S by E, Black Rock to starboard; low water about 08:00, flood making after — the tide turns under us and helps her out. Trefusis land three cables, opening. Watch: 27 on deck after all hands. Deck: MINE. Sails: topsail, main, jib set; fore staysail set at my order (it waited its turn).
Stood by until steady on the course.

07:15: standing order grammar learned — the mate may enter standing orders in his own rank; trigger forms: when/for/at/every; conditions are readings; after 'then' plain orders separated by ';' read at entry. Refusals learned: a standing order may not make a cry ('say X' is the captain's to say to a station); 'tell the officer' in a standing order is a station address = the captain's rank only. My alternatives in force: leadsman charged on deck (call each cast, under 5 fathoms loud), watch repeats to me; the captain may enter the 'lead warning' standing order himself if he wants it in the book. My standing orders live: 'lead every ten minutes'; my reckoning 50°10'N 5°02'W kept beside the master's. Deck: MINE (though the captain keeps the conn out of the sound for now). Course S by W gathering way 2-3 kn after the tack; depth by chart 10½ fathoms at low water; Trefusis land 3 cables abeam to starboard WNW, opening. Glass 29.92 steady.

Handover note (the watch so far): 07:15, morning watch. HAVE THE DECK since 07:13 (captain keeps the conn himself out of the sound, by his own word — I mind the lead, land and tideway and do not steer without his word; 'steer S by E' was refused to my rank as a course change). Got under way 07:09 larboard tack, tacked at 07:11, now starboard tack full and by, S by W 2-3 kn, all plain sail (topsail, main, jib set; fore staysail set at my order; light sails furled). Plan agreed with him: bear away to S by E for the sound on his word — I told him she is ripe and the Black Rock will be well to starboard of that course; low water about 08:00, flood making after, will help her out. My standing orders live: 'heave the lead every ten minutes'; leadsman charged on deck to call each cast aloud, under 5 fathoms loud enough to wake the master; my reckoning 50°10' N 5°02' W kept beside the master's (a cable E by N of it), to be said at noon. Standing-order grammar learned the hard way: my rank cannot enter 'tell the officer...' or 'say...' in a book; the captain may, if he wants 'lead warning' in the book — I offered him the exact form. The owners' letter: letter for a correspondent at Fayal in the master's keeping; policy void past 1 Aug — the season is good if we do not linger; business private, no names before the hands. Stores complete: water 5 tons/42 days, provisions 44 days. Glass 29.92 steady; fine; pilot cutter near, no need for her, captain's word. Watching: the lead, the land about Trefusis (3 cables, opening), the Black Rock (S, a mile and a half) when we bear away, the flood at 08:00.
Stood by until a word on deck.

07:17: 'Lead Warning' standing order — tried eight forms in my rank, all refused: 'tell the captain/watcher/master/lookout/officer/officer of the watch' — a standing order that addresses any station is the captain's rank only (he entered 'tell the officer...' himself at 07:16, and it stands); 'say...' refused (only the captain may say to a station); 'cry...' not an understood verb. Conclusion for the books: a cry on deck cannot be carried by the mate's standing order at all — the leadsman's voice is the working answer. The captain's 'Lead Warning' entry stands in the book (trigger: depth under 5 fathoms, tells the officer). Lead being heaved now.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 07:17, morning watch. Standing order 'Lead Warning' — my rank cannot enter it in any form; every 'tell the <station>' and 'say' is refused to a standing order from me; the captain's own entry stands in the book (07:16, 'when the depth is under 5 fathoms then tell the officer...'). Learned for the books. Ship's state: tacked and braced up starboard tack at S by E (169°), 3 kn, ebb half a knot, glass 29.93 rising; lead going in the chains. Black Rock a mile and a half to starboard of the course, Trefusis land opening on the larboard bow, Pendennis a mile SSW. Deck given back to the captain (he keeps the conn out of the sound). Watching: the lead's casts, the Black Rock as we stand down the sound, low water about 08:00 and the flood after.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Took the deck from the captain.
Stood by until a wind shift.

08:00, forenoon watch 8 bells, on watch. Course SE by S (146°), close hauled starboard tack, 6 kn, wind WSW 11 kn, glass 29.94 rising, fine. Clear of the harbour and the Old Wall (NW by N, 1½ miles) and the Black Rock (NW by N, 3 miles); nearest land St Anthony's Head astern, 2 miles. Captain conned the watch to 07:40 (fixes each few minutes, bore off twice to SSE then SE by S); I have the deck since 07:33, minding the sails. Dangers now all abeam or astern, the Manacles SW by S 4 miles next to mind as we make south. Run 5 miles since departure. Noon by the sun at 11:58. Lead cast on my order at 08:00 (last, 15 fathoms at 07:19). Standing order 'Lead Warning' in the book, never yet fired.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:10: topgallant set, yards braced up (54-58° from square), sheets trimmed — close hauled on the starboard tack, course SE by S/SE by E as she lies; wind WSW 10 kn, 6 kn; clear of all dangers, nearest land 3-4 miles; run 6 miles. Captain's correction on the record: the term is 'trim for close hauled' (my 'trim the sails' was accepted and did the same work). The Manacles SW by W 3½ miles next to mind as we stand south; low water past, flood making. Watching: the wind (WSW, might come up to W and let her luff), the glass (29.93 steady), noon sights at 11:58.
Stood by until a wind shift.

11:13, forenoon watch 6 bells: WIND SHIFTED — WSW by W to SW by W (hauled about a point since 08:10). Captain conned the forenoon: close hauled (08:11), full and by (08:16), gaff topsail set (08:21), S by E (08:22); fixes each hour moving the account, latest 10:43 (49°54'N 4°56'W, the account a mile out until it); come up half a point to S, braced sharp up, sheets trimmed. Now S (174°), close hauled starboard tack, wind 42° off the starboard bow, topgallant shaking — captain ordered the weather bowlines hauled at 11:08. Run 22 miles. Glass 29.97 rising, clear sky, fine. My own reckoning running 2½ miles SW of the master's — outside my trust; the master's fixes are the better figure. Noon by the sun 11:58 — no sight yet today. Lizard lights SW 4 leagues at 08:02, Black Head NW 3 leagues now: we are well down the coast. Dangers: none charted within 10 miles.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

Noon, 08 June: no sight — the sun hid in fog. By the master's account 49°47'N 4°56'W, run S by E 25 miles; my own reckoning 49°46'N 4°59'W, 2½ miles SW of his, within my trust. Fog came down 11:18, visibility a cable; I took in the topgallant and gaff topsail on my own word — plain sail only, ~4-5 kn, course S. No charted danger within 10 miles; no land in sight; lead going, no bottom. Glass 29.96, steady after rising; wind SW by W 10 kn. Flood making half a knot NE. Watching: the fog thickening or lifting, the lead, any sail or landfall from the lookout.
Stood by until a change in the sky.
Stood by until a change in the sky.

12:41: fog lifted — clear and fine, horizon again. Set the topgallant and main gaff topsail back on my own word. Course S (175°), ~4 kn, wind SW by W 10 kn, flood making NE ¾ kn, run since noon 3 miles. Glass 29.97. No land in sight, open water, no dangers within 10 miles. Watching: the wind and the weather; the captain on the quarterdeck.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

14:12: wind veered to W by N (mean W by S), 8-9 kn — on our starboard beam; the topgallant has been shaking, so I trimmed (yards braced up for the new wind, sheets hauled). Sky turned dark and gloomy, scud driving, squally, visibility down to a mile — watching for squalls and a further shift; 46 fathoms, no land in sight, no dangers within 10 miles. Run since noon 8 miles. Captain has been conned her all afternoon (come up a point, brace sharp up, quarter-point braces). Glass 30.01 rising.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a wind shift.

14:18: captain shaped the course for the Azores — 38°43'N 27°12'W, 1156 miles, full and by starboard tack; his standing order 'Hourly Shaping' in the book (every hour, shape the course for 38 43 N 27 12 W). Wind W by N 8 kn, close hauled, 4 kn, glass 30.02 rising. Earlier squally spell (dark, scud) has passed — clear again by the rollup? Watching: wind backing/veering for a fair wind to Horta; my reckoning run on hourly; the letter for Senhor Bettencourt in the master's keeping.
Stood by until a wind shift.

15:20, afternoon watch 6 bells: two squalls passed (14:58, 15:06 — wind veering a point to W by N, 12 and 16 kn, with rain; both passed to W 9 kn). Wind now W by S 9 kn, mean W 12; close hauled starboard tack on the Azores course (shaped for 38°43'N 27°12'W, full and by), 5 kn, course made good S by E. Glass 30.03 rising steadily, showers passing, hard-edged oily clouds. Run since noon 13 miles. No land in sight, no dangers. Captain's plan on record: full and by until wind forces us south (accepted) or backs through north or south and makes it fair. Watching: further squalls, the wind, the hourly shaping standing order.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until eight bells.
Stood by until eight bells.

Handover note (the watch so far): 16:00, first dog watch begins, 8 bells. Ship: close hauled on the starboard tack for the Azores (course shaped for 38°43'N 27°12'W by the captain's standing order 'Hourly Shaping', every hour), full and by — SW by W not layable, so she lies her closest. Wind W by S 8-9 kn, gentle; plain sail + topgallant + gaff topsail set; 4-5 kn; glass 30.03 rising; showers passed. Run since noon 16 miles; my reckoning 49°31'N 4°52'W, 2½ miles SW of the master's, within trust. No land, no dangers within 10 miles, 49 fathoms no bottom. Captain below in the cabin at 15:47, came up, told me his plan (full and by until wind forces south — accepted — or backs to fair). I have had a drink and a meal and am fresh. Squalls passed 14:58/15:06; more of the same kind may come — hard-edged clouds about. Watching: wind shifts toward fair, the hourly shaping, squalls.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 16:00, first dog watch, 8 bells. Deck given back to the captain for the dog watch. Ship as in my note: close hauled starboard tack for the Azores (38°43'N 27°12'W, the captain's 'Hourly Shaping' standing order active), full and by; wind W by S 8-9 kn, 4-5 kn; plain sail, topgallant and gaff topsail set; glass 30.03 rising; run since noon 16 miles; no land or dangers in sight; my reckoning 49°31'N 4°52'W, 2½ miles SW of the master's, within trust. I have eaten and drunk and will turn in below now, asleep until called, ready to take the deck when the master gives it. Watching when I wake: the wind for the fair wind he hopes for, the squalls from the hard-edged clouds, the hourly shaping.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

Woke rested 17:23, first dog watch 2 bells, off watch; the captain still has the deck. While I slept: a squall at 16:03 — wind veered a point to W, freshened to 11 knots with rain — passed 16:08, wind WSW 8 knots. Glass now 30.06, rising 6 hundredths in three hours; sky clear, weather fine, visibility to the horizon. She is standing SSE 154°, course made good SSE, run since noon 21 miles. The tide at slack water, the ebb to make. The moon twelve days old is up five degrees — too low for a lunar yet. The wind keeps in the west, so full and by on the starboard tack goes on; the hard-edged clouds have cleared and the squall was of the same kind as the last two. I turn in again asleep until called; when the master gives me the deck I will take the readings afresh and note whether he wants a lunar tried as the moon climbs.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

20:00, first watch 8 bells, change of the watch; still off watch, the captain has the deck. Wind WSW 7 kn, she stands SSE 154°, run since noon 34 miles; glass 30.10 and rising steady (now 4 hundredths in three hours); sky hazy, a smooth sea. The moon twelve days old is nineteen degrees up, in distance of Regulus: the readings say the moon serves — a lunar is to be had for the longitude for the first time this passage. When I next have the deck I will propose it to the captain, or take the sight if his word allows. Wind still westerly, so full and by goes on; the tide set by Ushant now in the almanac.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.
Stood by until a handover.
Took the deck from the captain.

21:22, first watch 2 bells. Took the deck from the captain for the night watch; he goes below once the lunar is worked. Lunar by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen: longitude 4° 54' W, trusted within 30 miles — reckoning was 4° 43' W, the account moved four cables W by S, no matter. Variation now 25° W by the sunset amplitude (was 21° 30' W by the 1794 chart) — allowed in the reckoning from now; my own reckoning 49° 07' N, 4° 45' W, 2 miles SW by S of the master's. Wind W, faded to 6 knots (8 at the dog watch); she stands S (180°), full and by starboard tack, the WSW course for the Azores not layable; glass 30.12 rising strongly, hazy, smooth sea, moonlit night — land made out at a league, none in sight, no danger within 10 miles. The captain's word by Mr Pascoe: square sail when the apparent may come abeam and course sou'westerly — apparent 57° on the bow, so it waits; hands handy. Tide allowance (ebb half a knot SW) holds till about a quarter past ten, then the Hourly Shaping takes it. Watching: the wind veering (W → W by N would bring the apparent near abeam and the square sail with it), any shift toward the fair wind he wants, the hourly shaping, the haze thickening. Pascoe looks for little wind before the forenoon.
Stood by until a wind shift.

21:25, first watch. The captain's word: mind the offing through the night — if speed increases while the course stays south or east of south and the wind holds westerly, we close the Breton shore; then wear to the larboard tack or get the course sou'westerly, by the reckoning even blind. He is below asleep until rested; wake him with 'tell the captain' only if something requires him. My plan for the watch: cast the lead on every hour with the shaping; keep my own reckoning run on; watch the wind for a veer (it would both lay the WSW course and open the offing) or a haul (it would square the wind more dead on the bow); square sail still waiting on the apparent abeam; wear in good time rather than late — she is slow (6 kn) and may miss stays. Glass 30.13 rising strongly. Next shaping due about 22:15.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the turn of the tide by the reckoning.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the square sail is set.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.

01:19, middle watch. Deep-sea lead by the captain's word (he belayed the hand lead): 56 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks; three fathoms of tide allowed — 53 on the chart; the account kept. First bottom this passage; the master's account confirmed. My own reckoning 48° 58' N, 4° 46' W, within two miles of his. She stands SW by W 232°, wind NW light (3-4 kn), all sail drawing, the square sail set since midnight and bowlines hauled on the captain's word. Glass 30.18-30.19, rising. Moon down to four degrees, no lunar. Watching: the Hourly Shaping at the next hour, the tide turning about high water at Ushant (a quarter past one) — after that the ebb gives us westing again.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the turn of the tide by the reckoning.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. Held the deck through the middle watch — the whole watch mine, the captain below but for one turn up at 02:43 when he ordered the sails trimmed; the yards braced three to the wind, 54-58° from square. Wind settled NW by N at 03:53, light breeze 5 kn; she stands SW by W 240°, all sail set, square sail drawing since midnight. Glass 30.21 rising (the small dip at 00:35 passed), clear after the haze, sunrise 03:55. Run since noon 54 miles but course made good only S 176° — the southing shows. Reckoning 48° 58' N, 4° 51' W; mine 48° 56' N, 4° 53' W, holding two miles SW of his. Deep-sea cast 01:19, 56 fathoms fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. The turn of the tide by the reckoning has not come; the flood allowance is down to a quarter knot NE. Watching: the Hourly Shaping hourly, the tide allowance turning, any shift toward the fair wind the captain wants (NW by N is near the fairest yet — the WSW course may nearly lay), the deep-sea lead by the captain's standing practice now.
Stood by until a glass.

04:30, morning watch 1 bell. The captain entered two standing orders at 04:02: 'trim on the course' (at steady on the course then trim the sails) and 'tend the sheets on the glass' (every glass, if not hove to, tend the sheets); 'trim on the course' fired 04:16, yards braced three to the wind, 54-58° from square. Wind hauled NNW 5 kn; she now stands WSW 246° — the Azores course nearly laid. Slack water, the ebb to make: the tide allowance's turn come at last after the flood's NE set all night. Run since noon 55 miles, course made good still S 177°. Glass steady at 30.21-22. My reckoning 48° 56' N, 4° 54' W. Watching: the standing orders' firing, the wind — if it steadies NNW-NW the fair wind the captain wants is here; the Hourly Shaping will shape WSW and she may lay it. The deep-sea lead now the practice; last cast 01:19.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until noon.
Stood by until a sounding.

08:14, forenoon watch. Deep-sea cast: 58 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept — the same ground as at 01:19, the shelf of the Channel confirming the reckoning. Run since noon 72 miles, course made good S by W 192° — the watch from 04:00 has given us the westing at last, W by S and WSW all through the forenoon, the wind N and N by W. She now stands W by S 254°, apparent 55-58° on the bow, 4-5 kn. The topgallant came in at 06:32 (shaking in the 52° close-hauled trim — would not draw) and hangs in the gear; it goes up again when she bears away or the wind frees. Glass 30.26 rising. My reckoning 48° 48' N, 5° 15' W, two miles SW by S of the master's. Next: noon sights at 11:57; if the wind backs further north and freshens, ask the captain whether to shake out more sail; the Hourly Shaping continues.
Stood by until noon.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until noon.

11:58, forenoon watch, noon. Day's work: lat by obs 48° 46' N (account was 48° 44' — the flood set us two miles NNE of allowed); course made good SSW, 86 miles; longitude by account 5° 34' W. My own reckoning had run to 48° 42' N, 5° 37' W, four miles outside my trust of the master's — set my slate to the noon fix: 48° 46' N, 5° 34' W. Lunar from last evening says 4° 54' W — some twenty miles east of the account; Mr Bowen will judge. Wind N 5-6 kn, apparent 81° on the bow, all sail set (topgallant re-set 10:30 by the captain's word, yards braced 53° then 46° from square); she stands SW by W, the Hourly Shaping steering WSW with the flood allowance. Glass 30.30 rising. Deep-sea cast 08:14: 58 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. Watching: the wind for the fair southerly the captain wants (a veer further east would lay the WSW course well), the flood's NE set holding us toward the shelf, soundings by the deep-sea lead.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 12:40, afternoon watch 1 bell. Deck given to the deck while I join the captain below in the gunroom for a bite and the chart. All quiet and well: all sail set and drawing, wind N by E 5-6 kn (veering easterly of north as the captain reads it), apparent 101-111° on the quarter abaft the beam, she stands SW by W; glass 30.29 steady; no land or dangers; deep-sea cast 08:14, 58 fathoms fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. Noon: lat by obs 48° 46' N, lon by account 5° 34' W, course made good SSW 86 miles; my slate set to the noon fix. The lunar of last evening (4° 54' W) is twenty miles east of the account — a matter for the master's judgment, on the table in the gunroom. Standing orders to be kept by whoever has the deck: 'Hourly Shaping' hourly for 38° 43' N 27° 12' W, 'trim on the course', 'tend the sheets on the glass'. Watching: the wind veering further east (the fair wind), the flood's NE set toward the shelf, and the topgallant drawing since 10:30.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a handover.

12:40, afternoon watch. Gone below to the gunroom with the captain for a bite and the chart; the deck with the deck, Mr Pascoe keeping it until we come up. My handover note is in the journal: all quiet, all sail set and drawing, wind N by E about the beam, glass 30.29; noon work — lat by obs 48° 46' N, lon by account 5° 34' W, SSW 86 miles since yesterday; the lunar of last evening twenty miles east of the account, for the master's judgment at the chart. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

12:41, afternoon watch. In the gunroom with the captain, over the whole chart. She sits 48° 46' N, 5° 34' W by the noon work; St Mary's NNW 25 leagues; the Azores course WSW, 1113 miles by the last shaping; the captain's pencilled aims and the fifty-mile circle about the islands on it; the lunar (4° 54' W) a shade east of the account's line, within doubt. Bite taken, chart gone over; my own reckoning stands at the noon fix.
Stood by until a handover.
Took the deck from the captain.

18:01, last dog watch 4 bells. Took the deck from the captain for the evening; he remains above until he wants rest, then below. Since noon (spent in the gunroom with him over the chart, a bite together): the wind has gone NNE and freshened to 6 kn, the yards nearly square (18-31° from square through the afternoon), she stands WSW 247°, course made good WSW 243°, 18 miles since noon; the ebb allowed SW three quarters. Run since noon 18 miles — the fair wind come at last, everything drawing, topgallant set. Glass 30.34 rising steadily. Reckoning 48° 38' N, 5° 58' W; my slate matches, two cables NE of his. Moon 13 days old, just up, one degree. St Mary's N by W 26 leagues. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (last 17:15, next 18:15), trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching: the wind for further veering east, the tide turn about 23:00, soundings (63½ fathoms by account, the last cast nine hours old — deep-sea cast when the shaping falls due), the topgallant set since 10:30 drawing.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Allowed by the captain: take a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.

21:46, first watch 3 bells. Lunar by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen (my request, his word): longitude by lunar 5° 29' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 6° 22' W — the master moved his account three leagues to the east, now 48° 31' N, 6° 08' W. My own slate (from the noon fix 5° 34' W, run on by the log-board) stands 48° 30' N, 6° 22' W, three leagues west of his corrected account, at the edge of my trust of it. I keep my slate uncorrected for an independent check and will speak of it at noon; the lunar and the account disagree by some 35-40 miles, both within the lunar's doubt. Also this watch: at 21:11 the sails lifted — wind came forward to N by E while the yards stood free; braced the yards in (54-58° from square) and the standing order re-braced at 21:16. She now sails free again, apparent on the beam, WSW 251°, made good SW by W, 35 miles since noon. Glass 30.35 steady. Moon 19° up, still in distance of Regulus — another set tonight would narrow the longitude. The tide turn by the reckoning due about 23:00.
Stood by until the turn of the tide by the reckoning.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

22:58, first watch 5 bells. The captain below to sleep until at least sunrise; I hold the deck through the night. All steady: wind NNE 8 kn, apparent on the quarter, she stands WSW 248°, all sail drawing, made good SW by W, 40 miles since noon. Glass 30.36, steady-to-rising. Tide: slack water, the flood to make — the turn of the master's tide came at 22:48; the flood will set NE and push us up toward the shelf through the night; soundings by the deep-sea lead as the shaping falls due. The moon in distance of Altair now (18° up); a second lunar this night would narrow the longitude — I may propose one when the moon is high enough and Mr Bowen sleeps, so it waits for his waking, or I take it if the master's word covers it (it was his word that allowed the last). Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. My slate: 48° 28' N, 6° 28' W, three leagues W of his corrected account (lunar 5° 29' W). Watching: the flood's NE set, any wind shift, the yards at each shaping (the sails lifted once at 21:11 when the wind came forward — braced in), the captain asleep till sunrise.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.
Stood by until a sounding.

00:12, middle watch. Deep-sea cast: 76 fathoms, grey sand and ooze; two and a half fathoms of tide allowed — 73½ on the chart; the account kept. The ground has changed character (fine grey sand with black specks → grey sand and ooze) as we run off the shelf south-westward; depth increasing on schedule. Middle watch begun, 8 bells struck, the watches changed; the captain asleep below until at least sunrise, the deck mine. All sail drawing on WSW, wind NNE about the quarter, 3-4 kn. The flood now three quarters of a knot to the NE — it will set us up toward the shelf through the small hours; soundings hourly as the shaping falls due. Glass 30.35 steady. Noon by the sun at 12:04. Watching: the flood's set, the wind, the noon sights.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.
Stood by until sunrise.
Stood by until sunrise.

04:04, morning watch. Sunrise; I have held the deck the whole night through (first and middle watches), the captain asleep below since 22:58, to wake at least at sunrise. The night quiet and honest: wind settled NNE-NE by N 6-7 kn, all sail drawing, the yards square (0° from square) and she standing SW by W 238° with the apparent well on the quarter; made good SW by W through the small hours, 54 miles since noon. Glass 30.36-30.37, steady through the night, hazy, a smooth sea. Soundings kept: 00:12, 76 fathoms grey sand and ooze (account kept); 01:25, 70 fathoms; 03:09, 69 fathoms — the ground character changed from the fine grey sand with black specks of the outer shelf to ooze as we come off it. My slate 48° 23' N, 6° 47' W, three leagues W of the master's corrected account (lunar 5° 29' W) — the disagreement holds, for his judgment at noon. Flood allowance fading (three quarters of a knot NE), the tide's last grip on us before the ebb. Watching: the captain waking (or his calling), the hourly shapings and trims, the noon sights, whether the wind backs to lay the course or freshens.

04:04, morning watch, sunrise — the night watch held whole, the captain below since 22:58. Summary of the night: wind settled NNE-NE by N, 6-7 kn, all sail drawing (yards square), she standing SW by W 238° most of the night, made good SW by W; 54 miles since noon; glass steady 30.35-30.37, hazy then clear, a smooth sea, easy. Soundings (deep-sea lead, each the account kept): 00:12, 76 fathoms, grey sand and ooze; 01:25, 70 fathoms; 03:09, 69 fathoms — the bottom character changed from fine grey sand with black specks (the outer shelf) to grey sand and ooze as we ran off the shelf. Flood allowance faded to three quarters of a knot NE by 04:00; high water at Ushant reckoned about 02:00, so the ebb follows and will give us westing. My slate 48° 23' N, 6° 47' W, three leagues west of the master's corrected account; his lunar (5° 29' W) says the account stands some 35 miles east of mine — both within its doubt, for his judgment at noon. Noon by the sun 12:04. Wind by NNE and the apparent on the quarter — the fair wind the captain wanted is here and steady. Watching: his waking, the Hourly Shaping (last 03:55?), the noon work, and any shift that puts the wind forward again — the sails lifted once last evening when it came forward.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sail made out.

06:30, morning watch 5 bells. Stranger made out: a brig on the starboard quarter, bearing N, four miles, standing SW by S under plain sail, no colours yet; first seen 05:08 abeam to starboard N by W six miles, hull below the horizon; the captain has been in the tops since 05:40 with the glass and made her out. She works to the south'ard and so will close or cross us; we stand WSW 250°, 3 kn. I keep her logged at every change; nothing to alter for, in my judgment — she may be a trader out of the Channel; keep watch on her colours and her course, and hail the captain of every change as a lieutenant of 1806 would. Also: the captain said I might rest when he takes the deck; I am a little drowsy after the whole night, and will stand easy when he relieves me — but not until he does, the deck is mine while he is aloft. The ebb now a knot to the SW; run since noon 62 miles. Noon by the sun 12:04.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a stranger's colours made out.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 08:00, forenoon watch, 8 bells. Deck given to the captain; I am drowsy after holding the whole night and go below to sleep. What he takes: all sail set and drawing on WSW 253°, wind NNE 8 kn, apparent 102° on the quarter, 4 kn; glass 30.36 steady; no land, deep-sea cast 03:09, 69 fathoms grey sand and ooze, the account kept; the ebb a knot and a half to the SW. The stranger: a brig on the starboard quarter, bearing NE, three miles, standing SW by S under plain sail, no colours yet — first seen 05:08; she has worked round from N to NE as we have gone off to the westward; I judge her a trader, to be watched, nothing to alter for. My reckoning 48° 16' N, 7° 05' W, three leagues W of the master's (his lunar 5° 29' W); noon by the sun 12:04, and the longitude question is his to judge at the noon work. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (last 07:15), trim on the course (last 07:17), tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching for me asleep: the brig's colours or course change, any wind shift, the noon sights — wake me for anything beyond the book.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

Woke rested 12:47, afternoon watch 1 bell, off watch; the captain has the deck. What came while I slept: the noon work — lat by obs 48° 13' N, lon by account 7° 08' W, course made good SW by W 82 miles. My own slate ran to 48° 10' N, 7° 24' W, three leagues W of his before the sight, and the observation puts me four miles N of his: I set my slate to the noon fix again (48° 13' N, 7° 08' W) and will speak of the longitude at the next noon. The brig (first seen 05:08 from the northward) has worked round on our larboard quarter, SE by E, two leagues, still standing SW by S under plain sail — we have crossed her track or she has crossed ours; no colours made out. The captain held the deck the forenoon; the standing orders kept their rounds; wind NE 6 kn, she stands WSW 244°, all sail drawing; glass 30.35, first fall in two days — worth watching. I turn in again asleep until called; when I take the deck I will read the glass's fall first of all.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

14:09, afternoon watch 4 bells. Took the deck from the captain (he below at the chart). Ship: all sail set and drawing, WSW 244°, wind NE by E 7 kn on the quarter, 3½ kn, glass 30.35 (fell 2 hundredths through the forenoon, now steady), clear, smooth sea, no land, no danger. Brig on the larboard quarter SE by E three leagues, standing SW by S, dropping astern — a passing trader, to be watched, nothing to alter for. Noon (12:05): lat by obs 48° 13' N (account 3½ miles S of it), lon by account 7° 08' W, made good SW by W 82 miles; my slate reset to the noon fix. The longitude question stands: account 7° 08' vs lunar 5° 29' W, near two degrees apart, both within the lunar's doubt; I proposed a second lunar at moonrise and the captain has gone to the chart — his word will come. The moon thirteen days old, down now, rises toward evening; when she is in distance of Regulus I will take the set if his word allows (it did last evening). My reckoning from the fix now 48° 07' N, 7° 32' W, four leagues W by S of his — the same leaning; watch it at the next noon. Watching: the glass (first fall in two days), the moonrise for the lunar, the brig astern, the Hourly Shaping.
Took the deck from the captain.
Stood by until a lunar.
Allowed by the captain: take a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.

16:00, first dog watch 8 bells. Still have the deck; the captain below since 14:10 at the chart, then to rest. The afternoon watch passed quiet: all sail set and drawing, WSW 244-245°, wind NE by E 6-7 kn well abaft the beam, 3 kn, glass 30.35 steady after the small forenoon fall. Run since noon 13 miles, made good WSW 245°. The brig has dropped out of sight astern — she stood on SW by S and we drew away from her to the westward; no colours ever made out, a passing trader. My slate from the noon fix: 48° 04' N, 7° 41' W, four leagues W by S of the master's account; his lunar 5° 29' W still stands against the account 7° 25' W — the moon is not yet up; the second lunar awaits her. Deep-sea cast due (last 03:09); the ground grey sand and ooze, 91 fathoms by account, coming off the shelf apace. Watching: the glass's tendency (it fell a hundredth in the forenoon, then steadied — the falling fast is not here), the moonrise for the lunar, the hourly shapings and trims, the deep-sea lead.
Stood by until a sounding.

16:13, first dog watch. Deep-sea cast: 91 fathoms, soft ooze; two and a half fathoms of tide allowed — 88½ on the chart; the account moved six cables to the east on it — the cast is confirmation the account ran too far west, and it bears out my suspicion since yesterday's noon: the longitude account has been running west of the truth, the lunar's 5° 29' W the nearer of the two. My own slate (7° 42' W) stands four leagues west of the master's and outside my trust; the soundings will settle it as the ooze deepens off the shelf. The bottom is now soft ooze — off the bank altogether. She runs WSW 244°, all sail drawing, 14 miles since noon, glass 30.35 steady. The moon rises toward evening; the second lunar when she comes into distance of Regulus, by the captain's word given at 14:10.
Stood by until a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.

20:00, first watch 8 bells. The moon is seven degrees up and fourteen days old — not yet fit for the lunar; by her rate of climbing she should be in distance within the hour or two, and I hold the deck for the set. The glass has now fallen 3 hundredths in three hours (30.32) — a real fall begins, after two days of rise; watch it against the standing orders, though no wind follows yet (NE by E 6 kn, all quiet, a smooth sea). She runs WSW 244-245°, made good the same, 25 miles since noon. The captain on deck as the watch changed; he asked for my estimate of the lunar's hour (I said about eight to half past, well placed by nine) and took an azimuth at 17:58 — variation now 24° W by azimuth, against 25° W by the amplitude of the 8th; he allows it from now. My slate: 47° 59' N, 7° 58' W, still four leagues west of his account and outside my trust of it; the soundings (91 fathoms soft ooze at 16:13, the account moved east six cables) keep saying the same. The moonrise lunar will settle between the two.
Stood by until a lunar.

23:16, first watch 6 bells. The second lunar is taken and cleared: Spica and the moon by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen — longitude by lunar 7° 44' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 7° 51' W, so the account moved seven cables E by N. This confirms the pattern: the first lunar (5° 29' W) and the account (7° 08' W then) disagreed by two degrees; this second lunar agrees with the present account within a mile — the master's tide-work is close tonight. My own slate (47° 56' N, 8° 08' W) now stands four leagues W by S of his and outside my trust of it: the divergence began at yesterday's noon and has grown; I mean to work my reckoning afresh from this evening's fix and speak to the captain at his waking — the two slates must be brought together or the difference owned. Also: the glass has fallen through the evening, 30.32 → 30.31, 2 hundredths in three hours — slow, but three hours of fall after two days of rise; the first watch has been quiet (wind NE 5 kn, all square, WSW 244°, 33 miles since noon). The captain took a lunar at 22:00 (his own order), the distances cleared by 23:16. Watching: the glass's further fall, my reckoning work-up, the captain's waking.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

00:16, middle watch 8 bells. Still hold the deck, the second night running. The first watch passed quiet: wind NE 5-6 kn, all sail set, yards square, she runs WSW 244-245° with the wind nearly dead astern (168° astern at 23:46 — the square sail and the gaff topsail doing the work); 35 miles since noon; glass fallen to 30.30-30.31 — three hours' fall then steady, no wind to speak of following it; a smooth sea. Soundings not taken since 16:13 (91 fathoms soft ooze); the account now 126 fathoms by chart — well off the shelf, into the deep water west of Ushant. The lunar of Spica (7° 44' W) confirms the master's account; my slate (8° 11' W, four leagues W by S outside my trust) diverges — I will work it up at noon from the fix and the log, and speak plainly to the captain of it. The captain on deck at the watch change; all hands fresh. Watching: the glass (if it falls fast, the standing orders wake me), the wind for any hauling forward, the noon work and the reckoning to be squared.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until sunrise.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. The middle watch held whole and quiet, the captain asleep below since 01:17 until sunrise. The night so far: wind NE-NE by E 5-6 kn nearly dead astern (168° astern), all sail set, yards square, she runs WSW 243-245°, 44 miles since noon; made good WSW. Glass fallen through the night, 30.30 → 30.27, about a hundredth the hour, steadily — the first settled fall of the passage; no wind to follow yet, a smooth sea, sky hazy. Depth by account 390 fathoms — we are off the shelf altogether, into the deep water west of Ushant; the deep-sea cast last taken 16:13 (91 fathoms soft ooze); with no bottom to be found at the lead's length now, soundings cease to confirm the account and the lunar must carry the longitude. My slate 47° 51' N, 8° 23' W, four leagues W by S of the master's and now within my trust again; the lunar of Spica (7° 44' W) is the truth to work from, and I will square my reckoning at noon from the fix. The moon is full tonight (fourteen days old) and down now; she rises toward evening in the first watch. Watching: the captain's waking at sunrise, the glass's fall (any hurry in it and the standing orders serve), the wind for hauling forward (then the yards), the noon sights.
Stood by until sunrise.
Stood by until a glass.

04:42, morning watch 1 bell. The glass has fallen fast: 7 hundredths in three hours, to 30.23, 4 hundredths in the last hour alone. The wind has hauled from NE through N round to E by S, light and variable airs, 3 knots, she has slowed to 2 kn, all sail still set. I sent the word below to the captain (he sleeps until sunrise, at his own asking; the glass falling fast and the wind round to the eastward are the kind of thing a lieutenant tells the master of). Depth by account 527 fathoms — well off the shelf, the lead's length will not find bottom. My slate 47° 50' N, 8° 25' W. Watching: squalls out of the east as the glass falls (the last three squalls came on a rising glass in westerly air — this is new weather), the yards for the wind coming forward of the beam, the captain's waking at sunrise.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.

08:00, forenoon watch 8 bells. Staying up till noon by the captain's word; I have eaten and am awake enough. The morning watch: the wind has hauled round the whole way — NE at midnight, E by S at 04:19, settled ESE by 05:25 and 07:39, now SE by E a light breeze 4 kn, gusty and variable; the yards braced up by degrees (11°, 26°, 41° from square) as it came forward. She now stands close hauled on the larboard tack, WSW, apparent 75° on the larboard bow. The glass has fallen all morning: 30.27 → 30.20, a hundredth the hour; the squall the falling glass foreboded has not come — the winds are all light airs and gusts. Depth by account 767 fathoms; the lead's length is useless now, we are in deep water. Run since noon 52 miles. My slate 47° 47' N, 8° 34' W, four leagues W by S of his. Noon by the sun at 12:10; the captain means me to see the noon sights. Watching: the wind's further haul to south (it would put the Azores course to leeward and square the problem), the gusts for a real squall (the captain's word: square sail and topgallant come in first, and only for a real squall), the glass.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until noon.

12:11, afternoon watch, noon. Day's work: lat by obs 47° 49' N (account was 47° 46', moved 2½ miles NE); course made good since yesterday WSW, 62 miles; longitude by account 8° 27' W — no tide in the day's work, the directions give none for these waters. My own slate had run to 47° 43' N, 8° 47' W, five leagues WSW of his and outside my trust: set my reckoning to the noon fix, 47° 49' N, 8° 27' W. The pattern of the last three noons (the account north of the observation by 2-4 miles) is broken today — the account lies south of the observation; with no tide to allow and deep water, the longitude now rests on the log alone, and the lunar of Spica (7° 44' W, taken 23:16) stands 43 miles east of the account — within its doubt, but it has leaned east twice now. Also: at 12:01 I took in the topgallant — shaking in the 53° close-hauled trim as the wind settled SE. The wind has worked SE by S through the forenoon, gusty and variable, glass down to 30.17 and steady the last hour; the squall never came. She is close hauled larboard tack on the WSW course, plain sail and square sail and gaff topsail, 3-4 kn. Staying up till noon done as asked; I'll ask the captain for rest when the forenoon's work is squared.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a handover.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 12:41, afternoon watch 1 bell. Deck given back to the captain; I go below to rest by his word. What he takes: all sail set but the topgallant (came in 12:01, shaking in the 53° close-hauled trim), plain sail + square sail + main gaff topsail, close hauled on the larboard tack, WSW 243°, wind SE-SSE 4 kn gusty and variable, apparent 59° on the larboard bow, 3-4 kn; glass 30.16 falling a hundredth the hour (the squall it threatened has not come), clear, smooth sea, no land, no danger, deep water (1254 fathoms by account — the lead is useless now, soundings cease). Noon: lat by obs 47° 49' N, lon by account 8° 27' W, made good WSW 62 miles; no tide in the day's work. Lunar of Spica (23:16 last night) 7° 44' W, 43 miles east of the account, within its doubt — the longitude leans east at both lunars. My slate set to the noon fix, a mile N by W of his. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching: the wind for hauling further south (the course would come to leeward), the gusts for a real squall (square sail and topgallant first, by his word of the morning), the glass's fall.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

15:42, afternoon watch 7 bells. Woke rested, off watch; the captain has the deck. While I slept: the wind has settled SE by S, still close hauled on the larboard tack (W made good SW by W 241°), the glass has fallen on — 30.16 → 30.12, 2 hundredths the last hour, the sky gone overcast: the weather the falling glass promised is gathering at last, though no squall yet. Run since noon 9 miles. My slate 47° 44' N, 8° 39' W, a mile N by W of his. The moon is full (14 days old) but the sky thick — no lunar tonight if this holds. I stay on the quarterdeck awake and easy; when the captain gives me the deck I take the readings afresh and mind the glass first of all.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

18:00, last dog watch 4 bells, change of the watch. Still off watch, the captain has the deck. The afternoon's news: the wind has backed SSE (from SE), still close hauled larboard tack, and the captain set the topgallant again at 16:04 — all sail now. The weather has thickened to drizzle, the sky overcast, the glass fallen to 30.10 — 4 hundredths in three hours, the fall steady and gaining pace; the moon full but the sky thick, so no lunar tonight. Depth by account 2066 fathoms — far into the deep water. Run since noon 14 miles, made good WSW 242°. My slate 47° 42' N, 8° 46' W, a mile N by W of his. Watching when I have the deck: the glass's fall (if it hurries, the standing orders and my own judgment serve — the squall the glass has promised all day may yet come out of the south-east), the wind for hauling further south or freshening, the topgallant and square sail for the gusts. I remain off watch until the captain gives me the deck; the dog watches are his.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Took the deck from the captain.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Nothing given over — the handover note stands as written in the journal at 18:00, last dog watch 4 bells: still off watch, the captain has the deck; the wind SSE close hauled larboard tack, all sail set, drizzle, the glass 30.10 fallen 4 hundredths in three hours, run since noon 14 miles made good WSW 242°, my slate 47° 42' N, 8° 46' W a mile N by W of his, no land no danger, the deep water 2063 fathoms.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

18:08, last dog watch. Took the deck from the captain. She: close hauled larboard tack, WSW ~242°, wind SSE 3-4 kn gusty, apparent 61° on the larboard bow, 2¼ kn, all sail set (topgallant re-set 16:04), drizzle, glass 30.10-30.11 fallen 3-4 hundredths in three hours, deep water 2063 fathoms (no sounding possible), no land, no danger. Run since noon 14 miles made good WSW. My slate 47° 42' N, 8° 46' W, a mile N by W of his; his lunar of Spica 7° 44' W stands 43 miles east of the account, the second lunar to lean east. Moon full, sky thick — no lunar tonight unless it clears. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (next ~18:15), trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. The captain's word for squalls: watch the gusts, square sail and topgallant come in first for a real squall, not for little gusts. Watching: the glass's fall (a hurry in it wakes the book), the wind for hauling further south (the course to leeward worsens) or freshening, the topgallant and square sail at the gusts, the moon for a clearing sky.
Stood by until a glass.
Took the deck from the captain.
Stood by until a glass.

18:33, last dog watch 1 bell. The captain's order for the watch: when the topgallant shakes, try 'brace the topgallant up half a point' before taking her in. Noted and will keep it. The watch so far: the Hourly Shaping fired 18:15, steer WSW 243°; the yards braced 54-58° from square and the sheets trimmed to 29-32° off the centreline; all sail set and drawing on 3 kn of NE-by-E-of-us SSE air. Glass 30.11 steady the last hour after the morning's fall; drizzle, a smooth sea. Run since noon 15 miles. My slate 47° 42' N, 8° 47' W, a mile N by W of his. Watching: the gusts for the squall (square sail and topgallant first), the topgallant for shaking (brace her up half a point first), the moon for a clearing sky and the lunar.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

20:00, first watch 8 bells. Still hold the deck (evening watch mine since 18:09). The evening: wind backed further to S by E, gusts 3-4 kn, close hauled larboard tack, WSW 243°; the topgallant shook and I braced the topgallant yard up half a point at 19:03 by the captain's standing instruction — drew again; but now the topsail and the topgallant both shake in the variable airs, apparent 48° on the bow, and the standing orders have braced the yards sharp (54-58°) each half hour against it. Glass fallen to 30.08, 4 hundredths in three hours, the fall quickening; drizzle, overcast, deep water 2133 fathoms. The moon full but thick. Run since noon 18 miles made good WSW 244°; my slate 47° 41' N, 8° 51' W. The captain prefers more canvas out in light airs, drawing with a light touch — so the topsails are kept on and worked, not handed, while they may be made to draw. Watching: the gusts (a real squall takes the square sail and topgallant first), the shaking canvas (brace up before handing, the captain's rule), the glass's fall, the moon for the lunar if the sky breaks.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

21:30, first watch 3 bells. Holding the deck. The wind has hauled to S by E (settled 20:53), still gusty, she now stands W by S 258° — the Hourly Shaping has found the course layable at last, close hauled larboard tack, and made good is WSW 245°, so she is footing to the westward on the Azores course. The square sail shakes in the gusts (the captain braced the yards sharp up at 20:00 and belayed his standing order 'trim on the course' at 20:02, leaving the trim to the tend-sheets order and the helm); the topgallant shakes too. Glass 30.07, fallen 3 hundredths in three hours and 2 the last hour — the fall continues quickening but no squall yet, the drizzle ceased, fine. Leeway 3-4°. Run since noon 21 miles. My slate 47° 40' N, 8° 55' W. The moon up ten degrees behind the cloud, thick sky — no lunar. Watching: the shaking square sail and topgallant (brace up before handing — the captain's rule), the gusts for the real squall, the glass's fall, the moon for the sky breaking.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells, the change of the watch. I hold the deck — evening watch and first watch both mine. The night's run: wind backed slowly through S by E to S, 3-5 kn gusty and variable, she now stands W by N 280° close hauled on the larboard tack, made good W by S 253°; the Hourly Shaping has brought her round from the close-hauled W by S to W by N as the wind freed and backed — the course is now laid with the wind south. 30 miles since noon. Glass 30.05, steady the last hour, the fall slower through the night (2 hundredths in three) — no squall come yet, overcast and fine, a smooth sea. Leeway 2-4°. My slate 47° 41' N, 9° 08' W, a mile N by W of his. The moon full and up seventeen degrees behind the cloud — no lunar while the sky is thick. The captain on the quarterdeck. Watching: the gusts for a real squall (the glass still falling slowly), the wind for hauling further east (it would free the course) or freshening, the square sail and topgallant in the variables (brace up before handing — the captain's rule), noon by the sun at 12:15.
Stood by until a glass.

Ordered on my own word, to avoid an immediate danger (she is taken aback, all sails backed and shaking, and losing her way): helm a lee.
Stood by until a word on deck.

Stood by until a sail shaking.

Noon, afternoon watch 8 bells. The forenoon held to the captain's orders: yards braced sharp up when the wind came forward (square sail yard 58°, topsail 64°, topgallant 66° from square) and the sheets trimmed by turns — short handed, all sails drawing after, no canvas handed. Two squalls in the forenoon (10:59, 11:13), both passed, wind SW by W then SW, gusts to 10 kn. The wind then backed to SW by S. Noon readings: SSE 160°, 3 kn, apparent 39° on the starboard bow, glass 30.01 steady (fell to 29.95 then steadied), run since noon 73 miles made good W by S 260°, reckonings within a mile (mine 47° 38' N 9° 54' W). Deep water 2314 f. Noon sights next.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a sail shaking.
Stood by until a wind shift.

12:54, afternoon watch 1 bell. The ship tacked at 12:18 (all hands, captain's evolution) — now larboard tack, heading W 272°, full and by; wind SSW 9 kn, apparent 41° on the larboard bow. Noon: lat by obs 47° 35' N (account hit it, moved five cables SSW); lon by account 9° 54' W; course made good W by S, 74 miles; my own reckoning 47° 38' N 9° 58' W, mile and a half N of the master's. A squall 12:41 passed 12:45, wind SW 10 kn. Glass 29.95 falling slowly, deep water 2313½ f. The topgallant still just shaking, the helmsman bearing off as she shakes — the captain's standing method. Watching: the wind for hauling or backing, the shaking sails, the glass.
Stood by until a wind shift.

14:41, afternoon watch 5 bells. Holding the deck, larboard tack full and by. The afternoon: two squalls (12:55 veered 2 pts to SW 13 kn with rain; passed 12:59, wind SW by S 10 kn), wind then backed SW by S. She now stands W by S 260°, 4 kn, apparent 41° on the larboard bow — the topgallant kept just shaking by the helmsman bearing off, the captain's method. Glass 29.93, fallen 2 hundredths in the last hour after steadying — watching it. Run since noon 11 miles made good W by N 285°. I have eaten (biscuit and cheese, first food since 08:00 yesterday). Watching: the glass's fall, the squalls, the wind for hauling south, the shaking sails.
Stood by until a squall.

16:00, first dog watch 8 bells. Holding the deck since 12:55. Larboard tack, full and by: she stands W by N 282° made good, 3 kn by the log, wind SW by S 8 kn gusty, apparent 40° on the larboard bow. The topsail and topgallant just shaking — the captain's standing method: while full and by let them shake, the helmsman bears off as they do. Glass 29.94, fallen steadily through the afternoon to steady — near 2 hundredths down since noon. Run since noon 16 miles. I have eaten (14:42). Watching: the wind for hauling south, the glass's fall, the squalls, the sails not coming to more than shaking.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a wind shift.

20:00, first watch 8 bells. Holding the deck since 12:55, the captain on the quarterdeck with me (he furl'd the square sail himself at 19:45-48 — it is furled now, not in the gear; the yards braced sharp up at 19:00-01: square sail 58°, topsail 64°, topgallant 66° from square; the topgallant taken in and reset 19:04-09, still just shaking — the captain's method holds). She stands W by N 281°, 5 kn, wind SW by S 10 kn gusty, apparent 41° on the larboard bow, heel 4°, sea getting up moderately, glass 29.95 (risen 2 hundredths in the last hour after the day's fall), run since noon 35 miles made good W by N 283°. Moon full but not risen; no lunar possible. Watching: the wind for hauling south, the shaking sails, the glass, the sea.
Stood by until a wind shift.

21:00, first watch 2 bells. Holding the deck; the captain on the quarterdeck. Wind freshened to 11 kn (gusts higher), still SW by S; she stands W 274° made good, heel 5° — a shade over press'd for the trim. Sunset 20:19; moon full risen one degree — too low for the lunar yet. Glass 29.97, risen 4 hundredths in three hours, rising again — the day's fall is gone. Sea moderate. Watching: the wind for freshening further (heel and shaking sails), the moon for the lunar distance, the glass.
Stood by until a wind shift.

21:16, first watch. Wind backed a point to SW at 10 kn; the captain has squared her away to WNW 287°. It is night, the full moon just two degrees up. The glass steady at +5 in three hours. Nothing to be done at this hour; the captain holds the deck and I say on. Watching: the moon climbing toward the lunar distance, the wind, the glass.
Stood by until a wind shift.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells. Still on deck with the captain since 12:55 yesterday — a long pull, but the sea is easy and the watches quiet. The wind got up through the first watch: mean 13 kn now, gusts to 17; she stands WNW 289° at 6 kn, heel 7° — a good deal over the trim, and the captain's 15-knot square sail rule nears (true mean 13, gusts 17). Glass 30.02, risen from 29.93 to 30.03 through the night, a hundredth down in the last hour. Run since noon 57 miles made good W by N 286°; reckoning 47° 50' N 11° 15' W, my slate a mile and a half N by W of the master's. A lunar was taken by Mr Bowen two days ago — Spica — giving 7° 44' W, trusted within 30 miles; the moon now sixteen days old and sixteen degrees up, in distance of Altair. Watching: the wind's rise toward the square sail, the glass, the moon.
Stood by until a wind shift.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 03:48, middle watch 7 bells, twilight. Deck given to the captain; I have held it since 18:09 of yesterday (evening, first and middle watches) and am feeling drowsy, so I give it up while he is on the quarterdeck. The wind shift that woke me: the wind has veered to SW by W, a moderate breeze of 11-12 knots, gusts to 14, and she now stands NW by W 301° — close reaching some 65° off the true wind, five knots through the water, leeway 4°, heel 5°, the topsail and topgallant still just shaking and the helmsman bearing off as they shake (his own method), fore-and-aft sails set, square sail furled. Glass 30.11 and rising, five hundredths in three hours, detached clouds, fine. Reckoning 48° 00' N, 11° 42' W, run since noon 78 miles, made good WNW 289°; my own slate a mile and a half N by W of his. Moon sixteen days old and nine degrees up — the lunar off until she climbs; the last was 7° 44' W by Spica two days ago. Noon by the sun 12:23. Watching for whoever has it: the shaking canvas, the wind for freshening further (heel and the square sail at 15 kn true), the wind's hauling for the Azores course, the noon sights. I go below to sleep.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

04:27, morning watch 8 bells. Woke in the gunroom by the captain's call; off watch. The cooper reports the leaguers in the ground tier leaking at the chimes where she has worked them — a good part of the water is in the well; the water stands at 3.7 tons, 31.5 days by the account, down from 4.4 tons. I know of no hands down in the ground tier in my watch (18:09-03:48); the rolling of these two days is my guess at the cause. She: NW by W 298°, close reaching, wind SW by W 11 kn, glass 30.13 rising fast (9 hundredths since the middle watch), run since noon 81 miles made good WNW 290°, my slate 48° 03' N 11° 47' W. Sunrise 04:26. Watching: the cooper's sounding of the well, the water's account, the noon sights at 12:23.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

Woke rested 08:24, forenoon watch, in the gunroom; off watch, the captain has the deck. What came while I slept: the ship tacked at 04:39 to the starboard tack (heading S 176°, all hands), the Hourly Shaping belayed at 04:37, the wind freshened to 14 kn SW — true now near the 15-knot mark for the square sail — heel 8°, rolling heavily, glass 30.22 rising strongly, run since noon 103 miles made good W by N 276°. The captain took an azimuth at 08:17: variation 25° W by azimuth, 13 June, allowed in the reckoning from now. Water still 3.7 tons. Watching when I take the deck: the wind for passing 15 knots true (the square sail), the heavy rolling, the water's account.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Took the deck from the captain.

08:25, forenoon watch 1 bell. Took the deck for the captain's nap (a half watch by his word). She: starboard tack full and by, S by E 166°, wind SW 14 kn gusts 16, apparent 15 kn 40° on the starboard bow, heel 8°, rolling heavily, 6 kn through the water. All sail set but the square sail (furled); topsail and topgallant just shaking by his method, the helmsman bearing off as they shake. Glass 30.19 rising. Reckoning 47° 41' N, 11° 41' W, run since noon 103 miles made good W by N 276°, my slate a mile and a half N of his. Water 3.7 tons, 31.1 days. Watching: the true wind for passing 15 knots (take in the square sail), the rolling and shaking sails, the water account with the cooper, the captain's waking.
Stood by until a glass.

08:57, forenoon watch 1 bell. Holding the deck for the captain's nap. She has fallen off to SSE 163° — the wind has worked forward to apparent 40° on the starboard bow, the helmsman bearing off as the canvas shakes (his method); true wind SW 14 kn gusts 16, six knots through the water, heel 8°, rolling heavily. Glass 30.21 rising, 7 hundredths these three hours. Reckoning 47° 38' N, 11° 40' W, run since noon 107 miles made good W 273°. Water 3.7 tons. Captain asleep in the cabin. Watching: the wind for passing 15 kn true (the square sail), the shaking canvas, the captain's waking at the half watch.
Stood by until the true wind exceeds 15 knots.

09:00, forenoon watch 2 bells. Holding the deck. True wind passed 15 kn — SW 15, gusts to 18, apparent 17, heading SSE 162°, heel 9°, rolling heavily. The topgallant is now shaking — the hand who had the watch has taken it in, or it hangs; the readings say it shaking. I'll order it taken in and stowed, and trim the sheets after. Glass 30.20 rising. Reckoning 47° 39' N, 11° 39' W, run since noon 108 miles. Water 3.7 tons. Captain asleep in the cabin. Watching: the wind for freshening further (heel and the square sail), the topgallant's trimming, the captain's waking.
Stood by until a glass.

09:32, forenoon watch 3 bells. Holding the deck since 08:26; the captain asleep below. The watch took in the topgallant at 09:04 — the gusts were pressing it (18 knots on a mean of 14 in the last hour's rollup). Now: true wind 14 kn from SSE, apparent 16 kn, she stands S by E 168°, topsail shaking still, fore-and-aft sails set, square sail furled. Glass 30.23 rising (5 hundredths in 3 hours). Reckoning 47° 36' N 11° 38' W; run since noon 110 miles, made good W 270° — the sea room good, depth 2235 f. Moon down, no lunar. Water 3.7 tons. I have drunk. Watching: the topsail for shaking (the captain's rule: bear off as she shakes; brace or hand only if it will not stop), the wind's further rise or backing, the captain waking at his word.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

10:33, forenoon watch 5 bells. The true wind has passed the mark: 16 knots from SW by S, mean 15, gusts higher — the square sail is already furled (came in last evening), so nothing more is wanted; she heels 10 degrees, the topsail shakes on the wind still and the helmsman bears off as it shakes by the captain's method. Glass 30.24 rising, 3 hundredths in the last hour. Reckoning 47° 30' N, 11° 36' W; run since noon 116 miles made good W 266°. Captain asleep below since 08:26. Watching: the wind for freshening further (heel rising), the topsail for coming to more than shaking, the captain's waking.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

12:04, afternoon watch 8 bells. Held the deck the whole forenoon; the captain still asleep below since 08:26. The forenoon passed steady: wind SW-SW by S 12-16 kn (peaked 16 at 10:33, eased back to 12-14), she stands S by E 160-171°, full and by, 5-6 kn, leeway 4°, heel 6-10°; topgallant taken in 09:04, topsail shaking by the captain's method, fore-and-aft sails set, square sail furled. Glass rising steadily to 30.27 (up a hundredth in the last hour) — the weather mending. Run since noon 126 miles made good W by S 258°. My slate 47° 22' N, 11° 31' W, two miles NNE of the master's account, within his trust. No land; St Mary's NE by E 86 leagues. Water 3.7 tons, 30.8 days. Noon sights by the sun come at 12:11 by my reckoning; the captain asleep but for the sights if he wakes for them. Watching: the wind for freshening, the topsail, the noon sights, the captain waking for the day's work.
Stood by until noon.

12:24, afternoon watch. Noon sights taken by the master (he below at the day's work) — lat by observation 47° 23' N, the account moved four miles N; course made good since yesterday W by S, 127 miles; longitude by account 11° 31' W; no tide in the day's work. My own reckoning 47° 20' N, 11° 30' W, the observed latitude three miles N of it. Glass 30.28 rising briskly (4 hundredths in the last hour), wind SW by S 13 kn, she stands SSE 156° full and by, 5 kn. The weather mends. Watching: the glass's rise for clearing airs or freshening, the wind for hauling south, the captain coming up from the day's work.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a word on deck.
