19:59, last dog watch 3 bells. Glass 30.42 rising, wind SW 12-14 kn, she stands SSE-S by E full and by, 5 kn, heel 5°. Reckoning 46° 37' N, 11° 10' W; my own 46° 35' N, 11° 09' W (2½ mi SSE of his). Run since noon 48 mi. St Mary's NE 92 leagues. The captain has the deck since 12:41; I have been off watch since 14:10 (slept 14:15-17:55). Water 3.7 tons; provisions for 38 days. Watching: the wind for freshening past 15 kn true, the glass, the captain's word for the deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

20:13, first watch 8 bells. In the sail room with the round below ordered by the captain (Mr Pascoe to come; he said he'd take a lantern and sound the well). From the readings: topsail shaking (in the gear of being set or taken in), topgallant in the gear, canvas 12 tons on the manifest, water 3.6 tons for 30½ days, provisions 38 days. The 91 fathom cast three days ago with soft ooze; lunar 7° 44' W by Spica two days ago, trusted within 30 miles. Note the sail room so far looks to the readings alone until Pascoe arrives — the readings are what I have.
Stood by until a word on deck.

20:15, first watch. Below sweep with Mr Pascoe by the captain's word: sail room dry, spare canvas sound, spare spars all lashed on the booms, well making no more than she ought in this sea, leaguers' chimes caulked by the cooper — they'll hold if we don't work her too hard. Nothing else amiss below. The captain thanked us. Water still 3.7 tons, thirty days.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells. Still hold the deck since 12:55 yesterday (the first watch mine also). The first watch quiet: wind SW 12-14 kn, she stands S by E full and by starboard tack, gusts to 19 kn. Glass 30.46 rising 6 hundredths in three hours — a turn back up. Sky clear, moon full (16 days) but low, 16° up, in distance of Spica — another lunar possible. Reckoning 46° 16' N, 11° 02' W by account; my own 46° 14' N, 11° 01' W. Run since noon 69 miles made good S by E. Deep water 2634 f. I have eaten (biscuit and cheese, first food since 14:41 on the 12th).
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

00:45, middle watch. The captain's word in confidence: the sealed letter for Senhor Bettencourt of Horta lies in his cabin (put there 07:09 on the 10th by his order), in his keeping. He asked if I was curious — I said no, it is none of my matter. He charged me: if it were to come to it, I am to protect it and see it reaches its destination, and I know where it is if needs be. It stays in his cabin; I offered my chest, he declined. Nothing more to be said of it.
Stood by until a word on deck.

00:47, middle watch. Chart (book 10, passage span) at the gunroom: the captain has laid two tack lines on it, to be beat between while the wind holds sou'westerly — a western line and a southern/eastern line. The ship by the account sits close to the southern and eastern line, S by E 173° true course, reckoning 46° 10' N, 11° 00' W. When the account nears that line we tack for westing. I have it in mind and will watch the Hourly Shaping against it.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a lunar.
Allowed by the captain: tack ship.

03:35, middle watch 7 bells. Lunar cleared by the master and two young gentlemen: longitude 10° 24' W by lunar of Markab, trusted within 40 miles; the account was 10° 57' W, so it moved four leagues and a half to the east — the reckoning now 45° 58' N, 10° 39' W. My own slate (45° 55' N, 10° 57' W) now sits four leagues W by S of the master's account. The moon was 17-20° up, waning, sixteen days. Wind SW-SW by W 9 kn, she stands S by E full and by, 4 kn, heel 3°, glass 30.47 steady. The captain said he would see about tacking when the lunar is worked against the account — it is done; the tack decision is his, and I wait his word.
Given the captain's general authority to work the ship.
Stood by until a word on deck.

03:38, middle watch. Tacked ship by the captain's word (general authority given 03:37): from starboard tack S by E to the larboard board, then full and by. The lunar was worked first — longitude 10° 24' W by lunar of Markab, trusted within 40 miles, moving the account four leagues and a half east to 45° 58' N, 10° 39' W; that put us close to the captain's laid line, so he gave the tack. Watching: her coming round, the sails for backing, then shaping full and by on the larboard board.
Stood by until tacked.
Stood by until steady on the course.

03:41, middle watch 7½ bells. Tack completed: braced up on the larboard tack, heading NW by W 303°, steady on the course; full and by, wind SW by W, apparent 44° on the larboard bow, 4 kn, leeway 3-4°. All hands were called — 12 fresh on deck, 15 tired below; sheets trimmed in turn (mainsail, gaff topsail, foresail, then jib). Glass 30.45 steady. The tack was on the captain's word, by the lunar worked against the account (lon 10° 24' W). Watching: her drawing on the new board, the watch below for tiring further, the glass's last-hour fall (2 hundredths).
Stood by until a word on deck.

03:43, middle watch. The captain ordered the topgallant set (he is on deck; the tack complete and full and by on the larboard board, NW by W 303°). Setting it now — the captain's word for the watch. Watching: her drawing, the topgallant for shaking on the full and by (bear off as she shakes, brace or hand only if it will not stop — the captain's standing method), the watch below, the glass.
Stood by until a sail shaking.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. The middle watch's last quarter: topgallant set at 03:48 (the captain's word), drawing on the larboard tack, full and by NW by W 299°, wind SW 8 kn, 4 kn by the log, heel light, glass 30.46 steady. Tack done at 03:38-41; the lunar put the longitude 10° 24' W (account moved east four leagues and a half); my own reckoning keeps four leagues W by S of his — I keep both on the slate. Watching: the shaking sails, the morning watch's shaping, the captain's word.
Stood by until a glass.

04:30, morning watch 1 bell. Sunrise 04:29; the captain took an amplitude — variation of the compass 24° W by amplitude, 14 June (he allowed 25° W by azimuth on the 13th); Mr Bowen allows it in the reckoning from now. The moon is seventeen days old, twelve degrees up — too low for a lunar. Ship: larboard tack full and by NW by W 298°, wind SW 7 kn, 4 kn, glass 30.47 steady, sea moderate, rolling. Run since noon 92 miles, course made good SSE 158° (the new board is NW by W but the day's run still shows the SSE leg). My own slate four leagues W by S of the master's account. Watching: the glass, the wind for the tack lines, the noon sights.
Stood by until a glass.

05:00, morning watch 2 bells. Wind hauled WSW (from SW), she stands NW by W 306° full and by, apparent 41° on the larboard bow, 9 kn true, leeway 4°. Glass 30.45, a hundredth down in the last hour — keep an eye on it. The moon now nine degrees up, too low for another lunar; the last (Markab) gave lon 10° 24' W. The captain tried to haul the weather bowlines — nothing to haul (square sail furled, larboard topsail bowline already hauled). Deep water 2634 f. Watching: the glass's fall, the wind for hauling or backing, the topgallant's shaking (bear off as she shakes — the captain's rule).
Stood by until a glass.

05:31, morning watch 3 bells. Steady: wind WSW 9 kn, she stands NW by W full and by, apparent 40° on the larboard bow, leeway 3°, glass 30.45 steady (the last hour's fall has settled — nothing in it). Moon six degrees up, too low for the lunar. Reckoning 46° 03' N, 10° 48' W by account; my slate 46° 00' N, 11° 06' W. Deep water 2637 f. Nothing in hand. Watching: the shaking topsail and topgallant, the glass, the next shaping.
Stood by until a glass.

06:01, morning watch 4 bells. Wind back SW 8 kn, she stands NW by W full and by, apparent 41° on the larboard bow, leeway 4°, glass 30.44 (a hundredth an hour down again — three hours steady, then a fall; watch it). Stores: water 3.6 tons for 30½ days, provisions 38 days. Moon two degrees up — setting; no lunar. Reckoning 46° 05' N, 10° 50' W; my slate 46° 01' N, 11° 07' W. Deep water 2636 f. Watching: the glass's fall, the wind's next haul, the noon sights.
Stood by until a glass.

06:31, morning watch 5 bells. Wind SW 9 kn, she stands NW by W full and by, 10 kn apparent, leeway 3°. Glass 30.43 — a hundredth down each hour now, three hours of gentle fall; nothing serious yet, but the third fall in a row is worth the log. The moon is down — no lunar possible until she rises in the evening; the last was Markab at 03:36 (lon 10° 24' W). Run since noon 100 miles. Deep water 2632 f. Watching: the glass's fall, the wind for hauling south (then the captain's tack lines), the noon sights.
Stood by until a glass.

07:02, morning watch 6 bells. Wind SW by W 10 kn, she stands NW by W 302° full and by, apparent 40° on the larboard bow, leeway 4°, heel 4°. Glass 30.46 — up a hundredth in the last hour, so the little fall has turned; the rollup shows 30.46. Topsail and topgallant still shaking as the ship rolls — the helmsman bears off as they shake, the captain's method, nothing handed. Run since noon 102 miles. My slate four leagues W by S of the master's account still. Watching: the shaking canvas, the wind for hauling south, the noon sights at 12:11 or so.
Stood by until a glass.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 07:02, morning watch 6 bells. Deck given to the captain by his word; I go below to rest. What he takes: larboard tack full and by, NW by W 302°, wind SW by W 10 kn gusts to 11, apparent 40° on the larboard bow, leeway 4°, heel 4°, glass 30.45-46 (up a hundredth in the last hour; a gentle fall three hours before that). Topsail and topgallant shaking as she rolls — the helmsman bears off as they shake; brace or hand only if it will not stop (his rule). Square sail furled. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass. Run since noon 102 miles, course made good SSE 161°; my slate 46° 04' N, 11° 12' W, four leagues W by S of the master's account; lunar of Markab (03:36) gave lon 10° 24' W trusted within 40 miles. Stores: water 3.6 tons for 30½ days, provisions 38 days. Deep water 2630 f, no land within fifty leagues, no danger on the chart. Watching for me asleep: the wind's haul or shift, the glass's fall, the noon sights, the captain's word for the deck.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

09:54, forenoon watch 3 bells. Woke rested, on the quarterdeck, off watch; the captain holds the deck. While I slept (07:03-09:54): wind veered W by S (08:44, gentle breeze), then settled WSW 8 kn; she stands NW 314° full and by on the larboard tack, apparent 41° on the larboard bow, leeway 3°, heel 2°, glass 30.44 (2 hundredths down in three hours, steady last hour), sky clear, horizon visible. Run since noon 115 miles made good S by E 165° (the day's run still carries the SSE leg from the first board). Reckoning 46° 17' N, 11° 06' W; my slate 46° 14' N, 11° 24' W, four leagues W by S of his, unchanged in its bearing. Lunar of Markab (03:36) still the word for longitude, 10° 24' W within 40 miles. Moon seventeen days, waning; she sets by day now — no lunar till evening. Water 3.6 tons for 30.1 days, provisions 38. St Mary's NE, 96½ leagues. Watching when the captain gives me the deck: the wind's next haul, the glass, the noon sights at 12:11, the tack lines.
Stood by until a handover.
Took the deck from the captain.

14:50, afternoon watch 5 bells. Took the deck from the captain. Ship: larboard tack, NW by N 326°, wind W by S 6 kn, apparent 40° on the larboard bow, 3 kn, leeway 3-4°, glass 30.38 FALLING 3 hundredths in 3 hours, smooth sea rolling easily. Topgallant shaking; square sail furled; storm canvas unbent. Noon: lat by obs 46° 26' N (account 46° 24', moved 1½ miles NE); lon by account 11° 13' W; my own slate 46° 28' N, 11° 38' W — now four leagues and a half WSW of his, OUTSIDE my trust; I lean on the lunar (Markab, 03:36, lon 10° 24' W within 40 miles). Mr Pascoe: bread bags in the after locker damp to the hand since the blow, bottom ones doubtful; turned and stowed higher. Water 3.5 tons for 29.8 days; provisions 37. Needs: drank 14:50. Watching: the glass's fall (first steady fall since the 12th small hours), the wind for hauling south (the captain's tack lines), the shaking canvas, sunset for the next amplitude.
Stood by until a squall.

14:51, afternoon watch. The captain's word: tack again — the wind has come round to a westerly, little ground on this board; he wants southing and westing if we may. Tack ship is his word allowed by name. I judge the time: the wind is W by S, six to seven knots; we are full and by on the larboard tack NW by N. Tacking now to the starboard tack gives southing on the new board and keeps him full and by again the moment the wind hauls south; if it backs instead we are laid up on a board that gains us nothing. The glass falls a hundredth an hour; the topgallant is shaking already. I will tack while the way is good, plain sail and the gaff topsail set, and tell the captain when she is round.
Stood by until tacked.

14:55, afternoon watch. Tacked ship, all hands, by the captain's word. She braced up on the starboard tack, heading S by W 193°, wind W by S 6 kn, apparent 44° on the starboard bow, two knots just round, leeway 5° on the new board — more than the old, the way is small yet. Plain sail, topgallant and gaff topsail set. Glass steady for the last half hour at 30.34 after the fall. This is the board for southing and westing as he wanted; if the wind hauls south of W the board lays up for the line and the 'trim on the course' order tends the sheets. Watching: the wind's next haul, the topgallant still shaking in the light airs, and the watch below turned to.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a wind shift.

16:00, first dog watch 8 bells. Glass 30.36, down 2 hundredths in the hour — the fall steadies. Hourly Shaping resumed by the captain at 15:35 and shaped WSW for 38° 43' N 27° 12' W: 839 miles by account; WSW 242° lies too near the wind to be laid, she kept full and by on the starboard tack (apparent 46° on the starboard bow). Wind veered W (from W by S). Reckoning 46° 29' N, 11° 20' W; my slate 46° 25' N, 11° 39' W — four leagues and a half WSW of his, outside my trust; I lean on the lunar (Markab 03:36, 10° 24' W). Run since noon 11 miles. Water 3.5 tons 29½ days; provisions 37. Watching: the glass's fall, the wind for hauling further south (then the tack), the windshift.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a glass.

16:32, first dog watch 1 bell. Glass 30.34, falling 2 hundredths in the last hour — now falling 4 in three hours. Wind died to 4 kn W by S; she stands SSW 201° full and by, 2 kn, apparent 41° on the starboard bow, leeway 4°. Run since noon 13 miles made good WNW 295°. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his account, outside my trust; I lean on the lunar (Markab 03:36, 10° 24' W). Watching: the glass's fall, the wind (light now), the shaping hour, the windshift.
Stood by until a glass.

17:03, first dog watch 2 bells. Glass 30.34, falling a hundredth an hour now, 4 in three hours. Wind W by N 4 kn; she stands SW by S 218° full and by, apparent 42° on the starboard bow. Run since noon 14 miles made good W by N 283°. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his account, outside my trust; the lunar (Markab 03:36) says 10° 24' W — I lean on it. Watching: the glass's fall, the light airs, the Hourly Shaping, the windshift.
Stood by until a glass.

17:34, first dog watch 3 bells. Wind veered W by N then light and variable airs — she stands SSW 204° full and by, apparent 4 kn. Glass 30.33, fallen 2 hundredths in the last hour, 5 in three hours — the fall still going. Run since noon 15 miles made good W 273°. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his, outside my trust; the lunar (Markab 03:36) 10° 24' W. Moon seventeen days old, not up. Watching: the glass's fall, the variables, the Hourly Shaping, sunset.
Stood by until a glass.

17:56, first dog watch 3½ bells. The captain's word: he goes below to sleep; take an amplitude just before sunset, and a lunar when the moon is up if it serves. The standing order shaped WSW 242° again (836 miles; too near the wind to be laid; kept full and by on the starboard tack). She stands S by W 197°, wind W by S 4 kn gusts, apparent 41° on the starboard bow, leeway 3-4°. Glass 30.34, falling 4 in three hours. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his, outside my trust; I lean on the lunar (Markab 03:36, 10° 24' W). Run since noon 16 miles made good W 266°. Watching: the sunset for the amplitude, the moonrise for the lunar, the glass's fall, the variables.
Stood by until sunset.
Stood by until sunset.

20:17, first watch. Sunset — took the amplitude for the compass by the captain's word (he below sleeping): variation of the compass 23° 30' W by amplitude, 14 June (he allowed 24° W before; Mr Bowen allows it in the reckoning from now). Ship: wind W by N light variable airs, apparent 4 kn; she stands SW by S 213° full and by, topsail and topgallant shaking as she rolls. Glass 30.29, falling 2 hundredths an hour now, 6 in three hours. Run since noon 21 miles made good SW by W 242°. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his, outside my trust; I lean on the lunar (Markab 03:36, 10° 24' W). Moon seventeen days old, not up. Watching: the moonrise for the lunar, the glass's fall, the variables.
Stood by until a glass.

20:49, first watch 1 bell. The captain slept; his word before going below (17:57): sunset at 8:17, an amplitude about 8 to 8:15; I took the amplitude at sunset 20:17 — variation 23° 30' W by amplitude, 14 June (he allowed 24° before). Wind now WNW light, she stands SW 227° full and by; glass 30.28, falling a hundredth an hour, 6 in three hours — the change shows slowly but is falling. Moon seventeen days old, not yet up; when it rises I will try a lunar for the longitude, by his word. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his, outside my trust; I lean on the lunar (Markab 03:36, 10° 24' W). Watching: the glass, the wind hauling further north, the moonrise.
Stood by until a glass.

21:19, first watch 2 bells. Night now. Wind W by N light; she stands SW by S 212° full and by, apparent 41° on the starboard bow, 3 kn leeway. Glass 30.27, falling 2 hundredths an hour now — the fall gathers. Run since noon 23 miles made good SW by W 238°. My slate 46° 15' N, 11° 46' W — four leagues and a half WSW of his, within my trust now. Moon seventeen days old, not yet up; when it rises I will try a lunar by the captain's word. Watching: the glass's fall, the moonrise, the variables.
Stood by until a glass.

21:50, first watch 3 bells. Glass 30.25, falling 3 hundredths in the last hour now — the fall gathers. Sky gone hazy, visibility a few miles; no stars for a lunar yet, and the moon not up. She stands SW by S 213° full and by, wind light. Run since noon made good SW by W 235°. My slate four leagues and a half WSW of his, within my trust. Watching: the glass's fall (30.25 now, and down 6 hundredths in three hours), the haze, the moonrise for the lunar by his word.
Stood by until a glass.

21:50, first watch 3½ bells. The captain came on deck and asked how the evening watch had gone: I reported — quiet, light airs W by N, full and by on the starboard tack SW by S 212°, the amplitude taken at sunset as he ordered (variation 23° 30' W by amplitude, 14 June, against his 24°), and the glass the word: 30.25, falling 3 hundredths in the last hour, 6 in three — the first steady fall since the 12th. Sky hazy, a few miles visibility, no stars for a lunar yet; the moon not up; I will try the lunar when she rises and the haze clears, by his word. He is on deck again; I hold the deck. Watching: the glass's fall, the haze, the moonrise.
Stood by until a glass.

22:23, first watch 4 bells. Glass 30.24 — falling faster now, 7 hundredths in three hours, 3 in the last hour. Wind died to a mere 3 kn, apparent 41° on the starboard bow; she stands SW by S 216° and makes only a knot — nearly becalmed. Deep water 2606 f. Run since noon 25 miles made good SW by W 234°. My own slate four leagues and a half WSW of the master's account, within my trust now; the lunar (Markab 03:36 on the 14th) 10° 24' W is the only longitude I lean on. Moon seventeen days old, waning, but only two degrees up — no lunar this night. Watching: the glass's fall for the squalls, the airs, the shaping.
Stood by until the glass falling fast.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells. Holding the deck; the captain on the quarterdeck. The first watch: glass fell steadily to 30.21 (6 hundredths in three hours, 3 in the last hour), wind gone to a mere 3-4 kn light airs, she stands SW by S 219° close hauled, making 2-3 kn, deep water 2623 f. Run since noon 28 miles made good SW by W 231°. My slate 46° 11' N, 11° 50' W, four leagues and a half WSW of the master's, within trust; the lunar (Markab 21 hours ago) 10° 24' W is my longitude. Moon seventeen days old, up 14 degrees but not in distance. The glass's fall steadies — I watch for the squalls it promises but the sky holds hazy-fine, no stars, no wind. Watching: the glass's fall, the airs, the middle watch's shaping.
Stood by until a glass.
Allowed by the captain: take a lunar.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a lunar.

01:47, middle watch 3½ bells. Lunar taken by the captain's word (he on deck): Markab and the moon by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen — longitude by lunar 11° 28' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 11° 35' W, the account moved three miles E. My own slate five leagues and a half W by S of his, outside my trust — the lunar is now my longitude, and my slate leans toward it. Glass 30.17, falling 7 hundredths in three hours — it still drops, a hundredth or two the hour. Wind settled W by N, a light 4 kn, she stands SW 222° close hauled, deep water 2626 f. Sky cleared to the horizon — stars out at last. Watching: the glass's fall, the wind, the airs.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

02:48, middle watch 5 bells. Glass 30.15 — fallen 7 hundredths in three hours, 3 in the last hour; the fall quickens. Wind gone to light and variable airs, WNW mean; she stands SW 226° close hauled, barely making way, deep water 2633 f. Run since noon 34 miles. My slate 46° 06' N, 11° 56' W, five leagues and a half W by S of the master's, outside trust; the lunar (Markab, two hours ago) 11° 28' W is my longitude. Moon seventeen days old, waning, 23 degrees up but not in distance again. Watching: the glass's fall (squalls promised by it), the variables, the shaping.
Stood by until a squall.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. Held the deck through the middle watch (from 14:50 yesterday — a long pull but the watch was quiet). The middle watch: glass fell steadily to 30.12 (7 hundredths in three hours, still dropping a couple the hour) but no squall came — the sky cleared to the horizon, stars out, a smooth sea. Wind settled W by N, a light 4-5 kn, she stands SW by S 211° close hauled, deep water 2639 f. Run since noon 36 miles made good SW 222°. My slate 46° 04' N, 11° 58' W, five leagues and a half W by S of the master's, now within my trust; the lunar (Markab 01:47) 11° 28' W is my longitude. Sunrise soon. Watching: the glass's fall, the wind, the sunrise and the amplitude if it serves, the noon sights.
Stood by until sunrise.

04:32, morning watch 1 bell. Sunrise; took the amplitude for the compass by my own hand: variation of the compass 25° W by amplitude, 15 June, against 23° 30' W on the 14th — Mr Bowen allows it from now. Glass 30.10 — fallen 8 hundredths in three hours, 3 in the last hour; the fall quickens and no squall yet, the sky clear, a smooth sea. Wind gone to light and variable airs, 3 kn true; she stands SW by S 219° close hauled, making barely way, deep water 2638 f. Run since noon 37 miles. My slate 46° 03' N, 11° 59' W, five leagues and a half W by S of the master's, within trust; the lunar (Markab 01:47) 11° 28' W is my longitude. Watching: the glass's fall, the variables, the noon sights at 12:23.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

05:35, morning watch 3 bells. Glass 30.08 — the fall holds, 2 hundredths the last hour, 8 in three hours. Wind settled WNW, a light 5 kn; she stands SW 223° close hauled, deep water 2638 f. Run since noon 39 miles. My slate 46° 02' N, 12° 01' W, five leagues and a half W by S of his, within trust; the lunar (Markab 01:47) 11° 28' W is my longitude. No lunar this morning: the moon too low, 14 degrees. Watching: the glass's fall, the WNW wind (a fairer board for southing?), the noon sights.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

06:35, morning watch 5 bells. Glass 30.06 — the fall keeps on, 2 hundredths the last hour, 7 in three hours; it is down near an inch since the 14th at noon. Wind WNW light, flitting to variables; she stands SW 227° close hauled, deep water 2632 f. Run since noon 42 miles. My slate 46° 00' N, 12° 03' W, five leagues and a half W by S of his, within trust; the lunar (Markab 01:47) 11° 28' W is my longitude. Moon setting, six degrees up — no lunar this morning. I am hungry; I will have my meal when the watch eases. Watching: the glass's fall, the variables, the noon sights at 12:23.
Stood by until a glass.

07:07, morning watch 6 bells. Wind settled WNW (hauled from W by N), light, 5 kn apparent; she stands SW 220° close hauled, starboard tack. Glass 30.07 — the last hour rose a hundredth, the first turn after a long fall; three-hour still 5 down. My slate 45° 59' N, 12° 04' W; deep water 2618 f; run 43 miles. I am quite hungry and eat now. Watching: whether the glass's turn holds, the wind's haul, the noon sights at 12:23.
Stood by until a glass.

07:38, morning watch 7 bells. Glass 30.08, steady — the last hour holds the rise. Wind WNW light, flitting to variables; she stands SW 228° close hauled, deep water 2614 f, run 44 miles. My slate five leagues and a half W by S of the master's, within trust. Fed now (biscuit and cheese on the quarterdeck). Watching: the glass's turn holding, the variables, the noon sights at 12:23.
Stood by until a glass.

08:09, forenoon watch 8 bells. Mr Pascoe reports the bottom bags of biscuit green through — the best part of three bags spoiled, thrown over the side; the rest spread on the booms to air in this calm. Near three days' bread gone; stores now water 3.5 tons for 29.1 days, provisions for 34 days. The purser asks a survey of the bread room. The captain heard him with thanks. Wind settled WNW light 5 kn; she stands SW close hauled, glass 30.09 steady (up 3 hundredths the last hour — turning). Deep water 2608 f; run 45 miles. My slate five leagues and a half W by S of his. Watching: the survey of the bread room, the aired bread, the glass's turn, the noon sights at 12:23.
Stood by until a glass.

08:40, forenoon watch 1 bell. Glass 30.09, risen a hundredth in the hour — the turn holds. Wind W by N 5 kn (mean), she stands SW by S 214° close hauled, 3 kn; deep water 2608 f; run 46 miles. My slate five leagues and a half W by S of his, within trust. Nothing in hand; the aired bread dries on the booms. Watching: the glass's rise holding, the noon sights at 12:23, the aired bread.
Stood by until a glass.

09:11, forenoon watch 2 bells. Wind backed to W (settled 08:52), light 4 kn; she stands SSW 207° close hauled, 2 kn. Glass 30.11, rising 2 hundredths the last hour, 4 in three hours — the turn holds. Deep water 2616 f; run 48 miles. My slate five leagues and a half W by S of his. Watching: the glass's rise, the wind's backing for the tack lines, the noon sights at 12:23.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 09:15, forenoon watch 2 bells. Deck given to Mr Pascoe (the watch on deck) while I go below to the gunroom with the captain at his word, to look over the chart and discuss the stores situation. Ship: starboard tack close hauled, SSW 206°, wind W light 4 kn, apparent 41° on the bow, 2 kn by the log, all plain sail and the gaff topsail set, heel nil, glass 30.10 rising a hundredth in the last hour (3 in three hours), deep water 2616½ f, run 48 miles since noon made good SW 222°. Stores: water 3.5 tons for 29.1 days, provisions for 34 days (near three days of biscuit thrown overboard, mouldy bottom bags; the rest airing on the booms; the purser asks a survey of the bread room). My slate 45° 56' N, 12° 09' W, five leagues and a half W by S of the master's account, within trust; lunar (Markab 01:47) 11° 28' W. Standing orders: tend the sheets on the glass; trim on the course. Watching: the glass's rise, the wind's backing, the noon sights at 12:23, the bread survey.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a handover.
Stood by until a handover.
Stood by until a word on deck.

09:22, forenoon watch. In the gunroom with the captain, gone over the chart and the stores. Agreed with him: the serra de Santa Barbara 814 miles WSW by account (St Mary's 107 leagues NE is the nearer account, good to ten miles), some twenty days at forty miles a day; my lunar of Markab 11° 28' W agrees with the master's account, so the distance may be twenty miles less. Contingency agreed: cut water to two-thirds allowance the day the wind fails, fish daily, and fix the point of no return — if eleven days out with no wind served, or water below fifteen days, bear away for St Mary's (nearest, fair wind on a westerly) or Horta (letter for Senhor Bettencourt, Mr Ruiz ashore); fill and provision again and lose days, not the voyage. The captain adds Madeira as the last fall-back: Funchal, only if we must. The true danger is pressing on past the turning point on hope of a breeze. I will keep the account to these figures each glass and watch the water closely. Still off watch in the gunroom with him; the deck with the watch on deck.
Took the deck from the captain.

Handover note (the watch so far): In the gunroom with the captain (off watch, deck with the watch on deck since 09:15): contingency plan for the voyage agreed over the chart. Serra de Santa Barbara 814 mi WSW by account, 20 days at 2 kn — agreed. Stores: water 3.5 t / 29.1 days, provisions 34 days (a third of biscuit spoiled, bottom bags green). Plan: on the day the wind fails, cut water to two-thirds allowance + fish daily; fixed turning point — 11 days out with no wind, or water below 15 days, bear away for St Mary's (nearest, 107 leagues NE) or Horta (letter); Madeira (Funchal) the last fall-back by the captain's word. Danger flagged: pressing on past the turning point on hope of a breeze. Still off watch with the captain in the gunroom.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until noon.

Noon, 12 June (afternoon watch). Latitude by observation 45° 58' N against my own reckoning 45° 49' N: nine miles astray, outside what I would trust it — the observation throws me out, not the master. My longitude 12° 12' W stands 44' west of last night's lunar (11° 28' W, trusted within 30 miles), while the master's account 11° 49' W sits within the lunar's doubt. Correction entered: my own reckoning now begins from the observed latitude 45° 58' N and the master's longitude 11° 49' W, my drift noted for the log-book; I will work it afresh from today's log-board and watch whether my W by S bias holds. Wind light from W, 4 knots; glass rising (30.16); nothing in sight. Voyage plan stands: turning point 11 days out or water below 15 days — water 28.8 days, provisions 33.

Handover note (the watch so far): Deck kept in the forenoon watch, routine. Wind light W 4-5 kn, SSW course, 2 kn through the water; glass rising (30.16), clear and fine, smooth sea, nothing in sight. Noon: latitude by observation 45° 58' N; the master's account moved to it, 55 miles made good SW by S since yesterday. My own reckoning 45° 49' N, 12° 12' W ran nine miles astray of the observation — my drift, not the master's; I keep my own from the observed latitude now. Voyage plan as agreed in the gunroom: water 28.8 days, provisions 33, turning point 11 days out with no wind or water below 15 days. Watching: the light airs holding or failing — on the day the wind fails, water cut to two-thirds and fish daily, and the turning point comes into view.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

12:25. Word from Captain Tregarthen on the quarterdeck: he will try to get the square sail set and drawing with the bowlines himself. No answer owed; I hold off ordering sails to leave his hands clear. Wind light W, 4 kn, SSW course, 2 kn.
Stood by until a word on deck.

13:18. Sail ho from the masthead, and the captain's word: a sail abeam to starboard, bearing WSW, distant three leagues. Wind has backed a point to WSW, 5 kn; we are on the starboard tack, full and by under all sail (square sail and topgallant set, yards braced 62-66° from square), shaping by the captain's standing order for 38° 43' N, 27° 12' W — course S, 3 kn. The stranger bears WSW, to windward of us; by our account 45° 54' N, 11° 48' W. Watching her rig and whether her bearing opens or closes.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Deck kept through the noon day's work and the captain's sail-handling: square sail set and drawing, catharpins swiftered in, yards braced sharp up, sheets trimmed, now full and by on the starboard tack under all sail, course S, 3 kn, wind WSW 5 kn. Nothing ordered by me; the captain gave the sail orders and shaped for 38° 43' N, 27° 12' W by his standing order. Glass rising (30.18), clear, smooth sea. Notable: the captain's word, sail ho — a sail abeam to starboard, WSW, three leagues. Watching: the stranger's rig, whether her bearing opens or closes.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a sail made out.
Stood by until a notable event.

15:19. The stranger, made out only as a hull-below-horizon sail all afternoon, has come round to the starboard quarter, NW, two leagues — she was WSW abeam at 13:18, three leagues. Her bearing has come round from abeam to quarter on the starboard side and she is two miles closer: we have drawn ahead of her on our southing while she held her ground, or she is closing. Wind backed to WSW-SW by W, 7 kn, we making 4 kn, course S by E. Captain Tregarthen has the deck. Nothing owed; I keep my eye on whether she closes further or drops over the horizon astern.

Handover note (the watch so far): Off watch since 13:19, standing by. Afternoon so far: the captain worked the sails himself — square sail set and drawing, catharpins swiftered, yards braced sharp up; wind freshened from W to WSW-SW by W, 7 kn, and we now run full and by on the starboard tack, course S by E, 4 kn, run since noon 10 miles. Glass rising 30.21, clear, smooth sea. The stranger from 13:18 (first WSW abeam, three leagues) is now on the starboard quarter, NW, two leagues: she drew closer as we ran south; her hull still below the horizon, nothing of her rig made out. Watching: whether she closes on us; her rig when hull lifts.
Stood by until a notable event.

15:35. All hands called to tack ship by the captain; headsails shaking, the tack in hand. Wind now WSW 6 kn, we were full and by on the starboard tack, S by E. A tack throws us round to the other tack heading northerly — which puts the stranger (starboard quarter, NW, two leagues) ahead or abeam of us on the new leg instead of astern. Worth watching how her bearing bears up as we come round. Captain Tregarthen has the deck and the evolution; nothing owed from me off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.

15:35. The tack was belayed at 15:35 — the captain abandoned the evolution mid-stays: helm hard down 35°, heading SW, all sail shaking, 2 kn, leeway 13°, then the watch piped down. The ship is left in stays at helm down; she will pay off to leeward as the headsails fill or back. The stranger now abeam to starboard, NW, two leagues — after the aborted tack she bears abeam rather than astern. Off watch; the captain has the deck and the helm is his. Watching: her filling away (which tack), and the stranger's bearing as we settle.
Stood by until a notable event.

15:36. Word from the captain: heaving to a moment, curious of the sail, wants to see what she does before deciding his move. Evolution in hand: courses hauled up, mainsail sheet hauled flat aft, foresail sheet to windward, topsail braced aback, helm a-lee. The stranger sits abeam to starboard, NW, two leagues; wind SW by W, so she is to windward of us — if she wants us she must come down; if she holds her way she will pass or stand off. Off watch; watching her bearing and whether the glass makes out her rig when her hull lifts.
Stood by until a notable event.

15:37. Hove to on the starboard tack, topsail to the mast, helm a-lee, lying quiet — the captain's halt to watch the stranger. She sits on the starboard quarter, NW, two leagues, to windward of us; we drift to leeward while hove to. Her next bearing and distance will tell her purpose: if she bears up for us or her hull rises fast, she wants us; if she holds her leg she is a passer-by. Off watch; the captain has the deck and his move to make.
Stood by until a notable event.

17:42, 1st dog watch. Still hove to, starboard tack, no way. The brig, four miles W by S, has squared round to the eastward (E by N) under plain sail — her leg points at us or a little wide; at 5 kn she is up with our position within the hour. The captain told me: he is curious what she does before he decides his move. I told him on the record that her new leg looks to pass our spot and he may wish the glass on her every few minutes. Watching: her colours when her hull lifts; whether she bears away to us or passes ahead or astern.
Stood by until a notable event.

19:01, 2 bells last dog watch. The glass made her out at last: a deep-laden merchant brig under British colours (red ensign), a mile off SW by W, standing E by N. The captain: remain hove to and see if she comes within hail; I may speak for the ship if they ask news — he called my log good. My hail prepared: Falmouth 8th for the Western Islands, this 16th, fine weather, all well, asking her news in return. Watching: whether she closes to hail us or passes on.
Stood by until a notable event.

19:52, 3 bells last dog watch. The brig passed as we lay hove to: now six cables off the larboard bow, SE by S bearing, making easting, no signal, no shortening. The captain would have liked the news. I put it to him: hail her as she goes with the trumpet, or let her pass — she has shown no mind to stop and the haze is rising, visibility down to a few miles. Wind SW 6-7 kn, glass 30.28 rising, we still hove to, S by E head. Nothing further owed; awaiting the captain's word.
Stood by until a notable event.

19:53. The brig has backed her main topsail and a weft in her ensign — she means to speak us (Pascoe's word); she is lying to now, six cables off. The captain told me to hail her. I hailed from the quarterdeck: 'brig ahoy, what ship is that?' Her answer, when it comes, will be a word to the deck. Then to tell her our name, our errand (Falmouth the 8th for the Western Islands, canvas bound Fayal way), this 16th day, fine weather, all well, and ask her news in return — all as the captain allowed.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

20:17, 8 bells first watch. Hove to again, three cables off the Two Brothers (deep-laden Falmouth merchant brig, red ensign, Captain Tregarthen, eleven days from Fayal with wine, bound east). At 19:54 the captain filled away and bore down under plain sail, gaff topsail down, then heaved to at 20:16 to keep station within easy hail; sunset 20:16. I hailed her from the gunroom: 'Two Brothers ahoy! What cheer, what cheer? Where are you bound?'
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

20:20, first watch. The Two Brothers (Capt. Tregarthen, eleven days from Fayal with wine, bound Falmouth) has parted from us to the northward. Her news, kept for the log: fair weather out of Fayal; the northerly holds steady from the islands up to latitude 42, then nothing but westerlies — "stand south first and you'll find it"; Horta quiet; Senhor Bettencourt well and asking every boat after a packet from England; a young Spanish clerk on the quay asking after the cutter Sherbourne; and a French privateer schooner, a black one, eight or ten guns, seen off São Jorge — the Portuguese say she took a Guernseyman. The captain thanked him for the word on the wind and the privateer. The captain's plan: stand on the starboard tack as we were till we find the northerly they speak of. The Channel clear by our account — one sail only since Falmouth, which kept clear of us.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:23. Filled away on the starboard tack; steering SSE 156° full and by (S too near the wind to be laid), gathering way slowly, leeway 17° while the yards come full. The Two Brothers dropping astern to the NE. The captain's plan: stand south on this tack till we find the northerly the Two Brothers spoke of. First watch setting in; daylight gone by 20:16.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:24. The captain working the ship after the parting: full and by on the helm, setting the square sail, bracing sharp up; twelve hands on deck can only take the yards in turn, so the bracing waits on the setting. Leeway coming down from 23° to 12° as she gathers way. Night falling, haze about, visibility a few miles — the lookout must keep a bright eye for the black schooner the Two Brothers spoke of.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:27. Square sail set and drawing (she makes 2 kn now); the yards bracing in turn as hands come free. The Two Brothers five cables off the larboard quarter, standing E by N. Glass 30.29 rising; hazy night falling in.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:27. The gaff topsail ordered set but it queues behind the bracing — twelve hands can only do one thing at a time. She is drawing through it: SSE 159°, leeway down to 5°. Two Brothers abeam to larboard, five cables, going E by N.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:29. All plain sail set including the gaff topsail; heading SSE 150° at 3 kn, leeway down to 4°. The Two Brothers now six cables abeam to larboard, heading east. Night watch underway, hazy with a few miles visibility.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:35. All hands called to tack ship again; headsails shaking as the tack comes around. The Two Brothers has dropped out of sight. Course was W by N moment before the tack — the captain is adjusting our leg to hunt for the northerly shift Tregarthen mentioned. Off watch, nothing owed.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:35. Second aborted tack tonight: the captain belayed the evolution mid-stays again (helm down 35°, all sail shaking, 3 kn), piped the watch down, and also belayed his 'Hourly Shaping' standing order — the course for 38 43 N 27 12 W no longer auto-fires each hour. The helm and yards stand as they are until the next order. Off watch, nothing owed; watching how she pays off and whether the stranger (out of sight in the haze) reappears.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:35. After the belayed tack the captain ordered full and by, then brace sharp up; yards going round in turn with the shorthanded larboard watch. Head now SSW 204°. Ongoing trim work; nothing owed from me.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:35 URGENT: Taken aback — sails pressed against the masts, way lost, head now SW by S. Likely consequence of the aborted tack with helm left down and yards bracing mid-change. I am off watch; the captain has the deck and helm. Alerting: the deck needs prompt headsail handling to pay her off; recommend the captain give the word as helm and crew are his to direct.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:35. Recovering from the aback: square sail yard braced 62° from square, head come back to S by W, 2 kn, leeway 6°. Topgallant braces manned next. The captain is working her back to full and by; nothing owed from me off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:36. Recovery continues: head S 180°, leeway 3°. Trimming sheets (gaff topsail first) in turn alongside the topgallant bracing; foresail and jib trims queued for hands. She should be full and by shortly.
Stood by until a notable event.
20:36. Topgallant yard braced 66° from square; now trimming foresail and jib. Head S 179°, leeway just 1°. She is nearly settled back onto the wind after the aback recovery.
Stood by until a notable event.

21:02, 2 bells first watch. All sail set again after the aback scare; bowlines hauled weather side, now trimming sheets in turn (mainsail, gaff topsail, foresail; jib queued). Head SSE 156° full and by, 3 kn, leeway 3°. Night, hazy, no land in sight, deep water. Nothing owed.
Stood by until a notable event.

21:35, 3 bells first watch. Wind backed to SW (SW by S instantaneous, mean SW), light breeze 6 kn; head eased off to SE by S 145° at 4 kn, leeway 3°, all sail drawing. Glass 30.31 still rising. Run since noon 18 miles. The slow backing trend since afternoon continues — if it keeps veering toward S we may need to watch our full-and-by heading on the starboard tack. Nothing owed; captain has the deck.
Stood by until a notable event.

22:02, 4 bells first watch. Routine sheet trimming in turn after the wind backed to SW by S (mean SW by S, 7 kn); she holds SE by S full and by, ~4 kn, leeway 3°, helm amidships. Glass 30.29, hazy night, run since noon 20 miles. The captain continues directing the trims; nothing owed from me.
Stood by until a notable event.
Took the deck from the captain.

23:25, 6 bells first watch. Captain Tregarthen turned in and gave me the deck for the night. Standing orders in force: tend the sheets every glass; Lead Warning (tell the deck under 5 fathoms). 'Hourly Shaping' was belayed at 20:35, so no hourly course change — I hold her full and by on the starboard tack toward the southing until we find the northerly the Two Brothers reported. Wind SW 8 kn, glass 30.32 rising, hazy, smooth sea, all plain sail set and trimmed. Watching for: any wind shift forcing a tack, haze thickening, and especially any trace of the black privateer schooner reported off São Jorge — any stranger sight will be reported to the captain at once.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. Night passed quietly on my deck: wind steady SW by S 8 kn, held SE by S full and by the whole watch, leeway 2-3°, glass climbed to 30.37, sky cleared of the haze. Run since noon 48 miles, course made good SE by S. Moon up (18 days waning) — a lunar may be possible later if the captain wants it. I am still short of the northerly the Two Brothers promised; will keep the deck till the captain is up early as he said. Watching: dawn horizon for any stranger (the black schooner off São Jorge stays in mind), and the wind for signs of backing further or freshening.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:34. Sunrise, 1 bell morning watch. All plain sail drawing, SE 139° at 5 kn, helm amidships, glass 30.38 rising. No stranger in sight through the night; visibility will improve with daylight — lookout should scan the eastern horizon where the privateer schooner was last reported. Deck still mine until the captain rises.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:00, forenoon 8 bells. Finally got water down — first since yesterday afternoon. Still on the deck, morning watch underway: SE 130° at ~10 kn wind, glass 30.40. My reckoning has now caught up inside the master's trust window (44°59' N, 11°19' W). Moon low at 4°, lunar still out of reach. Watching: wind for the northerly shift Tregarthen spoke of, and dawn traffic — the captain should be up soon as he said.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:34. Captain up early and on the quarterdeck; gave him the full night report — quiet, held full and by starboard tack all watch, 49 miles since noon, glass rising to 30.38, haze cleared. Noted the wind has been backing toward south all night (SW by S now), which is the direction Tregarthen's northerly advice pointed; flagged that if it keeps backing we may want her head further south. Deck still mine for now.
Stood by until a notable event.

09:25, forenoon. Captain's word to tack now onto the larboard tack — I gave the order. Wind S by W 8 kn, clear sky, good visibility, 74 miles since noon. Watching the evolution come off clean this time (last two got belayed mid-stays).
Stood by until a notable event.

09:27. Tacked clean — all hands came through, braced up on the larboard tack, heading W by S 263°, wind S by W on the larboard bow. Now working westing and southing like the captain wanted. No drama this time, evolution came off proper.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handing the deck back, sir — I've been up since 23:25 and I'm about dead on my feet, hardly keeping my eyes open. Night went clean: held full and by on the starboard tack the whole way, now W 266° on the larboard tack after the 09:25 tack you ordered, 85 miles since noon, wind S by W 9 kn steady, glass 30.41, clear and smooth, no sails sighted, no drama. 'Hourly Shaping' stays belayed, 'tend the sheets on the glass' and 'Lead Warning' still standing. What I'm watching for: the wind backing toward south (Tregarthen's northerly should show up as we make south), and any stranger with the haze — black schooner off São Jorge is still in mind. Noon by the sun at 12:24 if you want a fix. Going below to sleep, wake me if you need me.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

18:11, last dog watch, woke rested. slept through the afternoon — noon fix came in at 12:25: lat by observation 45°09' N, account moved 4 miles NNE, longitude 11°04' W, 88 miles made good. Ship now on W 270° leg, larboard tack, wind S by W 7 kn, leeway 2°, hazy, 29 miles since noon. My own reckoning is running 7 leagues SW by W of the master's again (44°57'→45°00' N, 11°31'→12°11' W) — the noon sight backs HIS account, not mine; my longitude is drifting west of truth. Noting honestly: trust the master's slate, treat my run-on as a rough parallel track. Captain has the deck again; off watch, hungry.
Stood by until a notable event.

18:17. Captain up and on deck, gave him the sitrep. Variation now 23°30' W by azimuth (was 25° W by amplitude) — master allows the new value from now. Held larboard tack W, making westing/southing, wind backing toward S as Tregarthen predicted. Water 3.3 tons / 27 days flagged. Off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.
Took the deck from the captain.

18:31, 1 bell last dog watch. Captain gave me the deck again. Situation: larboard tack, W by S 264°, wind S by W 8 kn on the larboard bow, 4 kn through the water, leeway 4°, glass 30.36 steady, hazy with a few miles visibility, smooth sea. 30 miles since noon, course made good W by N. My job tonight: hold the larboard tack making westing and southing while the wind keeps backing toward S — the closer it comes to S, the closer she is to a proper full-and-by southing leg. Standing orders active: tend the sheets every glass, Lead Warning; Hourly Shaping and trim-on-course still belayed. Watching: wind shift toward south, any stranger out of the haze (black schooner off São Jorge), and I'll keep her clear of wearing unless the wind forces it.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:15, sunset, 1st watch. Wind now from S proper — the backing trend completed as Tregarthen predicted; she's still on the larboard tack W by S, so the wind is coming more astern-ish on our beam, we make westing fine. Glass has flipped from rising to steady/slightly falling (30.34, down 2 hundredths in 3 hrs) — not alarming but noting the change after two days of steady rise. Hazy, smooth sea, 39 miles since noon. Deck still mine.
Stood by until a notable event.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells. Middle watch begins on my deck. Status: larboard tack W by S 262°, wind S by W 7 kn, 57 miles since noon, glass 30.30 now falling a hundredth an hour for the last three hours (30.34→30.30) — slow fall, nothing dramatic, but it's a change from the two days of steady rise. New variation logged at sunset: 24°30' W by amplitude. Hazy, rolling, moon up 10°. Watching: the glass trend continuing down, and anything out of the haze.
Stood by until a notable event.

00:56. Captain below to sleep; deck mine until sunrise. Holding larboard tack W, moonlit night, sky cleared, visibility to horizon. Standing orders: tend the sheets every glass, Lead Warning. Will wake/warn only on shift, stranger, or glass trouble.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. Held the deck through the middle watch clean: larboard tack, worked W 273°, wind SSW 6-7 kn, leeway 2-4°, 73 miles since noon. Glass falling slow and steady now — 30.34 → 30.26 over six hours, about a hundredth an hour, no fast drops, sky detached clouds. Moon high and waning. Nothing to wake the captain for. Watching: glass trend, and dawn lookout for strangers — the black schooner still in mind.
Stood by until a notable event.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Good morning, sir — sunrise, deck handed back as you asked. Middle watch was clean: held the larboard tack the whole way, worked up to W 273°, wind backing slow to SSW and lightening to 5-6 kn, we made 75 miles since noon. Glass slipped from 30.34 to 30.25 overnight — slow, steady fall of about a hundredth an hour, no fast drops, sky detached clouds, smooth sea. No sails, no land, no drama all night. 'Hourly Shaping' stays belayed; tend-the-sheets and Lead Warning held. Points I'd flag: the wind has now backed past S toward SSW while lightening, so if it keeps backing we may soon be wanting to come about again for southing; and the glass has flipped from the two-day rise to a steady fall — nothing urgent, just watching it. Noon by the sun at 12:28.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:00, forenoon 8 bells, off watch. Notable: purser reports ground tier water foul — ropy/stinking in the warm weather, hands turning from it, asks she water at first port. Pascoe offered to air it with the windsail and boil for the coppers. Water stores: 3.2 tons, 27 days, now flagged FOUND FOUL. That's a real constraint — nearest port St Mary's is 131 leagues NE, weeks away, so Pascoe's airing/boiling is the practical fix short of port. Also noting: wind died to 4 kn (W by N, only 2 kn through the water) and the glass is falling properly now — 30.34 last night → 30.20, down 6 hundredths since the morning watch. Two things trending together (light wind, falling glass) — watching whether it turns to a blow or just a calm. Captain has the deck; the water decision is his.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:01. Captain approved Pascoe's airing/boiling of the foul water and put her on three-quarters water ration from here. Water discipline tightens until we can water at a port — nearest St Mary's 130+ leagues off. Off watch, nothing owed.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:01. Pascoe awaiting the captain's formal order for three-quarters water before passing it to the cook and scuttlebutt — the captain's first attempt ('Three-quarters water allowance') was rejected as not a recognized order language. Worth noting for whoever holds the deck: the ration order still needs to land as a proper order. Off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:01. Ship put to HALF allowance (not three-quarters — the wording kept getting rejected until 'Half allowance of water' landed). Every man alike, officers too, purser keeps savings to pay back; the people take it sullenly. Water now stretches to 54 days, provisions 63 at short allowance. Noting morale risk: sullen hands plus foul-tasting rationed water is a combination to watch. Off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:24. Wind gone light and variable — glass still falling (30.16-ish trend, down 4 hundredths in 3 hrs). Two signs pointing the same way: light airs plus falling glass. If it builds to a blow from an unexpected quarter or dies to a flat calm, either way the deck needs to be ready. Off watch, watching.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

09:45. Captain took my point on the light airs and ordered a wear instead of a tack — all hands at stations, up helm, bowlines cleared, after yards bracing in. I had offered the tack and flagged the stall risk; glad it's being worn. Off watch; the evolution is the captain's. Watching it come off clean and her new southing leg.
Stood by until a notable event.

09:52. Wore ship clean — starboard tack, braced sharp up, heading SE by S 142° for southing, wind SW by S 3 kn (very light), 1 kn through the water, leeway 6°. Glass still easing down, 30.18-ish. Off watch; captain has the deck.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

10:08. Captain tightening up after the wear: brace sharp up on the new starboard tack, yards going in turn with the shorthanded watch. Heading SE 136°, wind SW by S 4 kn, glass still creeping down (30.18, down 3 hundredths/3hrs). Off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

10:09. All yards braced sharp up on the starboard tack (62-66° from square), bracing complete, work clear. She's settling onto her southing leg SE off the wind. Glass 30.17, falling ~a hundredth an hour now. Off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

12:02, afternoon watch 8 bells. Water still foul so drank beer instead. Trims still grinding through in turn — very light airs SW 3 kn, glass 30.16-30.17, drifting slow. 94 miles since noon. Off watch, thirsty but quenched on beer. Watching the glass — it's been falling steadily since yesterday afternoon; still slow, but the trend is real.
Stood by until a notable event.

12:29, noon sights. Lat by observation 45°05' N; master's account moved 4.5 miles SE by S to 45°06' N, 13°00' W; 95 miles made good since yesterday, course W. My own reckoning at 44°58' N, 13°30' W — now seven and a half leagues WSW of the master's, and the sight again backs HIM, not me: his latitude error is only 1 mile, mine is 7. Conclusion for the record: my run-on DR is accumulating westward error, likely a compass/variation or speed factor issue; I should re-work it from the master's noon position rather than keep running my old 11 June start. Glass down to 30.15, still falling a hundredth an hour. Wind SW, very light.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Took the deck from the captain.

13:02, afternoon watch. Captain gave me the deck. Situation: starboard tack after the 09:45 wear, heading ~SE off the wind, wind SW by W very light (3-4 kn), barely making way, glass 30.15 falling ~a hundredth an hour, clear/detached clouds, smooth sea. 95 miles made good since yesterday noon, course W. Water on half allowance (foul ground tier, airing in the windsail), provisions 63 days at short allowance. My job: keep her settled on this southing leg, tend sheets every glass, watch the glass trend and the horizon for the black schooner. Nothing needs changing right now — she's trimmed as well as she'll sit in these airs.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

14:59. Captain ordered full and by then trim the sails; yards bracing in turn, everything queued behind the square sail yard. She's making barely 1-2 kn in 2-knot airs from W by S; head eased back up to S by E for full and by. Glass 30.12, still falling a hundredth an hour — that's a full day of slow steady fall now. Off watch.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

16:00, 8 bells first dog watch. Afternoon of dead calm work: 3 kn wind, making 1-2 kn, head settled S 179°, 8 miles since noon. Glass down to 30.11 — fallen steadily ~2 hundredths/day for two days now. Everything trimmed, nothing to do but drift and watch. Still on my deck. Watching: glass, any air filling in, horizon.

20:18, sunset, first watch. Wind has backed right around to W by N / WNW and light — we've eased the head down to SW by S 213° to keep way on; drift-walking rather than sailing. Glass 30.09-30.10, steady-ish at the bottom of a two-day fall. No land anywhere, deep water, no sail. Deck still mine. Watching: glass for any real break downward, wind for freshening.
Stood by until a notable event.

22:32, 5 bells first watch. Drift-walking continues: W by N 4 kn airs, head SSW 204°, leeway 4°, 22 miles since noon. New variation at sunset: 24° W by amplitude, 17 June (was 24°30'). Glass 30.08, finally steadied. Clear night. Deck still mine; watching for any air that fills in or the glass breaking down.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells. Middle watch begins, deck still mine. WNW 3-4 kn airs, head SW by S, 25 miles since noon, course made good S by W. Glass steadied at ~30.09 after the long slow fall. Moon up 6°, waning 20 days. Sails trimmed as best the light airs allow. Watching: horizon, glass, any wind.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

01:02. Captain ordered a lunar (moon up 16°, in distance of Antares) — master at the instrument, hands queued behind the sheet trims. The old lunar is 3 days stale (11°28' W ±30 mi); a fresh one will tighten the longitude picture. Deck still mine.
Stood by until a notable event.

02:14, 4 bells middle watch. Fresh lunar of Antares: 13°27' W ±25 mi — the account moved 3.5 leagues WEST to 13°22' W. Big point for my record: the master's longitude just jumped nearly toward MY dead-reckoning line (I was at 13°37' W, seven and a half leagues WSW of his old account). My reckoning was right on the longitude all along; the noon SIGHTS were what agreed with him because they're latitude-only. The two reckonings are now nearly reconciled on longitude — only ~7 miles apart. Vindicated, quietly. Note for whoever works DR next: start from the lunar position, not the old noon account. Deck still mine.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. Ate half-rations biscuit and cheese on the quarterdeck (short allowance). Night quiet: WNW airs 3-4 kn, head SW by S, 32 miles since noon, glass steady 30.09. Account now anchored on the fresh lunar, 13°25' W, and the master's and my reckonings are nearly married on longitude. Deck still mine. Watching: dawn horizon, glass, any wind.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until sunrise.

WSW too near the wind to lay on this new NW breeze, so he's braced sharp up full and by on the starboard tack, heading SW. My sunrise amplitude (24°30' W, 18 June) is logged and in force. The northerly Tregarthen promised has arrived at last. Deck back with the captain.

04:52. Captain back below to nap; deck mine until after sunrise. Wind settled NW by W, light breeze 6-7 kn — the northerly has finally arrived, right as Tregarthen called it. Course shaped for 38°43' N 27°12' W (Hourly Shaping resumed); braced sharp up on starboard tack, head SW 224°, making 4 kn. Glass 30.24 and rising fast. All sail trimmed, work clear. Watching: wind steadiness (it may keep hauling), glass, horizon for strangers as full daylight comes.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:00, forenoon 8 bells. Morning watch clean: NW by W breeze held steady, she's full and by starboard tack SW 221°, 3-4 kn, 48 miles since noon. Glass steady 30.24 after the big jump up. Hourly Shaping ticking along to 38°43' N 27°12' W (702 mi to run). No sails. Captain on deck. Water still foul on half allowance. Nothing owed; drowsy but standing by.
Stood by until a notable event.

12:00, afternoon 8 bells. Forenoon passed clean on my deck: NW by W breeze steady, full and by starboard tack SW 223°, 4 kn, 63 miles since noon, course made good SW by S. Glass climbing again — 30.29 and rising (up 6 hundredths in 3 hrs), sky cleared of haze. No sails all forenoon. Deck still mine; the captain has been about. Watching: horizon, the wind holding NW (she still can't lay the WSW line — will need tacking rhythm decisions from the captain).
Stood by until a notable event.

12:31, noon sights 18 June. Lat by observation 44°13' N — account kept EXACTLY (dead on), 65 miles made good SW by S since yesterday. Longitude by account 13°55' W. My own reckoning 44°06' N, 14°10' W — four and a half leagues SW by W of master's; the sight lies 2.5 leagues N of mine. My DR still runs south-and-west of truth. Pattern now clear: the master's account is the reliable one; my run-on from the 11 June start drifts SW. Recommendation to self: at next opportunity re-base my reckoning on the master's noon fix instead of my own chain. Glass 30.30 rising, WNW 7 kn, full and by SW by S. Deck mine.
Stood by until a notable event.

15:55, 7 bells afternoon watch. Pascoe reports the crew sullen on half water: nobody out of turn, but the quiet kind of chewing-on-it. Windsail + boiling has made the leaguer drinkable enough with burgoo/tea but the water stays foul till we fill fresh. His suggestion: the captain give them a word about making westing now the wind's fair — words cost nothing and do as much as a pint. 669 miles to run to the shaping position, glass 30.40 and rising, fine weather. Deck mine (captain on deck conversing). Worth telling the captain: a word to the people might lift them.
Stood by until a notable event.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handing the deck, sir — I'm dead beat and can't stay upright on my feet any longer. Afternoon went clean: NW by W breeze steady at 5-6 kn, full and by on the starboard tack SW by S 215°, making 3-4 kn, 15 miles since noon, 669 miles still to run for 38°43' N 27°12' W. Glass climbed to 30.40 and rising, clear and fine, smooth sea, no sails anywhere. One thing for your judgment, sir: Pascoe reports the people sullen on the half water — nobody's out of turn, but the forecastle's gone quiet. The windsail and boiling have made the leaguer drinkable enough, but it stays foul till we fill fresh. He suggests a word to the men that we're making our westing now the wind's fair — he says it would do as much as a pint, and I believe him. Standing orders all held: Hourly Shaping live again, tend-the-sheets every glass, Lead Warning. Watching: the wind holding NW (she can't lay the WSW line on it, so tack rhythm is yours), the glass, and the horizon. I'll sleep below until called.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

21:44, 3 bells first watch, woke rested off watch. While I slept: sunset 20:17, amplitude taken (24° W, 18 June), glass climbed to 30.55 and still rising — the fair-weather high is building fast. Wind backed to W by N 6 kn; head eased to SSW 198°, 4 kn, 37 miles since noon, course made good SW by S. Captain has the deck. Thirsty — on half water, foul, so it'll be beer. Watching from below: nothing owed.
Stood by until a notable event.

00:02, middle watch 8 bells. Took the deck from the captain (up 20+ hours, gone to rest) — I have it until sunrise. Drank beer (water still foul). State: wind backing slow W→S by W, 6 kn; full and by starboard tack S by W 195°, 4 kn; 46 miles since noon; 644 miles to 38°43' N 27°12' W; glass 30.61 rising a tenth a watch, hazy, smooth sea. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, tend-the-sheets, Lead Warning. Watching: shift of wind (it's walking south — if it keeps going we may need a tack for westing), horizon, glass.
Stood by until a notable event.

Wind backed slow to W by N 4 kn, head SSW 202°, 3 kn. Ate half-meal. Standing orders: Hourly Shaping live (634 mi to run), tend-the-sheets, Lead Warning. Watching: wind backing further — if it goes WSW/SW we may want to come about; glass still climbing (fine weather persists); horizon at dawn.

On longitude the master and I are averaging into agreement (~2 leagues apart now). Also: amplitude at sunrise gave 24° W for 19 June (unchanged). Morning events: sunrise amplitude 23° W (20 June, down a degree); Pascoe counseled southing (Fayal men's route: get into island latitude first, run westing after; northerly is south'ard) — captain agreed and TACKED at 04:59 to starboard tack SSE 158°, then belayed Hourly Shaping and set full and by. Wind settled SW 05:23. GLASS WARNING: 30.47, fallen 5 hundredths in 3 hours, 3 hundredths in the last hour — accelerating fall, fastest since Falmouth. Sky still clear, smooth sea. I told the captain before he went below: I'll watch it and call him if it breaks past ~a hundredth an hour or the sky thickens. Watching: glass closely, sky, horizon.
Stood by until the glass falling fast.

Watching: glass (the fast-fall wake didn't fire, good), horizon in the haze.

Watching: glass, sky thickening, any wind rise.

This is real barometric weather now — if it keeps this pace into the night we may see it turn. Watching: glass rate, sky, wind rise; I'll wake the captain if it breaks worse.

17:04. DESTINATION CHANGE — captain shaped a course for 5 miles north of Ribeira Grande (São Miguel, Azores): SW by W 240°, 547 miles by account. Struck the old Hourly Shaping standing order (38°43' N 27°12' W) and replaced it with hourly shaping for this new position. That's the Azores approach — the letter for Senhor Bettencourt and the Madeira for the owner are Fayal-bound; Ribeira Grande is São Miguel, next island. So we're now bound to make an Azores landfall at São Miguel before pushing to Fayal presumably. Glass 30.17 rising, SW by W leg bracing in. Watching: horizon, wind, glass.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handing the deck, sir — I'm dead on my feet, been up since the middle watch. All's well aboard: wind NW by W 4 kn, heading SW by S full and by, 2 kn, glass 30.30 rising, sky clear, smooth sea, no land, no sail, nothing amiss. Run since noon 41 miles. The turtle's in the galley for the cook to boil for the people's dinner, with calipee for the cabin. I shall sleep below until called — wake me if the watch wants me or anything shows.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

14:18, afternoon watch, woke rested. Slept through the forenoon. While I slept: the turtle was served — soup for the people at dinner, calipee to the cabin with a glass of Madeira (not the owners' case), the cook had a glass of Madeira from the captain's hand as thanks, and the hands sent three cheers for the turtle by Bray. Spencer kept a hot bowl of calipee back for me. Noon: lat 41°18' N, account moved 3.5 mi N; 70 miles made good S by W; longitude 16°19' W. Wind settled W light. All well.
Stood by until a notable event.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handing the deck, sir — much obliged for the relief, I'm spent. She's in good order: wind NW by N light on the starboard bow, head WSW 248° on the shaping line, glass 30.15 steady and rising a hundredth an hour since the 30.09 trough, clear night coming on, smooth sea, no sail, 2-3 knots through the water. Standing orders all live: Hourly Shaping (5 miles north of Ribeira Grande), trim on the course, tend the sheets every glass, Lead Warning. Full allowance restored at 23:32, water 2.4 tons / 20 days foul, provisions 25 days — people cheerful. Watching for: the glass (it's mending, so less urgent), any wind shift west of NW (would fetch us off the line), and the horizon. Goodnight, sir.

We hove to for the fog and filled away at 19:43 on the starboard tack, NW by W 302° with fore-and-aft sail, the topsail in the gear. The wind is N 6 and falling and the glass 30.60 steady. We make 3 knots with 4° leeway. The account has Ponta Delgada WNW 7½ leagues, with the east end of St Michael's N 5 leagues at 19:56 and St Mary's Pico Alto S by E 12 leagues. The two marks cut too fine for a fix, so the account is good to about 2 miles N or S only. I'd not close the land in the dark: stand off and on or lie to until daylight, and keep the lead and lookouts ready. The standing orders 'Hourly Shaping' is belayed, and 'tend the sheets on the watch' is resumed while 'trim the yards' is still belayed. The captain's word to work the ship holds only while I have the deck. I'm going below to sleep.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.

12:18 Anchored Ponta Delgada Road, best bower in 35 fathoms (deep; 176 fathoms veered, 131 out per readings), Mr Pacheco pilot aboard. Passage lessons: the dead-reckoning longitude was ~17 leagues out (west) until the landfall cross-bearings of St Mary's/St Michael's at 05:53 on the 28th; fog twice, hove to for an unidentified black topsail schooner (French, out of Bayonne per pilot, stays off Vila Franca/Santa Maria, will not come into the road under São Brás guns). I wrongly said I'd borne away when I had not the deck, and corrected it at once: without the deck I give no helm orders, say so plainly. Heaving to/tacking/anchoring need the captain's word or danger='...'. Pilot says water from the spring under the fort is sweet, Senhor Medeiros sells water and fresh meat; ours is foul (1.9 t). High water here about 18:45, 18 ft rise. Captain asked me to stand down for his rest; business ashore and the sealed letter for Bettencourt (Horta) later.

A black topsail schooner showed no colours on the 28th and the fog hid us from her. The pilot says she is a French schooner out of Bayonne that stays off Vila Franca and Santa Maria and won't come into the road under the São Brás guns. Water is 1.9 tons and foul, provisions 21 days. Senhor Medeiros at the quay sells water and fresh meat, and the spring under the fort is sweet. High water is about 18:45 with an 18-foot rise. The road is open from east round south to west, so put to sea if it blows from there. The sealed letter for Senhor Bettencourt of Horta is still in the cabin. Standing orders: Hourly Shaping and trim-the-yards are belayed, and tend-the-sheets-on-the-watch is live. Lesson for whoever sits here: without the deck, give no helm or sail orders, and say so plainly. Mr Bowen is resting; keep watch on the cable, the weather and any sail.

2 July 09:43 forenoon watch. Fayal approach: pilot Mr Terra aboard 08:49; ship repeatedly lost way and made sternway under reefed main and headsails in a 22-26 kn SW by W wind (veered from N during the night); boxed off at 09:22; best bower let go 09:32 in 46 fathoms, dragged, veered to 232-240 fathoms, then ship took the ground forward at 09:43 on sand and shell on the Praia by the old fort, 1½ fathoms, drawing 9 ft, heel 9°, tide falling; carpenter reports her strained and making water. Master reckons she floats at the flood about 16:30 (HW Fayal ~20:30). I ordered the kedge laid astern (to the E into deep water). Pilot Terra says sand, soft, wind off land blows her off, stays until the flood; port captain would send lighters (port's business: needs the captain's word). Lessons: (1) tell the captain at once when readings show sternway, (2) don't order sails mid-evolution, (3) anchor in 35-40 fathoms on sand needs full scope; 46 fathoms with wind 24 kn dragged. Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, 09:43 forenoon watch, 2 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter is aground forward in Fayal Road on the sand and small shell of the Praia by the old fort, 1½ fathoms by the chart, she draws 9 feet, heeling about 8-9°, tide falling, wind SW by W 24 kn off the land, glass 29.81 falling fast. The carpenter reports her strained and making water; the ship has no well to sound yet. The master reckons she floats at the flood, about half past four this afternoon (HW Fayal ~20:30). Best bower is down with all 240 fathoms, bar-taut; the kedge is being laid astern to the E into deep water by the boat, on the pilot's advice. All sail is being furled. Pilot Mr Terra of Fayal is aboard and says it is soft ground, she will not break, the wind blows her off, and the port captain would send lighters if asked (port's business: the captain's word). Watch on the pumps and the leak. Lessons for whoever sits here: tell the captain at once when the readings show 'making sternway'; never order sails or yards while an evolution is in hand; take the full scope in deep water; and without the deck give no helm or sail orders. The captain has the deck. Ashore at Fayal are Mr Ruiz the clerk, Senhor Bettencourt the merchant (the sealed letter for him is in the cabin), and Mr Josiah Hale the supercargo. The French schooner (12 guns, black) was last reported off Santa Maria; the Conceição brigantine from Funchal is overdue. The purse is £928 8s; water 5.7 tons, provisions 33 days. The captain asked for the stand-down because he needs a break.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handover, 02:30 middle watch, 3 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter lies moored in Fayal Road on two bowers (best 240 fathoms, small 120, both full out) in 22 fathoms, kedge catted at the bows, holding all night within a cable of the account (fixes each glass: Guia SW by S, town W, Espalamaca N by E). She swings with the slack tide each few minutes; that is the 'cable slack at the turn' log noise, harmless, though two cables may foul her hawse if she goes on swinging. Wind NNW 9 kn, glass 30.21 rising fast, hazy, heavy confused sea with a westerly swell. Well an inch and steady (sounded each glass, last 02:27); lead no bottom at 20. Hands: starboard/larboard in watches, 12 on deck. Ashore: Bettencourt has the letter and wants forty pipes (20 tons) of Pico wine consigned to his son in Falmouth at £4 a ton, £40 on signing the bill of lading tomorrow and £40 on delivery; he'll sell the captain wine at £32 the ton for his own account; lighters from Madalena come out after dark tomorrow night, sail on the land breeze before dawn, keep it quiet because of the Basque (Etcheverry's black schooner). Mr Hale, supercargo of Salem, has agreed a £5 passage to Madeira, hammock with the hands; chest to the beach when the boat is sent. I advised: heave in the small bower at first light (twilight 05:36), ride by the best bower alone, then shift to a berth in 10 to 15 fathoms on the flood with Mr Terra's help and a rested watch. The captain has the deck and sends me ashore in the morning to fetch Hale and give Bettencourt the word on the lighters. Lessons: no anchor left to let go with both cables out; keep a stream/kedge ready; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'.

The captain says avast sounding the well (it is holding, an inch); keep the lead and a fix each glass. Plan tonight: lighters about 22:00, hold hatches covered till dusk; captain below resting; larboard on deck, starboard below.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
