16:47 3 July. Captain has the deck again and told me to rest before sunset. Fixes all day within a cable of the account (38° 32' N, 28° 37' W); variation 22° 30' W by azimuth (3 July); both bowers hold. Ate and drank at 16:47. Tonight: lighters ~22:00 from Madalena (two, 20 pipes each, Ruiz in the first with bill of lading + £40 gold; provisions 8 days from Bettencourt £10 and 2 butts of fresh water free; captain's own 8 pipes marked C, £128 to Ruiz when stowed); sail on the land breeze before dawn: needs the small bower weighed, the kedge catted, best bower hove in to short stay, topsail; remember hard lessons: tell the captain at once on 'making sternway'.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handover, 16:47 first dog watch, 3 July 1806. Sherbourne rides moored on two bowers (best 240 fathoms, small 120, both full out; kedge catted at the bows) in 22 fathoms; fixes each glass all day within a cable of the account (38° 32' N, 28° 37' W): Espalamaca N by E, town W, Magdalena E. Fog lifted 14:45, now clear, wind N by E 7 kn, glass 30.24 steady, moderate sea from the north. Well an inch and steady since the copper went on; you told me to avast sounding it. Variation 22° 30' W by azimuth (3 July). Water 5.5 tons, provisions 32 days. Tonight: Bettencourt's two lighters from Madalena (20 pipes each, six men and patrão each) alongside about 22:00 with Ruiz in the first, the bill of lading and £40 gold; also 8 days of provisions (£10) and two butts of fresh water free; your own 8 pipes marked C (£128 to Ruiz when stowed) and a present case of bottles; one hooded lantern at the gangway; the Frenchman in the brown coat is asking after us, so keep the hour quiet. The sail on the land breeze before dawn will need the small bower weighed, kedge catted, best bower hove short, topsail set; I'd call the larboard and starboard together for that. I have eaten and drunk and am going below to rest until called.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

02:14 4 July. Chart (whole): Azores cluster at left, our noon marks run from Falmouth top right down the Biscay coast and Portugal then SW across to the Azores; Madeira group alone at the bottom centre, about ESE of Fayal (roughly 330 miles south, 490-570 miles east by the picture/plain sailing). So Funchal bears about SE by E (≈122-125°) from Fayal, distance ≈ 600-670 miles. We are at 38° 27' N, 28° 36' W, running S at 4 kn with the wind N by W 10 kn astern; deep water (387 fathoms). I will haul up SE by E when the captain permits (he gave general authority to steer as needed).
Allowed by the captain: shape a course for.

04:04 4 July. Under way SE (140°) since 02:18, shaped for Funchal (668 miles ESE by account), the captain asleep till sunrise at least; wind NNW 8 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant, 4 kn, deep water (420 fathoms); account 38° 21' N, 28° 31' W; no danger within 10 miles. Lead standing order belayed. The captain wants me to hold this course while we clear the Azores, then shape direct once São Lourenço (St Lawrence) is behind us, and to wake him if the wind goes easterly.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until sunrise.
Stood by until a sail sighted.

06:45 4 July. Chart (passage span, 150 miles across, ship at centre 38° 12' N, 28° 22' W): the captain's pencilled lay line leaves the ship bearing ~122° true (ESE-SE by E) straight toward a point 10 miles S of Funchal road; I am steering SE (141°) so I'm ~19° south of that line. Azores islands lie north of us (Pico and Fayal, São Jorge, Graciosa, São Miguel NE far, Santa Maria not drawn but at about 36° 57' N, 25° 05' W). Own reckoning of the line: 652 miles; it would pass about 24 miles south of Santa Maria (the schooner's last reported ground) and about 9-10 miles south of Ponta do Pargo, the west point of Madeira. The wind N by W 10 kn gives a true wind angle of ~133° off the bow on 122°, a good run. A safer compromise would be to hold SE to 36°30' N then haul to ~114° (cost ~30 miles, passes ~80 miles south of Santa Maria).
Stood by until a word on deck.

06:47 4 July. Captain agreed: hold SE (140°) for now; we lay a new line once we may pass further clear of the Basque's grounds (south of Santa Maria / São Miguel). Plan: hold to about 36° 30' N, 26° 40' W, then haul to ESE (114°). Keep a masthead lookout, report any sail, check the account against landmarks (Pico N by W five leagues at 06:42).
Stood by until a sail sighted.
Stood by until a sail sighted.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handover, 13:37 afternoon watch, 4 July 1806. Sherbourne is under way for Funchal, steering SE (140-141°) and making good SE by S (142-147°) at 4 to 5 knots, with the wind N by W 11 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant set (main gaff topsail furled, storm canvas unbent), the yards braced 136° and the fore-and-aft sheets trimmed at 13:37. Clear, glass 30.25 steady. Noon observation: latitude 37° 54' N; the account moved a mile and a half NNW; account now 37° 51' N, 28° 01' W, good to two miles; Pico NNW 13 leagues, St George N 17, Caldeira NW by N 18, Santa Barbara NE by N 20; 1018 fathoms. Well an inch at the last sounding (not sounded since 02:00 by my orders; you can order it if wanted). Purse £842 15s; manifest 24 tons of Pico wine (20 for Bettencourt's son at Falmouth, 4 on your own account, marked C), room for 18; provisions 39 days, water 6.5 tons (54 days). Passenger: Mr Hale, £5 paid. Course plan agreed with you: hold SE to about 36° 30' N, 26° 40' W so we pass well south of Santa Maria and São Miguel and clear of the Basque's grounds, then haul to ESE (114°) for the point 10 miles south of Funchal road, Madeira 650 miles ESE. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch; 'heave the lead' is belayed (deep water). Watch: the masthead lookout reports every sail; none yet. Wake the captain for a sail, an easterly shift or the wind coming ahead, a strain warning, or land. Eaten and drunk at 12:01 (biscuit, cheese, scuttle-butt); going below to rest until called.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

16:06 4 July. Woke rested after sleeping 13:38–16:06. The captain holds the deck. Under way SE (141°) at 5 kn, the wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, account 37° 41' N, 27° 52' W, 1162 fathoms, no sail sighted; Pico NW by N 17 leagues, St George N by W 21, Santa Bárbara NNE 22. Plan: hold SE to about 36° 30' N, 26° 40' W then haul ESE (114°) for the point 10 miles south of Funchal road.
Stood by until a word on deck.

06:44 5 July 1806. Stand-down at the captain's word (he is taking a break; the game is saved). State: Sherbourne cutter under way for Funchal (shaped by the captain's word), steering SE by E (119°) since 00:03, making good SE (132°) at 5-6 knots by the log, wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant set; account 36° 54' N, 27° 44' W (really 26° 44' W by account), Ponta Delgada NE 23½ leagues, 1365 fathoms, glass 30.24 falling slightly, no sail sighted. Course plan: pencil line from the captain to a point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing São Lourenço by 20 miles; Madeira about 450 miles ESE. Purse £842 15s; 24 tons of Pico wine aboard (20 for Bettencourt's son in Falmouth, 4 for the captain on his own account, marked C); sealed letter for Falmouth in the captain's keeping; Mr Hale (supercargo, Salem) aboard for Madeira; provisions 39 days, water 6.4 tons. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch, trim the yards on the watch; 'heave the lead' (mate's) belayed. The French schooner (Etcheverry, Basque) was last said to be off Santa Maria; we are well south of her grounds. Lessons carried: no 'ring the bell' order exists; 'shape a course for' needs the captain's word by name for a new destination; 'how am I' shows hunger and thirst, so eat and drink ('Eat something', 'Drink some water') every watch; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'; keep the lead going near land; never weigh the last anchor in fog without the captain's word.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, 06:44 morning watch, 5 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter is under way for Funchal, steering SE by E (119°) and making good SE (132°) at 5-6 knots, the wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant set, glass 30.24 falling slightly, fair weather, no sail in sight. Account 36° 54' N, 26° 44' W, 1365 fathoms, Ponta Delgada NE 23½ leagues; we are well south of the Basque's reported grounds off Santa Maria. The captain's pencil line leads to a point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing São Lourenço by 20 miles; Madeira about 450 miles ESE. Aboard: 24 tons of Pico wine (20 for Bettencourt's son at Falmouth, 4 for the captain's own account, marked C), the sealed letter for Falmouth in the captain's keeping, Mr Hale (supercargo of Salem, passage paid £5), purse £842 15s, provisions 39 days, water 6.4 tons. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch, trim the yards on the watch; 'heave the lead' belayed in deep water (turn it on near land). The captain has the deck and is taking a break; he asked me to journal and stand down. For whoever sits here next: no 'ring the bell' order exists; a new destination needs the captain's word by name; eat and drink with 'Eat something' and 'Drink some water' each watch (check with 'how am I'); tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'; keep the lead going in uncertain water; never weigh the last anchor in fog without the captain's word.
Stood down by the officer of the watch: its own word.

captain.text: The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: the moon is sixteen degrees up and in distance of Regulus; a lunar may be taken this evening if he pleases, the last being a day old

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: the glass has fallen fast — seven hundredths in three hours to 30.23 — and the wind has hauled round to east by south and gone light and variable; she carries all sail in two knots of way and there is no hurry, but I would not be surprised at squalls out of the east as the glass drops, and thought you would wish to know it at once

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: the moon is seventeen degrees up and in distance of Markab — a lunar may be had this watch, if he pleases and the haze will let the stars be seen

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Tregarthen Aye sir, clear by our account, only one other sail sighted since we left Falmouth, and they stayed well clear of us on their own. Thank you for the word on the wind, and of the privateer.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: St Lawrence is 270 miles by account, about 46 hours at our 6-knot average, so the forenoon of the day after tomorrow. It could be 55 hours if the wind stays light and 40 if it freshens. Longitude is good to only 30 miles. I'll take a noon latitude at 12:51. Thank you for the note on formality.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: noon: latitude by observation 39° 01' N, so the account moved 3½ miles north. Course made good WSW, 147 miles in the day, longitude by account 20° 23' W. Ponta Delgada is 86½ leagues W by S. Wind N by W 11 knots, glass 30.15 steady, nothing in sight.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: I'll set the square sail if you wish it, sir, but I'd advise against it. The wind is N by W 11 knots and 62° on the starboard bow, and a course WSW has her close-hauled. A square sail won't draw, and it would be aback or shaking and slow her. It would pay if the wind came abaft the beam. Shall I still set it, or wait for a shift?

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: aye, sir, I'm on deck for the morning watch. I'm rested and ready, so you may go below and turn in. By the account she's on WSW 242°, 6¾ knots by the log, and the wind is NNW 10 with the glass at 30.32. The account puts us at 38° 12' N, 22° 18' W, with Ponta Delgada 54 leagues W by S. Nothing is in sight. Give me the deck when you're ready.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: noon is near and no sight of land yet. By the account we're at 37° 48' N, 23° 18' W, and Ponta Delgada is 37½ leagues W. The run was 155 miles since noon yesterday, with the wind NNW 10 and the glass 30.42 rising. She's rolling heavily, which may mean a swell from the northwest. I'll take the noon latitude and report it. Santa Maria's peak should show first, so I'll keep a lookout aloft.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: land in sight yet. By the account we're at 37° 48' N, 23° 18' W, with Ponta Delgada 37½ leagues W. The run was 155 miles in the day, wind NNW 10, glass 30.42 rising, and she's rolling heavily. I'll take the noon latitude and report it, and I'll keep a lookout aloft for Santa Maria's peak.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: sir, but the course is yours to alter, not mine. The wind is N and well forward of the beam, so hauling up for Ponta Delgada (W by account) costs us little. One warning: your Hourly Shaping order re-shapes for St Lawrence every hour, and it will undo a helm order you give for Delgada. If you want Delgada, the order wants changing or belaying. Wind N 10, glass 30.47, no land in sight.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: steering W has the wind 42° on the starboard bow and she's lifting. The square sails and topsail are shaking, and she's down to 4 knots with 4° of leeway. Two choices: (1) keep her away to WSW (about 245°) so the yards fill, or (2) take in the square sail and topgallant and hold W close-hauled. I'd rather keep away. Your word on the helm, sir, as the course is yours.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: at midnight Ponta Delgada is 16 leagues WNW by account, so about 8 hours at 6 knots. Our longitude is only good to 40 miles, so São Miguel could be nearer than that, and it's dark with the moon down. I advise a good lookout at the masthead and forward, and that we keep the lead ready. Since it's no moonlight I'd also shorten sail from about 03:00 so we raise the land at dawn rather than at night. Wind NNW 9, glass 30.54, nothing in sight. I'll call you at once on any sighting of land.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: at midnight Ponta Delgada is 16 leagues WNW by account, about 8 hours at 6 knots. Our longitude is good to only 40 miles, so São Miguel could be nearer, and it's dark with no moon. I advise doubled lookouts and the lead ready, and shortening sail from about 03:00 so we raise the land at dawn. Wind NNW 9, glass 30.54, nothing in sight. I'll call you at once on any sight of land.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: ho, sir. The lookout has the Pico Alto of St Mary's bearing SW by W, 15 leagues, and the high land of the east end of St Michael's NW by W, 23 leagues. That doesn't agree with our account, which put Ponta Delgada 8½ leagues NNW. By these two bearings we're a good deal further east than the account allowed, so the longitude was out by well over 40 miles. I'd take a fix from these bearings and re-shape for Ponta Delgada. I'd also keep her as she goes until you decide. Wind N by W 8, glass 30.57, clear, nothing else in sight.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: at 8 bells we're on WNW 292°, close-hauled under fore-and-aft sail, making only 3 knots and 3° leeway with the wind N 7 and falling. Ponta Delgada is WNW 19 leagues, so at this speed it's 19 hours or more. The glass is 30.59 steady. If the wind stays light I'd consider the square sails again whenever it comes abaft the beam, or a long board. I'll keep the watch and a lookout, and call you on any sail or shift.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: the wind has backed to N by E 8 knots, which eases us on WNW 287°. By the account the Formigas (the Ants) lie SW by S, three leagues, and the shoal south-east of them S by W, three leagues, and it's hazy with a few miles' visibility. We're heading away from them on WNW and the wind lets us hold that or better, so I see no danger, but I'd not stand to the south. I've told the lookout to watch for breakers. Ponta Delgada is WNW 16½ leagues.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: ho, sir: a sail abeam to larboard, bearing SW by S, two leagues. She's to leeward of us and I can't yet make out her colours or her rig. St Michael's east end is NW by N, 8 leagues, and the Pico Alto of St Mary's S by W, 9 leagues. I'll report her colours when they show and watch her bearing for closing.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: has come down, sir, with visibility a cable. The schooner was last glassed 5 miles off to the SW and is lost in it. She showed no colours and had hauled her wind toward us earlier, and Mr Pascoe doesn't like her. We're on WNW 292° at about 3 knots with the wind N 7. The nearest land is St Michael's, about 10 leagues WNW by the fix, so there's no lee-shore danger yet, but I'd put a lookout on the bows and keep the hands ready. Shall I call all hands to quarters, or heave to? Both are yours to order.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Pascoe's advice, sir: in this fog we might haul our wind a point or two and keep quiet, with no bell and no hailing, so the schooner steers for where she last saw us bound and passes astern. It's for you to decide. Lookouts are posted in each bow and on each quarter. I'll hold the course until you give the word.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: heaving to is the captain's manoeuvre and I can't give it on a word relayed. Please say "you may heave to" or give the order yourself, and I'll have it done quietly at once. Until then I'm holding WNW 292°.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: don't think we're clear yet, sir. The fog was still thick at 5 o'clock, visibility a cable, with nothing sighted or heard and the lookouts at both bows and quarters. We've drifted about 11 miles since noon, mostly leeway (17° or so), and the account has Ponta Delgada NW by W 9½ leagues. I'd give it a glass more, or until the lookout sees a mile or more, then fill away and make sail. If the fog lasts into the dark I'd rather lie to than close the land blind. Shall I fill away now or wait? Say the word and I'll do it quietly.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: fog has cleared, sir, and the horizon is open. The east end of St Michael's bears N, 5 leagues, and the Pico Alto of St Mary's S by E, 12 leagues. The wind has veered to NNE 8, fair for Ponta Delgada, which is NW by W 8½ leagues by account. The schooner isn't in sight. Sunset is near, though, and I'd not close the land in the dark. I propose to fill away now, set the square sail, and run down so as to be off the port by about midnight, then stand off and on until daylight. Your word, sir, or shall I fill away and make sail?

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Mr Pascoe hears church bells faint on the starboard bow, about NW by W, and takes them for Ponta Delgada at Sunday Mass. That agrees with the account, which has Ponta Delgada Road WNW 2½ leagues. We're hove to in fog with visibility a cable and 172 fathoms of water by the chart. The coast is high and steep-to, so I'd not close it blind. I advise waiting for the fog to lift, with the lead going, and then standing in on the bearing the bells give. I don't have the deck, sir; it's yours.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: she was taken aback at 09:25 with the wind 66-73° on the starboard bow, the jib set and the mainsail loosed. I've borne away a point on my own word to fill her and gather way. Ponta Delgada Road bears NW 3 miles by account (good to 5), visibility a few miles and hazy, no bottom at 184 fathoms. I'll hold her away until she has steerage way, then await your word.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, the kedge is laid out 90 fathoms SE by E and the hawser taut to the capstan; it came home along the ground at 10:23, she lies too hard on to be hove off before more water. The wind has shifted to WNW (26 kn, squally, glass 29.80 and falling fast), now 15 degrees on the larboard bow; mean still SW by W. The well has three inches and is gaining slowly, which the carpenter reckons a few inches on sand. All sail furled. The flood serves from about a quarter past two; I would heave again on the kedge at the half-tide. I am watching the well each glass and the cable's strain.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 12:05: she lies as before, well an inch and steady, pumped out at each glass, cable 0.01 of its rating. The wind is W by N, 28 knots, mean 31, squalls of 34 with rain; the glass 29.82, risen 2 hundredths in the last hour but still falling fast over three. The hands are reported worn out, 27 on deck and none at work; if you wish it, a part of them might be sent below to rest before the flood, when we must heave on the kedge at the half-tide, about 17:45 by the master's reckoning or sooner by the pilot's.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 13:05: a heavy sea has got up from the west and she pitches heavily on the ground; wind W 30 kn, mean 29, glass 29.83 steady. Well an inch and steady, pumped dry at each glass. The flood should begin to serve about 14:15. I would watch the well closely if she pounds as the sea builds, and have the hands rested for heaving on the kedge at the half-tide.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye aye, sir. A word for your weighing, as I see it: gusts are 34 to 40 knots, and a topsail laid aback in them will strain the topmast hard and may drive the kedge home again; I would wait for the half-flood, and if you do back it, have it clewed up at the first sign of her moving, as Mr Pascoe says. Once afloat she rides by the best bower with all 240 fathoms out and the Praia under her lee, so I would have the small bower cleared away at the bow with its cable bent and ready to let go before the kedge is weighed, and take in the best bower promptly to a short scope, or she may drag back on the sand. The well stands at an inch and steady; the glass is rising slowly, 29.84.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 13:38: she lies as before, well an inch and steady, heel 3°, a heavy sea from the west, wind W by S 29 kn (a moderate gale), glass 29.82 steady. Heaving short was belayed at 13:13 with the kedge on the bottom, 90 fathoms out; nothing is in hand. The flood should be making from about 14:15; the master is at the day's work below. I have not touched the kedge or the sails. Say the word when you would have me work the gear, and I would rest the larboard watch till then.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 15:13: well dry, pumped out at each glass. The kedge is hove short, 12 fathoms out with the cable a-stay; she is still aground forward, heel 2°, wind W 28 kn, glass 29.87 rising. The flood has been making since about 14:15, and by the pilot she should feel it by the half-tide and float some time before 17:00. I will report the moment the readings change from 'aground'. When she floats, the best bower has all 240 fathoms out; the small bower is still at the bows.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 16:00: still aground forward, heel 3°, a heavy sea pitching her on the ground, wind W 29 mean, gusts to 36, glass 29.86 rising slowly. The well has two inches and is gaining a little since the last pumping; the carpenter has not pumped her this glass yet. The kedge is hove short at 12 fathoms. By the pilot's reckoning of high water about 20:30 and the flood from about 14:15, she should lift in the next hour or so; I will report the moment she floats. Mr Pascoe's advice was to back the topsail only at the half-flood with hands standing by to clew it up.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 16:09: the topsail is set and shaking, straining at the bolt-ropes in the gusts of 31 to 36 knots; she is still aground, heel 1°, no way on, the cable bar-taut, well two inches. I see you are taking the topsail in already, which I think right at this strain. I'll sound the well each glass and watch for her to move.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 17:47: the lead gave four fathoms and a half, sand and small shell, which tripped the Lead Warning; the water is the tide's and the account holds, the fix of 17:02 within half a cable. She is still aground forward, heel 2°, no way on, the cable bar-taut at 0.01, wind W 23 kn lulling, glass 29.90 rising. Well dry at the last pumping (17:44). Storm trysail and storm jib are bent and furled; the topsail hangs in the gear, the mainsail and jib are unbent. The flood has run three and a half hours and she is not yet afloat, so I would expect her to lift within the hour; the kedge is hove short at 12 fathoms with the topsail ready to back when you say.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 18:41: the topsail aback is straining at the bolt-ropes in a gust of 30 knots (mean 24, W); she is still aground forward, no way on, heel 0°, the kedge short at 12 fathoms, well an inch (pumped dry 18:32). Lead four fathoms and a half in the chains. I have not touched the sail, as it is yours; I would clew it up if the strain worsens or a squall comes, and would not leave it standing aback unattended since she may start suddenly and go astern onto the kedge. Mr Pascoe looks for her to lift about seven or eight bells of the first watch.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 19:21: she is AFLOAT, hove off by the kedge on the flood, riding by the best bower with the cable slack (240 fathoms out), well an inch (dry at 19:02), lead four and a half. But the topsail is still aback (one reef) with the kedge hove short at 12 fathoms: she has no way on yet, but if she gathers sternway she will go back over her own kedge, and the Praia is a cable on the larboard bow. I would clew up the topsail now and weigh the kedge, then heave in the best bower to a short stay. Wind W by N 22 kn, glass 29.95. Shall I take in the topsail?

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 19:24: the topsail is taken in. She is afloat and has swung her head to W (274°) with the helm over at 35 degrees, wind W by N 23 kn, so she is head to wind and land (the Praia) bears right ahead at a cable, but the wind blows from the land and she has no way on. The best bower's cable is slack at 240 fathoms; the kedge is short at 12 fathoms and weighing is in hand. Well an inch. The glass is rising fast, 29.97. I would have the best bower hove in to a short scope and the small bower ready at the cathead, and the helm put amidships, in case she gathers sternway on the slack cable before the bower bites.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, she is MAKING STERNWAY at 4 knots, heading NW by W with the wind W by N 23 kn, as the readings stand at 19:35: the best bower's cable is slack at 240 fathoms and cannot check her, and the small bower is being let go in 21 fathoms and a half (veering to 106 fathoms). The Point of Espalamaca is three cables abeam to starboard, no land is close astern in the open water to the ESE (the Bank of Fayal lies SSE two miles, 8 fathoms at the account), and the well is an inch. The topsail is in the gear. Once the small bower bites I would check her with it and heave the best bower short to its scope, as the deep water makes it a long job.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 19:37: urgent line 'the small bower is dragging' came while the cable was still being veered: 77 fathoms of 106 out, so it should bite as the scope runs out. She is still making sternway at 3 knots, heading NW by W, the wind W by N 24 kn, 10 fathoms by the chart under her and falling away to the ESE; the Point of Espalamaca is three cables on the starboard bow, the Bank of Fayal SSE two miles. The best bower's cable lies slack, 240 fathoms out. I have given no order while the anchoring is in hand. If the small bower does not hold at full scope I would veer to the clinch rather than let her run on, and consider setting the topsail to give her steerage.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 19:38: the small bower has bitten and she is stopped: speed 0, no way on, 106 fathoms of the small bower and all 240 of the best bower out, her head NW by W with the wind WNW 23 kn. The fix is the account again, within two cables; the Point of Espalamaca is three cables on the starboard bow, the Magdalena shoals and the Bank of Fayal are to the SE at a mile and a half. She is in 14 to 23 fathoms, deep for the holding; both cables are long and the best is bar-taut at 0.04. I have given no further order. My suggestion is to ride as she is through the evening with a hand at the lead and a cast each half-hour for dragging, rest the hands by watches since they are worn out, keep the pumps each glass, and heave in to a better berth in the roads nearer the town in the morning watch when she has rested; I will do whatever you direct about the best bower.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Understood, sir: I keep the deck, keep her moored, and unmoor only in the worst case while you are ashore. Two things as I see them at 19:40: she dragged about two cables ESE between 19:36 and 19:39 and stopped when the small bower bit, but the log has not yet said 'holds again', and both cables are now out to the end (240 on the best bower, 120 on the small), so there is no anchor left to let go; the Bank of Fayal lies SSE a mile and a half. If you can, wait a quarter hour to see her hold before you leave her. I will keep the lead going each half-glass, the pumps each glass (well an inch), the hands in watches, and a fix at each bell, and if she comes home toward the Bank I shall set the topsail, weigh the small bower and stand off under way, which is the worst case you name. Give me the boat's time ashore and back if you can, and tell me what hands go with you.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Thank you, sir, I stand corrected: 'how am I' said I was thirsty and hungry, last fed at 06:01. I have taken a biscuit and cheese and a drink at the scuttle-butt on the quarterdeck, and I'd urge the same on you and the hands. She holds as she lies, speed 1 kn at most, leeway 20 degrees, the lead giving 4½ fathoms in the chains. I keep the deck.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 19:45: fix of this minute puts her within a cable of the account: she holds on the two bowers though she sheers (heading WSW, 36° on the starboard bow, speed under 1 kn, helm over); no bottom at 20 fathoms. I have piped down so the larboard watch has the deck and the starboard may rest and eat; the pumps next at the glass, the lead each half-glass.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Welcome aboard, sir. Report at 02:27: she has ridden the night on both bowers (240 and 120 fathoms out), no dragging, every fix within a cable of the account, well an inch and steady, lead no bottom at 20. Wind NNW 9 kn, a gentle breeze and falling light, glass 30.19 rising fast; a heavy confused sea with a westerly swell. She lies head to the N with the Point of Espalamaca four cables right ahead on the slack cable, so she is swinging with the turn of the tide. The kedge hangs at the bows. The log has no word from Mr Hale or Bettencourt's lighters yet. I hold the deck by your general authority and give it back whenever you say.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, the slack at the turn is no annoyance and no danger of itself: with the wind down to 9 knots the tide is swinging her about her bower and the cable only goes slack at each turn, and it has held all night within a cable. My advice is to shift the berth, but not now. (1) It is 02:30, hazy, and the hands are not rested; the best bower is 240 fathoms out in 22 fathoms, a long steep heave, and the berth we want is in 17 fathoms or less near the town, among the whalers' anchors, so I would not shift in the dark without the pilot. (2) Bettencourt's lighters come tomorrow night, so there is the whole day to shift and nothing is gained by hurry. (3) Nearer the town also means nearer Etcheverry's friends ashore, and Bettencourt asked for quiet; our berth is out of the way. (4) A real objection to staying two-anchored is that she is swinging round with the tide and may foul her hawse, so at first light (twilight from 05:36) I would heave in the small bower, ride by the best bower alone, then with Mr Terra aboard shift to the berth he names, in 10 to 15 fathoms, on the flood, with the full watch fresh. I'll keep her as she is until you say, with the lead and fixes going.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Back aboard, sir, with Senhor Bettencourt's letter for his son at Falmouth, now before you. His answer: two lighters from Madalena, twenty pipes each, six men and a patrão apiece, away at dusk and alongside about ten tonight; Ruiz in the first lighter with the bill of lading to sign and £40 in gold; one hooded lantern at the gangway only, the fall and slings rigged beforehand, since a pipe is half a ton; we lie where we are, out of sight of the quay. He would not take the Madeira: he wants it from your hand. Ruiz reports no schooner in the Road, the black schooner far east off Santa Maria last week, but a Frenchman in a brown coat posing as a wine buyer stood the watermen drinks last night asking what the English cutter carried and when she sailed, and went out toward the beach at Porto Pim an hour before midnight. Mr Hale, who was asked too and said nothing, is fit and his chest is corded behind the tavern bar; he did not come off in this boat, so he's to come to the quay. I advise a double lookout tonight, nobody to speak of the hour, and the boat's crew armed.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Welcome aboard, sir. 09:10 report: she rides as you left her on both bowers (240 and 120 out), well an inch, the glass 30.20 steady, wind N by W 9 kn; fog down since 07:48, visibility a cable and nothing in sight, so no fix can be taken (the account stands); the last cast no bottom. The boat is hoisted in; Mr Pascoe's heeling work (guns and water to larboard, masthead tackle to the boat, copper on the forefoot) has not been started that I can see, the hands having been on the boat and the lead; I have given no order for it as it is yours. The fog should serve tonight's lighters but means a lookout on the quarterdeck and a bell rung for the boats; the Bank of Fayal is SSE 1.5 miles.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 14:46: the fog has lifted, clear, visibility to the horizon, wind NNE light. Fix at once: Espalamaca N by E, the town W, the Magdalena E, lines met within a cable, the account kept (38° 32' N, 28° 37' W), so she has not dragged. Both bowers hold, well an inch, lead no bottom. Nothing sail-like in sight but the Peak of Pico (ESE, four leagues) and the Caldeira (NW by W, six miles), and three more marks I have not read. I'd still keep the larboard watch easy on deck and the starboard below till the lighters at ten, and keep the hatches covered until dusk so the shore sees nothing laid out.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 20:00: I have the deck. Fix of this minute: Espalamaca N by E, town W, Magdalena E, within half a cable of the account; both bowers hold; the lead is going. Wind N by W 9 kn, clear, bright moon. The lighters are due about 22:00 and the freight is already written up in the manifest. I'll call the starboard watch at 21:30 to rig the whip and slings and take off the hatches, and keep the lantern hooded; and at the first sight of a boat I will hail her and report. I'd also be glad to know the Pico wine rule: your eight pipes marked C are to be paid to Mr Ruiz when stowed, £128, and Bettencourt's £40 freight is to come in gold in the first lighter, so I'll have the purse and the bill of lading ready for you at the gangway.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 20:05: fog has come down again, visibility a cable and nothing in sight, so fixes are off. She holds on the account and the last cast gave no bottom. The fog suits our secrecy but may keep the lighters from finding us at ten. I'd have a lookout forward and one aft, and a hand with the lead, and when we hear oars, a single bell stroke and the hooded lantern at the gangway to bring them in; I'll do that when you say or at the first sound of oars.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye, sir. 22:08: the bell has been struck once as you ordered, though the ship's grammar has no order for it ('ring the bell' and 'strike the bell' are refused), and Mr Ruiz's account of the stroke says the second lighter is a cable astern with the creak of heavy oars. I have the lookouts at the quarter and the hooded lantern at the gangway. The first lighter's four tons are struck down; the manifest reads 4 tons, room for 38. Purse £854 18s after Ruiz's £128 and the £40 freight. Forty pipes (20 tons) for Falmouth come next, then the provisions and two butts of water; I'll have the hold's whip and slings manned by the starboard watch and see that the pipes are chocked and stowed low and well forward and aft to keep her trim. The fog hides us from the quay; with this wind (NNW 8 kn) and the land breeze to come we could weigh before dawn.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 22:13: all forty pipes are below (the manifest reads 24 tons of Pico wine, room for 18), and Mr Ruiz says the bread, beef, beans and the two butts of water are lying in the lighter's stern sheets and need only be sent for; they come up the side when asked. I will not try 'send for' myself, as sending for provisions is for your word. Do you wish me to have them hoisted in? I would not leave the lighter alongside long, with the fog and a Frenchman about. After that I propose we weigh: heave short the best bower and the small, cat the kedge, set the topsail and stand out on the land breeze before dawn, if you consent, since the wine is stowed, the provisions are aboard and the fog hides us.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 22:38: provisioning is done: 8 days of provisions stowed (provisions now for 40 days), 1 ton of water in (6.5 tons, 55 days), Mr Ruiz has gone down the side and the Madalena lighters are pulling away toward the Guia. The manifest reads 24 tons of Pico wine, room for 18; purse £842 15s. The ship is still moored, wind N by W 10 kn, glass 30.24, fog thick, moon 24° high behind the cloud. She is deeper by 24 tons, so she will answer slower on weighing. I await your word to heave short on the small bower and then the best bower; with only a gentle breeze I'd weigh the kedge first and the small bower next, but not before the hands are called and the fog allows us to see the Point.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, the small bower is aweigh (23:04) and she is MAKING STERNWAY at 1 knot, the best bower cable slack at 240 fathoms, heading NNW with the wind N by W 9 kn, fog thick, depth unknown (no bottom in the last cast), moon behind the cloud. With the small bower up and the best bower slack, the Praia is to the SW and the Point of Espalamaca NE, so sternway takes her SSE toward the Bank of Fayal (1½ miles). I suggest you heave in the best bower now to a short stay so it bites, or let me heave the lead and call the hands to the capstan; I am waiting for your word since you said wait on the best till the fog clears.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 23:22: the fog has thinned to a haze with visibility a few miles; Espalamaca N by E four cables, the town W eight cables, the Guia SW by S seven cables, and a fix within half a cable of the account, so we have not dragged. The small bower is catted and fished; she rides by the best bower with 216 fathoms out and the strain 0.00, heaving short in hand; the kedge is aweigh at the bows. Wind N 9 kn, glass 30.25, moon 17° up. I await your word to weigh the best bower and make sail on the land breeze for Funchal.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 00:14: the best bower is aweigh, no anchor down, the small bower and kedge at the bows. She has no way on yet, heading N 358° with the wind N by W 10 kn and 13° on the larboard bow, the topsail aback and the storm trysail and storm jib shaking. The land of Fayal is three cables on the larboard bow (NW by W), Espalamaca NNE eight cables, the Bank of Fayal SSE a mile and a half, 17½ fathoms at the last cast. She is deep with 24 tons of wine, so she'll be slow to pay off; mind the land ahead if she falls off to larboard. I hold the deck and am ready if you want a hand with the lead, the yards or the helm.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye, sir: entered in the book as 'heave the lead' by the mate, every glass then heave the lead. It will fire every half hour; say the word and I'll belay it in open water. For the present she is under way, SE by E (129°) at the helm, the Mount of Our Lady of the Guide SW by W six cables, eight cables abeam to starboard; the Bank of Fayal S by E a mile ahead on our starboard bow if we hold SE by E, depth 22 fathoms at the account, the flood carrying us a knot and a half to the NE by the master's reckoning, wind N by W 8 kn on the larboard quarter, with the storm trysail and storm jib set with the topsail. Both bowers are catted and fished.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye sir, I agree: 00:46, by the account she is 38° 31' N, 28° 36' W, the Bank of Fayal SE by S six cables, the Mount of Our Lady of the Guide on the starboard quarter at seven cables W by N, course made good S by E (168°), no bottom at 20 fathoms, a depth of 33 fathoms at the chart. The chart (33 fathoms and a half at low water here, 22½ to 49½ within doubt) bears out that the Bank gives no trouble at nine feet draught, but the account shows us set south and west by the ebb-and-flood swirl round the Guia, so S or S by W gives it a berth of at least a mile before we haul to the east for Funchal. Funchal lies SSE from here some 440 miles by my reckoning: SE by S is the line, so after the Bank I would haul up to SE by S with the wind N by W on the larboard quarter, topsail, trysail, storm jib, fore staysail and foresail set. The standing order to heave the lead every glass is in the book if you want it belayed once we are in deep water.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 01:40: the mainsail is set in the trysail's place and the jib in the storm jib's place; she carries plain sail (topsail, mainsail, fore staysail, foresail, jib) with the storm canvas unbent and stowed, and the light sails furled. Running S (175°) at 3 knots with the wind N by W 10 kn dead astern, the Bank of Fayal now N by W a mile and a half astern, deep water (241 fathoms by the chart), the flood setting us NE a knot and a half. The account is 38° 29' N, 28° 36' W, good to a mile NNE-SSW. When you want, I'd set the topgallant and square sail to use the following wind, which I do not do without your word; and the standing order for the lead is in the book to be belayed, as we are in deep water.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 02:10: topgallant and square sail are set (01:46 and 01:51), plain sail with the main gaff topsail furled, running S at 4 knots with the wind N 10 kn right astern, the account 38° 27' N, 28° 36' W, 353 fathoms by the chart, Fayal four and a half miles astern; no sail in sight. A correction to what I said at 00:46: Funchal lies not SSE but about SE by E (roughly 122°, near 670 miles), 354 miles south and some 570 miles east of Fayal by my plain sailing (cos of the mean latitude 35½° on 11° 42' of longitude), so S takes us down the meridian rather than toward the island, and the northerly wind is on our quarter for SE and abaft the beam for E by S. Now that we are clear of the Bank with deep water and a fair breeze I'd haul up to SE by E and make about 4 knots; I'll steer it if you will give me the helm, and belay the lead standing order, which is not needed in these depths.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Thank you, sir. I looked at the chart (whole): Madeira lies alone at the bottom centre, about SE by E (≈122-125°) from Fayal, some 600 to 670 miles, our noon marks run Falmouth, Biscay, Portugal and the Azores; my earlier 'SSE 440 miles' was wrong. Funchal is a new destination to the game's book, so the 'shape a course' order is refused me; please allow it by name ('you may shape a course for Funchal') or give me the compass course and I'll steer SE by E (129° by account allowing variation 22° 30' W when steering by compass: magnetic course ≈ SE by E ½ E). Meanwhile she runs S at 4 kn with the northerly wind astern; every glass southward costs us time on the line.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, 02:17: course shaped for Funchal by your word: ESE by account (118°), 668 miles, the line crosses the land about the west point of Madeira so we shall haul up to clear Ponta do Pargo and the Porto Moniz coast near the end; steady on ESE (116° heading, 118° ordered), wind N by W 9 kn on the larboard quarter, the yards braced to 100° and the fore-and-aft sheets trimmed, topgallant and square sail set, 4 knots. The lead standing order 'heave the lead' is belayed in these depths (400 fathoms); I'll turn it on again when we raise Madeira. I'll keep the deck; the starboard watch has it and the larboard below.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye, sir: 02:18, borne away two points to SE (140° ordered, heading SE by S 141°), the yards braced 30° from square, wind N by W 10 kn on the larboard quarter, 5 knots by the log, plain sail with square sail and topgallant, no bottom at 400 fathoms. I'll hold SE (140°) through the Azores and well to the south of Pico and São Jorge, and haul up for Funchal as you direct once Sao Lourenço (the east end of Madeira) bears true; the standing order for the lead is belayed.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye aye, sir, good night. 02:42: SE (140°) at 3-5 kn, the wind NNW 8-9 kn on the larboard quarter, topgallant, square sail, topsail, main, jib and staysail set, 433 fathoms, the account 38° 26' N, 28° 34' W; Fayal two leagues astern; all quiet and no sail in sight. I will keep her on this course, and wake you if the wind shifts easterly or comes ahead, a sail is sighted, the strain rises, or the land comes in sight. I have eaten and drunk.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Good morning, sir. Seen from here too: the fix at 05:56 puts the account three cables to the SE by S, 38° 15' N, 28° 25' W, so the account is sound; Pico N four leagues (my 4 leagues at the first sighting 05:38 N by E), the Caldeira of Fayal NW by N eight leagues, and the high land of St George NE by N eleven leagues, 1005 fathoms by the chart. She is on SE (140° steering) with the wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, 5 knots, making SSE (152°) over the ground, so the current is setting us a point or so south of our heading. With Pico and St George on our bow we have the whole of the Azores clear to the north; Santa Maria and São Miguel lie ENE of us at 150 miles and more, and the black schooner was last heard of off Santa Maria. I would keep this course to S of the island tracks, as you directed, and haul to ESE when we are to the south of São Miguel's latitude, about 37° 30' N.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, I've looked at the passage chart: your pencil line leaves us bearing 122° true for the point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing Ponta do Pargo and Sao Lourenco well; I'm steering SE (141°), 19° south of it. The line is clean of dangers and the wind N by W 10 kn is a good 133° off the bow for 122°, so we can lay it and sail faster. My only doubt is the Basque: it passes about 24 miles south of Santa Maria around 36° 35' N, the place where the black schooner robbed the fishing boat last week and where Hale said she waits for Gomes's brigantine south of Sao Miguel. My own choice would be to hold SE (141°) a day more to about 36° 30' N, 26° 40' W, then haul to ESE (114°) which passes some 60 miles south of Santa Maria and costs under ten miles of passage; with a clear horizon, the masthead lookout and the Falmouth cutter's speed at 5 knots, either is fair. Your word: lay 122° now, or hold SE a day first? I'll steer whichever.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, noon (12:00) 4 July: no sight of the sun yet to report but the sky is clear, with streaked cloud high up; a fix at noon puts us at 37° 55' N, 28° 08' W (account 37° 54' N, 28° 04' W), good to two miles, with the Caldeira of Fayal NW by N 15 leagues, St George N 16 leagues, the Serra de Santa Barbara NE by N 20 leagues and the Peak of Pico NNW 11 leagues; deep water (940 fathoms). Run since yesterday's noon 47 miles; the last glass made 4.2 knots SE (141°), wind NNW 10 kn on the larboard quarter, the course made good SE by S (146°). Provisions 39 days, water 6.5 tons (54 days). No sail in sight. We hold SE to about 36° 30' N, then haul to ESE (114°) as agreed; we are 80 miles from that turn, some 17 hours at this rate.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye, sir: 00:03, steady on SE by E (119° ordered, heading 118°) at your word, the turn made from SE; wind N by W 9 kn now 105° on the larboard quarter, yards braced and fore-and-aft sheets trimmed, leeway 1°, speed about 4 knots; the account 37° 12' N, 27° 24' W. By your pencil line we clear Sao Lourenco by twenty miles. The Azores clear to the north; no sail in sight.

The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Aye, sir, noted: the standing orders to tend the sheets and to trim the yards now fire at each change of the watch; I tend in between as needed. 00:43: SE by E (119°) at 4 kn, wind NNW 10 kn on the larboard quarter, 37° 10' N, 27° 20' W by account, Ponta Delgada ENE 29 leagues, 1434 fathoms, no sail, nothing in sight.

master.text: Anchored Carrick Road, Falmouth, 05:00, morning watch 2 bells. Best bower down, 8½ fathoms where let go, veered to 43 (five times the depth). Fixed by cross bearings at 50°10' N, 5°02' W, good to a cable; account agrees within half a cable. Bearings: Trefusis Pt abeam to larboard ESE 3 cables; Trefusis Pt WNW 5 cables; Pendennis Pt SW½S a mile; Mylor Pt N by E a mile; Falmouth WSW a mile; St Anthony's Head SE½S two miles. Nearest land three cables to larboard. Tide: ebb making, a kn and a quarter to the S by W; high water Ramhead about 2 p.m. by the epitome (moon 11 days old, near springs, rise 15 ft). Dangers about: the Governor SSW 7 cables, Lugo rock SE½S 7 cables, Black Rock S 1½ miles. Deck: the captain's; sails all furled; 12 hands on deck, fresh. Glass 29.90, not yet watched an hour; fine weather, moderate sea.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

05:05, morning watch: the captain's word — checks of papers, provisions, water, hands, made and reported: water 4 tons (33.6 days), provisions 30 days for 30 men (we muster 27, so stretched), 12 tons canvas, room for 30, purse £180, all hands fresh. Nothing expended. Captain says we get under way for FAYAL if all is prepared. Deck still the captain's; sails furled, best bower down 43 fathoms, small bower and kedge at the bows. Note: Mr Ruiz and Senhor Bettencourt are ashore at Fayal (letter for Bettencourt in the master's keeping). Wind W by S 11 knots — fair on the quarter for a southern passage to Fayal. Standing by for the word.
Stood by until a word on deck.

05:11: the captain's word — the two ashore at Fayal are no men of ours, the business is private, and no names are to be spoken if an errant ear is about. Taken note of; I named them in my report, a fault of discretion — I'll speak of 'the correspondent at Fayal' only. Important cargo bound for Fayal. I confirmed stores sufficient and told him the hold allows 30 tons more and water could be topped by the boat; he will consider, morning is early. Anchor still down, 43 fathoms; wind W by S 11 knots, fair for Fayal on the port quarter if we go south. Standing by for the word to weigh.
Stood by until a word on deck.

05:13: captain demands a ton of water (£0 2s, alongside in 6 min) and 14 days provisions (£21, alongside in 42 min). Purse £180 -> £158 18s. He means to send the boat ashore for trade rumours — something cheap on the market. My part: receive and stow the stores, book them in the purser's books; have the boat ready. Ebb making in the Road, sets S by W — boat will find it on her beam to the town. Deck still the captain's. Anchor down, 43 fathoms best bower. Wind W by S 11 knots. Business private — speak no names.
Stood by until a word on deck.

05:18: boat away for the prices and news (captain's order), crew out. Water was due alongside ~05:18, provisions ~05:54 — I'll receive and stow, book in the purser's books. Notable: the Black Rock showing S, a mile — a danger. We ride at anchor so no risk; but the ebb sets S by W toward it, so when we weigh I'll recommend a berth west of it or waiting for the flood, and the lead going. Wind W by S 11 knots, glass 29.92 steady, fine. Deck still the captain's.
Stood by until a word on deck.

06:41, 5 bells morning watch: the owners' letter (Rogers and Son) read by the captain, his question — what say you of it. My answer: the season is fair — 54 days to the policy's end (1 Aug), Fayal is 8-9 days each way, so sail soon and there's a fortnight in hand. Stores ample (water 42 days, provisions 44 after this morning's casks). Wine bounded by the purse (£158 18s), not the hold (room for 30 tons more); if the canvas fetches well at Fayal the fund grows. Urged weighing on this ebb, W by W wind fair for a southing, standing west of the Black Rock and round St Anthony's Head. Discretion: no names before the hands. Provisions for 14 days stowed at 05:54, booked. Boat back alongside 06:39, hoisted in, at the booms; prices brought off (same list), quay talk: timber and coal dear at St Mary's — rumour only. Deck still the captain's.
Stood by until a word on deck.

06:43: the captain's plan for getting under way — get under way on the larboard tack, wear as she makes way, bear away S by E out of the sound. My working: loose main and topsail, heave short, cast and gather way on the larboard tack, wear (wind passes round the stern to the starboard quarter/beam) and settle S by E — a wear, not a tack, so no risk of missing stays; the ebb (a kn and a quarter, S by W) sweeps her south through it. Cautions I gave him: Trefusis land ESE two cables lies under her head mid-wear (lead going, Pascoe at the sheets); after the wear S by E passes east of the Black Rock — she draws 9 feet, lead tells the water. Stores complete: water 5 tons/42 days, provisions 44 days. Boat at the booms. Deck still the captain's; standing by for it to be given to work the evolution.
Stood by until a word on deck.

07:11, 6 bells: under way since 07:09, larboard tack, best bower catted and fished. Captain tack-ship: to come round to the starboard tack and steer S by E for the sound, Black Rock to starboard — instead of the wear he first spoke of. Helm a-lee, all hands (20 on deck). Watch points I gave him: Trefusis land right ahead 3 cables mid-tack (ebb sweeps her clear); if she misses stays, wear instead of trying twice; after paying off, S by E with Black Rock to starboard, lead going. Water 4½ fathoms at low water by chart at the position, low water about 8 a.m., then the flood makes. Pilot cutter standing out toward us under British colours — asked whether to hail her; no pilot wanted for Fayal, as I take it. Deck still the captain's.
Stood by until filled away.
Stood by until filled away.
Took the deck from the captain.

07:13 — I HAVE THE DECK. Captain's word with it: on the lead regularly, minding the land and the tideway; no pilot wanted. Ship state: larboard tack — no, starboard tack now after the tack at 07:11 (headed SW by S under way 3 kn, leeway settling from 42° to 3°). Sails: main, jib set; fore staysail ordered set by me; topsail was aback/shaking mid-tack, filling. Course to shape: S by E, Black Rock to starboard, out of the sound. Nearest land: Trefusis land 3 cables W by N (opening). Pilot cutter N a mile larboard bow, no need for her. Glass 29.91 falling a hundredth. Depth by chart at account: 8½ fathoms at low water; low water about 08:00, flood making after. My plan: lead every 10 min and every two fathoms of change after the first; watch the tideway; steer S by E when she has way on. Deck: MINE.

07:14: The tack is made, starboard tack, full and by, hands recovering. Captain keeps the conn himself out of the sound ("worry not on the conn for now, sir") — so I mind the lead, the land and the tideway, and do not steer. Standing order given: lead every ten minutes. My reckoning set: 50°10' N, 5°02' W, a cable E by N of the master's, kept beside it, to be said at noon. Course for the sound when the captain gives the word: S by E, Black Rock to starboard; low water about 08:00, flood making after — the tide turns under us and helps her out. Trefusis land three cables, opening. Watch: 27 on deck after all hands. Deck: MINE. Sails: topsail, main, jib set; fore staysail set at my order (it waited its turn).
Stood by until steady on the course.

07:15: standing order grammar learned — the mate may enter standing orders in his own rank; trigger forms: when/for/at/every; conditions are readings; after 'then' plain orders separated by ';' read at entry. Refusals learned: a standing order may not make a cry ('say X' is the captain's to say to a station); 'tell the officer' in a standing order is a station address = the captain's rank only. My alternatives in force: leadsman charged on deck (call each cast, under 5 fathoms loud), watch repeats to me; the captain may enter the 'lead warning' standing order himself if he wants it in the book. My standing orders live: 'lead every ten minutes'; my reckoning 50°10'N 5°02'W kept beside the master's. Deck: MINE (though the captain keeps the conn out of the sound for now). Course S by W gathering way 2-3 kn after the tack; depth by chart 10½ fathoms at low water; Trefusis land 3 cables abeam to starboard WNW, opening. Glass 29.92 steady.

Handover note (the watch so far): 07:15, morning watch. HAVE THE DECK since 07:13 (captain keeps the conn himself out of the sound, by his own word — I mind the lead, land and tideway and do not steer without his word; 'steer S by E' was refused to my rank as a course change). Got under way 07:09 larboard tack, tacked at 07:11, now starboard tack full and by, S by W 2-3 kn, all plain sail (topsail, main, jib set; fore staysail set at my order; light sails furled). Plan agreed with him: bear away to S by E for the sound on his word — I told him she is ripe and the Black Rock will be well to starboard of that course; low water about 08:00, flood making after, will help her out. My standing orders live: 'heave the lead every ten minutes'; leadsman charged on deck to call each cast aloud, under 5 fathoms loud enough to wake the master; my reckoning 50°10' N 5°02' W kept beside the master's (a cable E by N of it), to be said at noon. Standing-order grammar learned the hard way: my rank cannot enter 'tell the officer...' or 'say...' in a book; the captain may, if he wants 'lead warning' in the book — I offered him the exact form. The owners' letter: letter for a correspondent at Fayal in the master's keeping; policy void past 1 Aug — the season is good if we do not linger; business private, no names before the hands. Stores complete: water 5 tons/42 days, provisions 44 days. Glass 29.92 steady; fine; pilot cutter near, no need for her, captain's word. Watching: the lead, the land about Trefusis (3 cables, opening), the Black Rock (S, a mile and a half) when we bear away, the flood at 08:00.
Stood by until a word on deck.

07:17: 'Lead Warning' standing order — tried eight forms in my rank, all refused: 'tell the captain/watcher/master/lookout/officer/officer of the watch' — a standing order that addresses any station is the captain's rank only (he entered 'tell the officer...' himself at 07:16, and it stands); 'say...' refused (only the captain may say to a station); 'cry...' not an understood verb. Conclusion for the books: a cry on deck cannot be carried by the mate's standing order at all — the leadsman's voice is the working answer. The captain's 'Lead Warning' entry stands in the book (trigger: depth under 5 fathoms, tells the officer). Lead being heaved now.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 07:17, morning watch. Standing order 'Lead Warning' — my rank cannot enter it in any form; every 'tell the <station>' and 'say' is refused to a standing order from me; the captain's own entry stands in the book (07:16, 'when the depth is under 5 fathoms then tell the officer...'). Learned for the books. Ship's state: tacked and braced up starboard tack at S by E (169°), 3 kn, ebb half a knot, glass 29.93 rising; lead going in the chains. Black Rock a mile and a half to starboard of the course, Trefusis land opening on the larboard bow, Pendennis a mile SSW. Deck given back to the captain (he keeps the conn out of the sound). Watching: the lead's casts, the Black Rock as we stand down the sound, low water about 08:00 and the flood after.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Took the deck from the captain.
Stood by until a wind shift.

08:00, forenoon watch 8 bells, on watch. Course SE by S (146°), close hauled starboard tack, 6 kn, wind WSW 11 kn, glass 29.94 rising, fine. Clear of the harbour and the Old Wall (NW by N, 1½ miles) and the Black Rock (NW by N, 3 miles); nearest land St Anthony's Head astern, 2 miles. Captain conned the watch to 07:40 (fixes each few minutes, bore off twice to SSE then SE by S); I have the deck since 07:33, minding the sails. Dangers now all abeam or astern, the Manacles SW by S 4 miles next to mind as we make south. Run 5 miles since departure. Noon by the sun at 11:58. Lead cast on my order at 08:00 (last, 15 fathoms at 07:19). Standing order 'Lead Warning' in the book, never yet fired.
Stood by until a wind shift.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:10: topgallant set, yards braced up (54-58° from square), sheets trimmed — close hauled on the starboard tack, course SE by S/SE by E as she lies; wind WSW 10 kn, 6 kn; clear of all dangers, nearest land 3-4 miles; run 6 miles. Captain's correction on the record: the term is 'trim for close hauled' (my 'trim the sails' was accepted and did the same work). The Manacles SW by W 3½ miles next to mind as we stand south; low water past, flood making. Watching: the wind (WSW, might come up to W and let her luff), the glass (29.93 steady), noon sights at 11:58.
Stood by until a wind shift.

11:13, forenoon watch 6 bells: WIND SHIFTED — WSW by W to SW by W (hauled about a point since 08:10). Captain conned the forenoon: close hauled (08:11), full and by (08:16), gaff topsail set (08:21), S by E (08:22); fixes each hour moving the account, latest 10:43 (49°54'N 4°56'W, the account a mile out until it); come up half a point to S, braced sharp up, sheets trimmed. Now S (174°), close hauled starboard tack, wind 42° off the starboard bow, topgallant shaking — captain ordered the weather bowlines hauled at 11:08. Run 22 miles. Glass 29.97 rising, clear sky, fine. My own reckoning running 2½ miles SW of the master's — outside my trust; the master's fixes are the better figure. Noon by the sun 11:58 — no sight yet today. Lizard lights SW 4 leagues at 08:02, Black Head NW 3 leagues now: we are well down the coast. Dangers: none charted within 10 miles.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

Noon, 08 June: no sight — the sun hid in fog. By the master's account 49°47'N 4°56'W, run S by E 25 miles; my own reckoning 49°46'N 4°59'W, 2½ miles SW of his, within my trust. Fog came down 11:18, visibility a cable; I took in the topgallant and gaff topsail on my own word — plain sail only, ~4-5 kn, course S. No charted danger within 10 miles; no land in sight; lead going, no bottom. Glass 29.96, steady after rising; wind SW by W 10 kn. Flood making half a knot NE. Watching: the fog thickening or lifting, the lead, any sail or landfall from the lookout.
Stood by until a change in the sky.
Stood by until a change in the sky.

12:41: fog lifted — clear and fine, horizon again. Set the topgallant and main gaff topsail back on my own word. Course S (175°), ~4 kn, wind SW by W 10 kn, flood making NE ¾ kn, run since noon 3 miles. Glass 29.97. No land in sight, open water, no dangers within 10 miles. Watching: the wind and the weather; the captain on the quarterdeck.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

14:12: wind veered to W by N (mean W by S), 8-9 kn — on our starboard beam; the topgallant has been shaking, so I trimmed (yards braced up for the new wind, sheets hauled). Sky turned dark and gloomy, scud driving, squally, visibility down to a mile — watching for squalls and a further shift; 46 fathoms, no land in sight, no dangers within 10 miles. Run since noon 8 miles. Captain has been conned her all afternoon (come up a point, brace sharp up, quarter-point braces). Glass 30.01 rising.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a wind shift.

14:18: captain shaped the course for the Azores — 38°43'N 27°12'W, 1156 miles, full and by starboard tack; his standing order 'Hourly Shaping' in the book (every hour, shape the course for 38 43 N 27 12 W). Wind W by N 8 kn, close hauled, 4 kn, glass 30.02 rising. Earlier squally spell (dark, scud) has passed — clear again by the rollup? Watching: wind backing/veering for a fair wind to Horta; my reckoning run on hourly; the letter for Senhor Bettencourt in the master's keeping.
Stood by until a wind shift.

15:20, afternoon watch 6 bells: two squalls passed (14:58, 15:06 — wind veering a point to W by N, 12 and 16 kn, with rain; both passed to W 9 kn). Wind now W by S 9 kn, mean W 12; close hauled starboard tack on the Azores course (shaped for 38°43'N 27°12'W, full and by), 5 kn, course made good S by E. Glass 30.03 rising steadily, showers passing, hard-edged oily clouds. Run since noon 13 miles. No land in sight, no dangers. Captain's plan on record: full and by until wind forces us south (accepted) or backs through north or south and makes it fair. Watching: further squalls, the wind, the hourly shaping standing order.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until eight bells.
Stood by until eight bells.

Handover note (the watch so far): 16:00, first dog watch begins, 8 bells. Ship: close hauled on the starboard tack for the Azores (course shaped for 38°43'N 27°12'W by the captain's standing order 'Hourly Shaping', every hour), full and by — SW by W not layable, so she lies her closest. Wind W by S 8-9 kn, gentle; plain sail + topgallant + gaff topsail set; 4-5 kn; glass 30.03 rising; showers passed. Run since noon 16 miles; my reckoning 49°31'N 4°52'W, 2½ miles SW of the master's, within trust. No land, no dangers within 10 miles, 49 fathoms no bottom. Captain below in the cabin at 15:47, came up, told me his plan (full and by until wind forces south — accepted — or backs to fair). I have had a drink and a meal and am fresh. Squalls passed 14:58/15:06; more of the same kind may come — hard-edged clouds about. Watching: wind shifts toward fair, the hourly shaping, squalls.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 16:00, first dog watch, 8 bells. Deck given back to the captain for the dog watch. Ship as in my note: close hauled starboard tack for the Azores (38°43'N 27°12'W, the captain's 'Hourly Shaping' standing order active), full and by; wind W by S 8-9 kn, 4-5 kn; plain sail, topgallant and gaff topsail set; glass 30.03 rising; run since noon 16 miles; no land or dangers in sight; my reckoning 49°31'N 4°52'W, 2½ miles SW of the master's, within trust. I have eaten and drunk and will turn in below now, asleep until called, ready to take the deck when the master gives it. Watching when I wake: the wind for the fair wind he hopes for, the squalls from the hard-edged clouds, the hourly shaping.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

Woke rested 17:23, first dog watch 2 bells, off watch; the captain still has the deck. While I slept: a squall at 16:03 — wind veered a point to W, freshened to 11 knots with rain — passed 16:08, wind WSW 8 knots. Glass now 30.06, rising 6 hundredths in three hours; sky clear, weather fine, visibility to the horizon. She is standing SSE 154°, course made good SSE, run since noon 21 miles. The tide at slack water, the ebb to make. The moon twelve days old is up five degrees — too low for a lunar yet. The wind keeps in the west, so full and by on the starboard tack goes on; the hard-edged clouds have cleared and the squall was of the same kind as the last two. I turn in again asleep until called; when the master gives me the deck I will take the readings afresh and note whether he wants a lunar tried as the moon climbs.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

20:00, first watch 8 bells, change of the watch; still off watch, the captain has the deck. Wind WSW 7 kn, she stands SSE 154°, run since noon 34 miles; glass 30.10 and rising steady (now 4 hundredths in three hours); sky hazy, a smooth sea. The moon twelve days old is nineteen degrees up, in distance of Regulus: the readings say the moon serves — a lunar is to be had for the longitude for the first time this passage. When I next have the deck I will propose it to the captain, or take the sight if his word allows. Wind still westerly, so full and by goes on; the tide set by Ushant now in the almanac.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.
Stood by until a handover.
Took the deck from the captain.

21:22, first watch 2 bells. Took the deck from the captain for the night watch; he goes below once the lunar is worked. Lunar by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen: longitude 4° 54' W, trusted within 30 miles — reckoning was 4° 43' W, the account moved four cables W by S, no matter. Variation now 25° W by the sunset amplitude (was 21° 30' W by the 1794 chart) — allowed in the reckoning from now; my own reckoning 49° 07' N, 4° 45' W, 2 miles SW by S of the master's. Wind W, faded to 6 knots (8 at the dog watch); she stands S (180°), full and by starboard tack, the WSW course for the Azores not layable; glass 30.12 rising strongly, hazy, smooth sea, moonlit night — land made out at a league, none in sight, no danger within 10 miles. The captain's word by Mr Pascoe: square sail when the apparent may come abeam and course sou'westerly — apparent 57° on the bow, so it waits; hands handy. Tide allowance (ebb half a knot SW) holds till about a quarter past ten, then the Hourly Shaping takes it. Watching: the wind veering (W → W by N would bring the apparent near abeam and the square sail with it), any shift toward the fair wind he wants, the hourly shaping, the haze thickening. Pascoe looks for little wind before the forenoon.
Stood by until a wind shift.

21:25, first watch. The captain's word: mind the offing through the night — if speed increases while the course stays south or east of south and the wind holds westerly, we close the Breton shore; then wear to the larboard tack or get the course sou'westerly, by the reckoning even blind. He is below asleep until rested; wake him with 'tell the captain' only if something requires him. My plan for the watch: cast the lead on every hour with the shaping; keep my own reckoning run on; watch the wind for a veer (it would both lay the WSW course and open the offing) or a haul (it would square the wind more dead on the bow); square sail still waiting on the apparent abeam; wear in good time rather than late — she is slow (6 kn) and may miss stays. Glass 30.13 rising strongly. Next shaping due about 22:15.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the turn of the tide by the reckoning.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the square sail is set.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.

01:19, middle watch. Deep-sea lead by the captain's word (he belayed the hand lead): 56 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks; three fathoms of tide allowed — 53 on the chart; the account kept. First bottom this passage; the master's account confirmed. My own reckoning 48° 58' N, 4° 46' W, within two miles of his. She stands SW by W 232°, wind NW light (3-4 kn), all sail drawing, the square sail set since midnight and bowlines hauled on the captain's word. Glass 30.18-30.19, rising. Moon down to four degrees, no lunar. Watching: the Hourly Shaping at the next hour, the tide turning about high water at Ushant (a quarter past one) — after that the ebb gives us westing again.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the turn of the tide by the reckoning.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. Held the deck through the middle watch — the whole watch mine, the captain below but for one turn up at 02:43 when he ordered the sails trimmed; the yards braced three to the wind, 54-58° from square. Wind settled NW by N at 03:53, light breeze 5 kn; she stands SW by W 240°, all sail set, square sail drawing since midnight. Glass 30.21 rising (the small dip at 00:35 passed), clear after the haze, sunrise 03:55. Run since noon 54 miles but course made good only S 176° — the southing shows. Reckoning 48° 58' N, 4° 51' W; mine 48° 56' N, 4° 53' W, holding two miles SW of his. Deep-sea cast 01:19, 56 fathoms fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. The turn of the tide by the reckoning has not come; the flood allowance is down to a quarter knot NE. Watching: the Hourly Shaping hourly, the tide allowance turning, any shift toward the fair wind the captain wants (NW by N is near the fairest yet — the WSW course may nearly lay), the deep-sea lead by the captain's standing practice now.
Stood by until a glass.

04:30, morning watch 1 bell. The captain entered two standing orders at 04:02: 'trim on the course' (at steady on the course then trim the sails) and 'tend the sheets on the glass' (every glass, if not hove to, tend the sheets); 'trim on the course' fired 04:16, yards braced three to the wind, 54-58° from square. Wind hauled NNW 5 kn; she now stands WSW 246° — the Azores course nearly laid. Slack water, the ebb to make: the tide allowance's turn come at last after the flood's NE set all night. Run since noon 55 miles, course made good still S 177°. Glass steady at 30.21-22. My reckoning 48° 56' N, 4° 54' W. Watching: the standing orders' firing, the wind — if it steadies NNW-NW the fair wind the captain wants is here; the Hourly Shaping will shape WSW and she may lay it. The deep-sea lead now the practice; last cast 01:19.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until noon.
Stood by until a sounding.

08:14, forenoon watch. Deep-sea cast: 58 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept — the same ground as at 01:19, the shelf of the Channel confirming the reckoning. Run since noon 72 miles, course made good S by W 192° — the watch from 04:00 has given us the westing at last, W by S and WSW all through the forenoon, the wind N and N by W. She now stands W by S 254°, apparent 55-58° on the bow, 4-5 kn. The topgallant came in at 06:32 (shaking in the 52° close-hauled trim — would not draw) and hangs in the gear; it goes up again when she bears away or the wind frees. Glass 30.26 rising. My reckoning 48° 48' N, 5° 15' W, two miles SW by S of the master's. Next: noon sights at 11:57; if the wind backs further north and freshens, ask the captain whether to shake out more sail; the Hourly Shaping continues.
Stood by until noon.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until noon.

11:58, forenoon watch, noon. Day's work: lat by obs 48° 46' N (account was 48° 44' — the flood set us two miles NNE of allowed); course made good SSW, 86 miles; longitude by account 5° 34' W. My own reckoning had run to 48° 42' N, 5° 37' W, four miles outside my trust of the master's — set my slate to the noon fix: 48° 46' N, 5° 34' W. Lunar from last evening says 4° 54' W — some twenty miles east of the account; Mr Bowen will judge. Wind N 5-6 kn, apparent 81° on the bow, all sail set (topgallant re-set 10:30 by the captain's word, yards braced 53° then 46° from square); she stands SW by W, the Hourly Shaping steering WSW with the flood allowance. Glass 30.30 rising. Deep-sea cast 08:14: 58 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. Watching: the wind for the fair southerly the captain wants (a veer further east would lay the WSW course well), the flood's NE set holding us toward the shelf, soundings by the deep-sea lead.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 12:40, afternoon watch 1 bell. Deck given to the deck while I join the captain below in the gunroom for a bite and the chart. All quiet and well: all sail set and drawing, wind N by E 5-6 kn (veering easterly of north as the captain reads it), apparent 101-111° on the quarter abaft the beam, she stands SW by W; glass 30.29 steady; no land or dangers; deep-sea cast 08:14, 58 fathoms fine grey sand with black specks, the account kept. Noon: lat by obs 48° 46' N, lon by account 5° 34' W, course made good SSW 86 miles; my slate set to the noon fix. The lunar of last evening (4° 54' W) is twenty miles east of the account — a matter for the master's judgment, on the table in the gunroom. Standing orders to be kept by whoever has the deck: 'Hourly Shaping' hourly for 38° 43' N 27° 12' W, 'trim on the course', 'tend the sheets on the glass'. Watching: the wind veering further east (the fair wind), the flood's NE set toward the shelf, and the topgallant drawing since 10:30.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Stood by until a handover.

12:40, afternoon watch. Gone below to the gunroom with the captain for a bite and the chart; the deck with the deck, Mr Pascoe keeping it until we come up.
