My handover note is in the journal: all quiet, all sail set and drawing, wind N by E about the beam, glass 30.29; noon work — lat by obs 48° 46' N, lon by account 5° 34' W, SSW 86 miles since yesterday; the lunar of last evening twenty miles east of the account, for the master's judgment at the chart. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

12:41, afternoon watch. In the gunroom with the captain, over the whole chart. She sits 48° 46' N, 5° 34' W by the noon work; St Mary's NNW 25 leagues; the Azores course WSW, 1113 miles by the last shaping; the captain's pencilled aims and the fifty-mile circle about the islands on it; the lunar (4° 54' W) a shade east of the account's line, within doubt. Bite taken, chart gone over; my own reckoning stands at the noon fix.
Stood by until a handover.
Took the deck from the captain.

18:01, last dog watch 4 bells. Took the deck from the captain for the evening; he remains above until he wants rest, then below. Since noon (spent in the gunroom with him over the chart, a bite together): the wind has gone NNE and freshened to 6 kn, the yards nearly square (18-31° from square through the afternoon), she stands WSW 247°, course made good WSW 243°, 18 miles since noon; the ebb allowed SW three quarters. Run since noon 18 miles — the fair wind come at last, everything drawing, topgallant set. Glass 30.34 rising steadily. Reckoning 48° 38' N, 5° 58' W; my slate matches, two cables NE of his. Moon 13 days old, just up, one degree. St Mary's N by W 26 leagues. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (last 17:15, next 18:15), trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching: the wind for further veering east, the tide turn about 23:00, soundings (63½ fathoms by account, the last cast nine hours old — deep-sea cast when the shaping falls due), the topgallant set since 10:30 drawing.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Allowed by the captain: take a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.

21:46, first watch 3 bells. Lunar by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen (my request, his word): longitude by lunar 5° 29' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 6° 22' W — the master moved his account three leagues to the east, now 48° 31' N, 6° 08' W. My own slate (from the noon fix 5° 34' W, run on by the log-board) stands 48° 30' N, 6° 22' W, three leagues west of his corrected account, at the edge of my trust of it. I keep my slate uncorrected for an independent check and will speak of it at noon; the lunar and the account disagree by some 35-40 miles, both within the lunar's doubt. Also this watch: at 21:11 the sails lifted — wind came forward to N by E while the yards stood free; braced the yards in (54-58° from square) and the standing order re-braced at 21:16. She now sails free again, apparent on the beam, WSW 251°, made good SW by W, 35 miles since noon. Glass 30.35 steady. Moon 19° up, still in distance of Regulus — another set tonight would narrow the longitude. The tide turn by the reckoning due about 23:00.
Stood by until the turn of the tide by the reckoning.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

22:58, first watch 5 bells. The captain below to sleep until at least sunrise; I hold the deck through the night. All steady: wind NNE 8 kn, apparent on the quarter, she stands WSW 248°, all sail drawing, made good SW by W, 40 miles since noon. Glass 30.36, steady-to-rising. Tide: slack water, the flood to make — the turn of the master's tide came at 22:48; the flood will set NE and push us up toward the shelf through the night; soundings by the deep-sea lead as the shaping falls due. The moon in distance of Altair now (18° up); a second lunar this night would narrow the longitude — I may propose one when the moon is high enough and Mr Bowen sleeps, so it waits for his waking, or I take it if the master's word covers it (it was his word that allowed the last). Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. My slate: 48° 28' N, 6° 28' W, three leagues W of his corrected account (lunar 5° 29' W). Watching: the flood's NE set, any wind shift, the yards at each shaping (the sails lifted once at 21:11 when the wind came forward — braced in), the captain asleep till sunrise.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.
Stood by until a sounding.

00:12, middle watch. Deep-sea cast: 76 fathoms, grey sand and ooze; two and a half fathoms of tide allowed — 73½ on the chart; the account kept. The ground has changed character (fine grey sand with black specks → grey sand and ooze) as we run off the shelf south-westward; depth increasing on schedule. Middle watch begun, 8 bells struck, the watches changed; the captain asleep below until at least sunrise, the deck mine. All sail drawing on WSW, wind NNE about the quarter, 3-4 kn. The flood now three quarters of a knot to the NE — it will set us up toward the shelf through the small hours; soundings hourly as the shaping falls due. Glass 30.35 steady. Noon by the sun at 12:04. Watching: the flood's set, the wind, the noon sights.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sounding.
Stood by until sunrise.
Stood by until sunrise.

04:04, morning watch. Sunrise; I have held the deck the whole night through (first and middle watches), the captain asleep below since 22:58, to wake at least at sunrise. The night quiet and honest: wind settled NNE-NE by N 6-7 kn, all sail drawing, the yards square (0° from square) and she standing SW by W 238° with the apparent well on the quarter; made good SW by W through the small hours, 54 miles since noon. Glass 30.36-30.37, steady through the night, hazy, a smooth sea. Soundings kept: 00:12, 76 fathoms grey sand and ooze (account kept); 01:25, 70 fathoms; 03:09, 69 fathoms — the ground character changed from the fine grey sand with black specks of the outer shelf to ooze as we come off it. My slate 48° 23' N, 6° 47' W, three leagues W of the master's corrected account (lunar 5° 29' W) — the disagreement holds, for his judgment at noon. Flood allowance fading (three quarters of a knot NE), the tide's last grip on us before the ebb. Watching: the captain waking (or his calling), the hourly shapings and trims, the noon sights, whether the wind backs to lay the course or freshens.

04:04, morning watch, sunrise — the night watch held whole, the captain below since 22:58. Summary of the night: wind settled NNE-NE by N, 6-7 kn, all sail drawing (yards square), she standing SW by W 238° most of the night, made good SW by W; 54 miles since noon; glass steady 30.35-30.37, hazy then clear, a smooth sea, easy. Soundings (deep-sea lead, each the account kept): 00:12, 76 fathoms, grey sand and ooze; 01:25, 70 fathoms; 03:09, 69 fathoms — the bottom character changed from fine grey sand with black specks (the outer shelf) to grey sand and ooze as we ran off the shelf. Flood allowance faded to three quarters of a knot NE by 04:00; high water at Ushant reckoned about 02:00, so the ebb follows and will give us westing. My slate 48° 23' N, 6° 47' W, three leagues west of the master's corrected account; his lunar (5° 29' W) says the account stands some 35 miles east of mine — both within its doubt, for his judgment at noon. Noon by the sun 12:04. Wind by NNE and the apparent on the quarter — the fair wind the captain wanted is here and steady. Watching: his waking, the Hourly Shaping (last 03:55?), the noon work, and any shift that puts the wind forward again — the sails lifted once last evening when it came forward.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a sail made out.

06:30, morning watch 5 bells. Stranger made out: a brig on the starboard quarter, bearing N, four miles, standing SW by S under plain sail, no colours yet; first seen 05:08 abeam to starboard N by W six miles, hull below the horizon; the captain has been in the tops since 05:40 with the glass and made her out. She works to the south'ard and so will close or cross us; we stand WSW 250°, 3 kn. I keep her logged at every change; nothing to alter for, in my judgment — she may be a trader out of the Channel; keep watch on her colours and her course, and hail the captain of every change as a lieutenant of 1806 would. Also: the captain said I might rest when he takes the deck; I am a little drowsy after the whole night, and will stand easy when he relieves me — but not until he does, the deck is mine while he is aloft. The ebb now a knot to the SW; run since noon 62 miles. Noon by the sun 12:04.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a stranger's colours made out.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 08:00, forenoon watch, 8 bells. Deck given to the captain; I am drowsy after holding the whole night and go below to sleep. What he takes: all sail set and drawing on WSW 253°, wind NNE 8 kn, apparent 102° on the quarter, 4 kn; glass 30.36 steady; no land, deep-sea cast 03:09, 69 fathoms grey sand and ooze, the account kept; the ebb a knot and a half to the SW. The stranger: a brig on the starboard quarter, bearing NE, three miles, standing SW by S under plain sail, no colours yet — first seen 05:08; she has worked round from N to NE as we have gone off to the westward; I judge her a trader, to be watched, nothing to alter for. My reckoning 48° 16' N, 7° 05' W, three leagues W of the master's (his lunar 5° 29' W); noon by the sun 12:04, and the longitude question is his to judge at the noon work. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (last 07:15), trim on the course (last 07:17), tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching for me asleep: the brig's colours or course change, any wind shift, the noon sights — wake me for anything beyond the book.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

Woke rested 12:47, afternoon watch 1 bell, off watch; the captain has the deck. What came while I slept: the noon work — lat by obs 48° 13' N, lon by account 7° 08' W, course made good SW by W 82 miles. My own slate ran to 48° 10' N, 7° 24' W, three leagues W of his before the sight, and the observation puts me four miles N of his: I set my slate to the noon fix again (48° 13' N, 7° 08' W) and will speak of the longitude at the next noon. The brig (first seen 05:08 from the northward) has worked round on our larboard quarter, SE by E, two leagues, still standing SW by S under plain sail — we have crossed her track or she has crossed ours; no colours made out. The captain held the deck the forenoon; the standing orders kept their rounds; wind NE 6 kn, she stands WSW 244°, all sail drawing; glass 30.35, first fall in two days — worth watching. I turn in again asleep until called; when I take the deck I will read the glass's fall first of all.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

14:09, afternoon watch 4 bells. Took the deck from the captain (he below at the chart). Ship: all sail set and drawing, WSW 244°, wind NE by E 7 kn on the quarter, 3½ kn, glass 30.35 (fell 2 hundredths through the forenoon, now steady), clear, smooth sea, no land, no danger. Brig on the larboard quarter SE by E three leagues, standing SW by S, dropping astern — a passing trader, to be watched, nothing to alter for. Noon (12:05): lat by obs 48° 13' N (account 3½ miles S of it), lon by account 7° 08' W, made good SW by W 82 miles; my slate reset to the noon fix. The longitude question stands: account 7° 08' vs lunar 5° 29' W, near two degrees apart, both within the lunar's doubt; I proposed a second lunar at moonrise and the captain has gone to the chart — his word will come. The moon thirteen days old, down now, rises toward evening; when she is in distance of Regulus I will take the set if his word allows (it did last evening). My reckoning from the fix now 48° 07' N, 7° 32' W, four leagues W by S of his — the same leaning; watch it at the next noon. Watching: the glass (first fall in two days), the moonrise for the lunar, the brig astern, the Hourly Shaping.
Took the deck from the captain.
Stood by until a lunar.
Allowed by the captain: take a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.

16:00, first dog watch 8 bells. Still have the deck; the captain below since 14:10 at the chart, then to rest. The afternoon watch passed quiet: all sail set and drawing, WSW 244-245°, wind NE by E 6-7 kn well abaft the beam, 3 kn, glass 30.35 steady after the small forenoon fall. Run since noon 13 miles, made good WSW 245°. The brig has dropped out of sight astern — she stood on SW by S and we drew away from her to the westward; no colours ever made out, a passing trader. My slate from the noon fix: 48° 04' N, 7° 41' W, four leagues W by S of the master's account; his lunar 5° 29' W still stands against the account 7° 25' W — the moon is not yet up; the second lunar awaits her. Deep-sea cast due (last 03:09); the ground grey sand and ooze, 91 fathoms by account, coming off the shelf apace. Watching: the glass's tendency (it fell a hundredth in the forenoon, then steadied — the falling fast is not here), the moonrise for the lunar, the hourly shapings and trims, the deep-sea lead.
Stood by until a sounding.

16:13, first dog watch. Deep-sea cast: 91 fathoms, soft ooze; two and a half fathoms of tide allowed — 88½ on the chart; the account moved six cables to the east on it — the cast is confirmation the account ran too far west, and it bears out my suspicion since yesterday's noon: the longitude account has been running west of the truth, the lunar's 5° 29' W the nearer of the two. My own slate (7° 42' W) stands four leagues west of the master's and outside my trust; the soundings will settle it as the ooze deepens off the shelf. The bottom is now soft ooze — off the bank altogether. She runs WSW 244°, all sail drawing, 14 miles since noon, glass 30.35 steady. The moon rises toward evening; the second lunar when she comes into distance of Regulus, by the captain's word given at 14:10.
Stood by until a lunar.
Stood by until a lunar.

20:00, first watch 8 bells. The moon is seven degrees up and fourteen days old — not yet fit for the lunar; by her rate of climbing she should be in distance within the hour or two, and I hold the deck for the set. The glass has now fallen 3 hundredths in three hours (30.32) — a real fall begins, after two days of rise; watch it against the standing orders, though no wind follows yet (NE by E 6 kn, all quiet, a smooth sea). She runs WSW 244-245°, made good the same, 25 miles since noon. The captain on deck as the watch changed; he asked for my estimate of the lunar's hour (I said about eight to half past, well placed by nine) and took an azimuth at 17:58 — variation now 24° W by azimuth, against 25° W by the amplitude of the 8th; he allows it from now. My slate: 47° 59' N, 7° 58' W, still four leagues west of his account and outside my trust of it; the soundings (91 fathoms soft ooze at 16:13, the account moved east six cables) keep saying the same. The moonrise lunar will settle between the two.
Stood by until a lunar.

23:16, first watch 6 bells. The second lunar is taken and cleared: Spica and the moon by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen — longitude by lunar 7° 44' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 7° 51' W, so the account moved seven cables E by N. This confirms the pattern: the first lunar (5° 29' W) and the account (7° 08' W then) disagreed by two degrees; this second lunar agrees with the present account within a mile — the master's tide-work is close tonight. My own slate (47° 56' N, 8° 08' W) now stands four leagues W by S of his and outside my trust of it: the divergence began at yesterday's noon and has grown; I mean to work my reckoning afresh from this evening's fix and speak to the captain at his waking — the two slates must be brought together or the difference owned. Also: the glass has fallen through the evening, 30.32 → 30.31, 2 hundredths in three hours — slow, but three hours of fall after two days of rise; the first watch has been quiet (wind NE 5 kn, all square, WSW 244°, 33 miles since noon). The captain took a lunar at 22:00 (his own order), the distances cleared by 23:16. Watching: the glass's further fall, my reckoning work-up, the captain's waking.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

00:16, middle watch 8 bells. Still hold the deck, the second night running. The first watch passed quiet: wind NE 5-6 kn, all sail set, yards square, she runs WSW 244-245° with the wind nearly dead astern (168° astern at 23:46 — the square sail and the gaff topsail doing the work); 35 miles since noon; glass fallen to 30.30-30.31 — three hours' fall then steady, no wind to speak of following it; a smooth sea. Soundings not taken since 16:13 (91 fathoms soft ooze); the account now 126 fathoms by chart — well off the shelf, into the deep water west of Ushant. The lunar of Spica (7° 44' W) confirms the master's account; my slate (8° 11' W, four leagues W by S outside my trust) diverges — I will work it up at noon from the fix and the log, and speak plainly to the captain of it. The captain on deck at the watch change; all hands fresh. Watching: the glass (if it falls fast, the standing orders wake me), the wind for any hauling forward, the noon work and the reckoning to be squared.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until sunrise.

04:00, morning watch 8 bells. The middle watch held whole and quiet, the captain asleep below since 01:17 until sunrise. The night so far: wind NE-NE by E 5-6 kn nearly dead astern (168° astern), all sail set, yards square, she runs WSW 243-245°, 44 miles since noon; made good WSW. Glass fallen through the night, 30.30 → 30.27, about a hundredth the hour, steadily — the first settled fall of the passage; no wind to follow yet, a smooth sea, sky hazy. Depth by account 390 fathoms — we are off the shelf altogether, into the deep water west of Ushant; the deep-sea cast last taken 16:13 (91 fathoms soft ooze); with no bottom to be found at the lead's length now, soundings cease to confirm the account and the lunar must carry the longitude. My slate 47° 51' N, 8° 23' W, four leagues W by S of the master's and now within my trust again; the lunar of Spica (7° 44' W) is the truth to work from, and I will square my reckoning at noon from the fix. The moon is full tonight (fourteen days old) and down now; she rises toward evening in the first watch. Watching: the captain's waking at sunrise, the glass's fall (any hurry in it and the standing orders serve), the wind for hauling forward (then the yards), the noon sights.
Stood by until sunrise.
Stood by until a glass.

04:42, morning watch 1 bell. The glass has fallen fast: 7 hundredths in three hours, to 30.23, 4 hundredths in the last hour alone. The wind has hauled from NE through N round to E by S, light and variable airs, 3 knots, she has slowed to 2 kn, all sail still set. I sent the word below to the captain (he sleeps until sunrise, at his own asking; the glass falling fast and the wind round to the eastward are the kind of thing a lieutenant tells the master of). Depth by account 527 fathoms — well off the shelf, the lead's length will not find bottom. My slate 47° 50' N, 8° 25' W. Watching: squalls out of the east as the glass falls (the last three squalls came on a rising glass in westerly air — this is new weather), the yards for the wind coming forward of the beam, the captain's waking at sunrise.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until a squall.

08:00, forenoon watch 8 bells. Staying up till noon by the captain's word; I have eaten and am awake enough. The morning watch: the wind has hauled round the whole way — NE at midnight, E by S at 04:19, settled ESE by 05:25 and 07:39, now SE by E a light breeze 4 kn, gusty and variable; the yards braced up by degrees (11°, 26°, 41° from square) as it came forward. She now stands close hauled on the larboard tack, WSW, apparent 75° on the larboard bow. The glass has fallen all morning: 30.27 → 30.20, a hundredth the hour; the squall the falling glass foreboded has not come — the winds are all light airs and gusts. Depth by account 767 fathoms; the lead's length is useless now, we are in deep water. Run since noon 52 miles. My slate 47° 47' N, 8° 34' W, four leagues W by S of his. Noon by the sun at 12:10; the captain means me to see the noon sights. Watching: the wind's further haul to south (it would put the Azores course to leeward and square the problem), the gusts for a real squall (the captain's word: square sail and topgallant come in first, and only for a real squall), the glass.
Stood by until a squall.
Stood by until noon.

12:11, afternoon watch, noon. Day's work: lat by obs 47° 49' N (account was 47° 46', moved 2½ miles NE); course made good since yesterday WSW, 62 miles; longitude by account 8° 27' W — no tide in the day's work, the directions give none for these waters. My own slate had run to 47° 43' N, 8° 47' W, five leagues WSW of his and outside my trust: set my reckoning to the noon fix, 47° 49' N, 8° 27' W. The pattern of the last three noons (the account north of the observation by 2-4 miles) is broken today — the account lies south of the observation; with no tide to allow and deep water, the longitude now rests on the log alone, and the lunar of Spica (7° 44' W, taken 23:16) stands 43 miles east of the account — within its doubt, but it has leaned east twice now. Also: at 12:01 I took in the topgallant — shaking in the 53° close-hauled trim as the wind settled SE. The wind has worked SE by S through the forenoon, gusty and variable, glass down to 30.17 and steady the last hour; the squall never came. She is close hauled larboard tack on the WSW course, plain sail and square sail and gaff topsail, 3-4 kn. Staying up till noon done as asked; I'll ask the captain for rest when the forenoon's work is squared.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a handover.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 12:41, afternoon watch 1 bell. Deck given back to the captain; I go below to rest by his word. What he takes: all sail set but the topgallant (came in 12:01, shaking in the 53° close-hauled trim), plain sail + square sail + main gaff topsail, close hauled on the larboard tack, WSW 243°, wind SE-SSE 4 kn gusty and variable, apparent 59° on the larboard bow, 3-4 kn; glass 30.16 falling a hundredth the hour (the squall it threatened has not come), clear, smooth sea, no land, no danger, deep water (1254 fathoms by account — the lead is useless now, soundings cease). Noon: lat by obs 47° 49' N, lon by account 8° 27' W, made good WSW 62 miles; no tide in the day's work. Lunar of Spica (23:16 last night) 7° 44' W, 43 miles east of the account, within its doubt — the longitude leans east at both lunars. My slate set to the noon fix, a mile N by W of his. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping, trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. Watching: the wind for hauling further south (the course would come to leeward), the gusts for a real squall (square sail and topgallant first, by his word of the morning), the glass's fall.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

15:42, afternoon watch 7 bells. Woke rested, off watch; the captain has the deck. While I slept: the wind has settled SE by S, still close hauled on the larboard tack (W made good SW by W 241°), the glass has fallen on — 30.16 → 30.12, 2 hundredths the last hour, the sky gone overcast: the weather the falling glass promised is gathering at last, though no squall yet. Run since noon 9 miles. My slate 47° 44' N, 8° 39' W, a mile N by W of his. The moon is full (14 days old) but the sky thick — no lunar tonight if this holds. I stay on the quarterdeck awake and easy; when the captain gives me the deck I take the readings afresh and mind the glass first of all.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

18:00, last dog watch 4 bells, change of the watch. Still off watch, the captain has the deck. The afternoon's news: the wind has backed SSE (from SE), still close hauled larboard tack, and the captain set the topgallant again at 16:04 — all sail now. The weather has thickened to drizzle, the sky overcast, the glass fallen to 30.10 — 4 hundredths in three hours, the fall steady and gaining pace; the moon full but the sky thick, so no lunar tonight. Depth by account 2066 fathoms — far into the deep water. Run since noon 14 miles, made good WSW 242°. My slate 47° 42' N, 8° 46' W, a mile N by W of his. Watching when I have the deck: the glass's fall (if it hurries, the standing orders and my own judgment serve — the squall the glass has promised all day may yet come out of the south-east), the wind for hauling further south or freshening, the topgallant and square sail for the gusts. I remain off watch until the captain gives me the deck; the dog watches are his.
Stood by until the change of the watch.
Took the deck from the captain.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Nothing given over — the handover note stands as written in the journal at 18:00, last dog watch 4 bells: still off watch, the captain has the deck; the wind SSE close hauled larboard tack, all sail set, drizzle, the glass 30.10 fallen 4 hundredths in three hours, run since noon 14 miles made good WSW 242°, my slate 47° 42' N, 8° 46' W a mile N by W of his, no land no danger, the deep water 2063 fathoms.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

18:08, last dog watch. Took the deck from the captain. She: close hauled larboard tack, WSW ~242°, wind SSE 3-4 kn gusty, apparent 61° on the larboard bow, 2¼ kn, all sail set (topgallant re-set 16:04), drizzle, glass 30.10-30.11 fallen 3-4 hundredths in three hours, deep water 2063 fathoms (no sounding possible), no land, no danger. Run since noon 14 miles made good WSW. My slate 47° 42' N, 8° 46' W, a mile N by W of his; his lunar of Spica 7° 44' W stands 43 miles east of the account, the second lunar to lean east. Moon full, sky thick — no lunar tonight unless it clears. Standing orders live: Hourly Shaping (next ~18:15), trim on the course, tend the sheets on the glass, Lead Warning. The captain's word for squalls: watch the gusts, square sail and topgallant come in first for a real squall, not for little gusts. Watching: the glass's fall (a hurry in it wakes the book), the wind for hauling further south (the course to leeward worsens) or freshening, the topgallant and square sail at the gusts, the moon for a clearing sky.
Stood by until a glass.
Took the deck from the captain.
Stood by until a glass.

18:33, last dog watch 1 bell. The captain's order for the watch: when the topgallant shakes, try 'brace the topgallant up half a point' before taking her in. Noted and will keep it. The watch so far: the Hourly Shaping fired 18:15, steer WSW 243°; the yards braced 54-58° from square and the sheets trimmed to 29-32° off the centreline; all sail set and drawing on 3 kn of NE-by-E-of-us SSE air. Glass 30.11 steady the last hour after the morning's fall; drizzle, a smooth sea. Run since noon 15 miles. My slate 47° 42' N, 8° 47' W, a mile N by W of his. Watching: the gusts for the squall (square sail and topgallant first), the topgallant for shaking (brace her up half a point first), the moon for a clearing sky and the lunar.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

20:00, first watch 8 bells. Still hold the deck (evening watch mine since 18:09). The evening: wind backed further to S by E, gusts 3-4 kn, close hauled larboard tack, WSW 243°; the topgallant shook and I braced the topgallant yard up half a point at 19:03 by the captain's standing instruction — drew again; but now the topsail and the topgallant both shake in the variable airs, apparent 48° on the bow, and the standing orders have braced the yards sharp (54-58°) each half hour against it. Glass fallen to 30.08, 4 hundredths in three hours, the fall quickening; drizzle, overcast, deep water 2133 fathoms. The moon full but thick. Run since noon 18 miles made good WSW 244°; my slate 47° 41' N, 8° 51' W. The captain prefers more canvas out in light airs, drawing with a light touch — so the topsails are kept on and worked, not handed, while they may be made to draw. Watching: the gusts (a real squall takes the square sail and topgallant first), the shaking canvas (brace up before handing, the captain's rule), the glass's fall, the moon for the lunar if the sky breaks.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

21:30, first watch 3 bells. Holding the deck. The wind has hauled to S by E (settled 20:53), still gusty, she now stands W by S 258° — the Hourly Shaping has found the course layable at last, close hauled larboard tack, and made good is WSW 245°, so she is footing to the westward on the Azores course. The square sail shakes in the gusts (the captain braced the yards sharp up at 20:00 and belayed his standing order 'trim on the course' at 20:02, leaving the trim to the tend-sheets order and the helm); the topgallant shakes too. Glass 30.07, fallen 3 hundredths in three hours and 2 the last hour — the fall continues quickening but no squall yet, the drizzle ceased, fine. Leeway 3-4°. Run since noon 21 miles. My slate 47° 40' N, 8° 55' W. The moon up ten degrees behind the cloud, thick sky — no lunar. Watching: the shaking square sail and topgallant (brace up before handing — the captain's rule), the gusts for the real squall, the glass's fall, the moon for the sky breaking.
Stood by until a glass.

00:00, middle watch 8 bells, the change of the watch. I hold the deck — evening watch and first watch both mine. The night's run: wind backed slowly through S by E to S, 3-5 kn gusty and variable, she now stands W by N 280° close hauled on the larboard tack, made good W by S 253°; the Hourly Shaping has brought her round from the close-hauled W by S to W by N as the wind freed and backed — the course is now laid with the wind south. 30 miles since noon. Glass 30.05, steady the last hour, the fall slower through the night (2 hundredths in three) — no squall come yet, overcast and fine, a smooth sea. Leeway 2-4°. My slate 47° 41' N, 9° 08' W, a mile N by W of his. The moon full and up seventeen degrees behind the cloud — no lunar while the sky is thick. The captain on the quarterdeck. Watching: the gusts for a real squall (the glass still falling slowly), the wind for hauling further east (it would free the course) or freshening, the square sail and topgallant in the variables (brace up before handing — the captain's rule), noon by the sun at 12:15.
Stood by until a glass.
