Stood by until a notable event.

11:20, forenoon watch. SAIL HO! A sail abeam to starboard, bearing W, distant five miles. Wind WSW 4 kn, heading S 180°, glass 30.30 steady. Nothing else in sight, open water, no land within a league. Watching: whether she closes, her rig when her hull lifts, and whether the captain wants a change of course.
Stood by until a notable event.

11:22, forenoon watch. The stranger made out: a brig, standing to the north-eastward (NE by E), under plain sail, bearing W five miles — crossing from west to east. Wind W by S 4 kn, heading S 183°, glass 30.30 steady. She should pass ahead of us across our bow if she holds her leg. Watching: whether she closes or crosses clear, her rig, and whether any further stranger appears.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

12:43, afternoon watch. The brig (NE by E under plain sail) is now on the starboard quarter, bearing N, five miles — she has passed astern of us as we ran south. Noon: lat 40°25' N, account moved 3 mi N; course made good S, 60 miles; longitude 16°24' W. Wind W by S 4 kn, heading S by W 186°, glass 30.30 steady. Watching: whether she drops over the horizon astern, and whether any stranger appears.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:13, first watch. Sunset. The brig that passed astern has dropped out of sight (last glass at 15:21: right astern, four leagues). We are 82 miles further along: 40°12' N, 16°26' W by account, 12 miles since noon, heading S 182° at 2 kn, glass 30.46 steady, hazy with a few miles visibility, smooth sea. Moon two days from change — dark nights coming. Nothing in sight.
Stood by until a notable event.

05:12, morning watch 2 bells. Sunrise. New day's work: lat 39°55' N, 16°27' W by account; 29 miles since noon (yesterday), heading S by W 192° at 1 kn, glass 30.43 rising, sky hazy. Ate and drank on the quarterdeck. The date's slipped past a week at sea; run since noon yesterday 29 miles. Watching: the glass rising, wind, and whether any stranger appears.
Stood by until a notable event.

05:13, morning watch. All hands called to wear ship — the captain altering her leg. Wind W by S, amplitude at sunrise gave 25° W (25 June, up from 24°30'). Head swinging from S by W through the wind; glass 30.44 steady. Watching: the wear coming off, and what tack/heading he settles her on.
Stood by until a notable event.

05:21, morning watch. Wear complete: braced sharp up on the larboard tack, heading NNW (332°), 2 kn, leeway 5° — she's reaching up to the northward again. Wind W 4 kn. Glass 30.43 steady, sky clear. The captain's northerly-leg pattern continues: beat up NNW for a spell, then wear and run south. Nothing in sight, open water. Watching: her heading, the glass, and whether any stranger appears.
Stood by until a notable event.

05:39, morning watch. SAIL HO — a brig right ahead, bearing NW, four miles, standing to the southward (S by W) under plain sail: head-on approach, closing tracks. We head NW by N at 2 kn, wind WSW 3 kn, glass 30.30. This is the first stranger since the Two Brothers yesterday. Watching: her bearing and distance closely — head-on means early decision. The captain (Mr Bowen) has the deck; the lookout's hail will reach him. If she bears down or alters toward us, report at once.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

08:51, forenoon watch. SAIL HO — a sail on the larboard quarter, bearing S by W, two leagues. We're on the larboard tack heading NW by N; she's abaft our beam to leeward. Wind WSW 5 kn, glass 30.30. This is likely the same American-coloured brig we met head-on at 05:39 — she was standing S by W and we tacked past her. Watching: whether she alters toward us, and whether any further stranger appears.
Stood by until a notable event.

12:43, afternoon watch. The brig on our larboard quarter has dropped below the horizon — nothing in sight now. Noon: lat 40°04' N, account moved 2 mi S by E; course made good SW by S, 43 miles; longitude 16°35' W. Wind light (2 kn), head NW 316°, glass 30.39 steady. I am very tired — will sleep below until called. Nothing owed.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.
Took the deck from the captain.

18:01, last dog watch. Took the deck from the captain (awake 40 hours, gone to the gunroom to sleep). I have the deck. She lies NNW 334° on the larboard tack, W airs 2 kn, glass 30.35, smooth sea, 8 miles since noon. Standing orders live as the book holds them: Lead Warning; 'trim on the course', 'tend the sheets', 'Hourly Shaping' (5 miles N of Ribeira Grande) all currently belayed. Madeira rationed out to the crew as ordered (12 bottles, gill a man, dinner today and tomorrow, Pascoe seeing it shared fairly). Water 2.4 tons at short allowance, foul. Watching: the wind backing or freshening, and the horizon for any stranger; wake the captain only for a drastic shift or a sight.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:00, 8 bells first watch. First watch begins on my deck. She holds NW by N 328° full and by, 2 kn, wind W by S, glass 30.34 steady. Nothing in sight, hazy with a few miles visibility. Captain asleep in the cabin. Watching: wind for drastic shift (wake him per his word), horizon, glass.
Stood by until a notable event.

20:14, sunset, first watch. Wind backed to WSW, head eased NW 318°, glass 30.34 falling a hundredth an hour. Nothing in sight. Deck mine; captain asleep. Watching: wind for drastic shift (wake him per his word), glass, horizon.

00:00, 8 bells middle watch. Middle watch underway on my deck. She's gone to NNW 332° full and by, wind W by S 4 kn, glass 30.31 falling 2 hundredths an hour. 13 miles since noon, nothing in sight, captain asleep in the cabin. The northerly-leg pattern continues — reaching north now. Watching: wind for drastic shift (wake him), horizon, glass.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:00, 8 bells morning watch. Middle watch passed quietly on my deck: beat up the whole watch, now N by W 346° full and by, wind W by N 4 kn, 17 miles since noon, glass 30.29 steady. Captain came on deck 00:00. Nothing in sight. Watching: the glass rising, wind, and whether any stranger appears.

04:48, morning watch. All hands called to wear ship — the wind has come NNW 9 kn on gusts and the northerly finally has some strength in it; glass jumped 8 hundredths in three hours (30.30→30.38), risen 9 hundredths in the last hour. Head swinging S by W through the wind. This is the northerly Tregarthen promised arriving in earnest. Watching: the wear coming off clean and the new tack's heading.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:56, morning watch. DESTINATION SET: the captain shaped a course for the port of St Lawrence — WSW by account, 437 miles. Hourly Shaping re-entered in the book for that port (the Ribeira Grande order from yesterday 17:04 already replaced). Wind settled NW by N, a gentle breeze at 10 kn gusting to 9 mean — the northerly is properly arrived now. Glass dropped sharply with the shift (30.38→30.21, down 9 hundredths in 3 hrs) — a front passing, but wind is fair for westing. All hands up for the wear. Watching: her settling onto the WSW leg, the glass steadying, and the new port's line.

04:56, morning watch. Wear complete — braced for the course ordered on the STARBOARD tack, heading WSW 245°. The port of St Lawrence is now the shaped course (437 miles WSW), Hourly Shaping re-entered for that port. Wind NW by N 9 kn on the starboard bow, we making 5 kn. This is a proper reaching leg with the northerly at last — good westing. Glass fell to 30.21 with the shift. Watching: her speed on the new tack, glass steadying, and the horizon.
Stood by until a notable event.
Stood by until a notable event.

04:58, morning watch. Yards braced 54°-58° from square on the starboard tack, sheets trimming in turn. She's settling onto the WSW leg for St Lawrence at speed — 10 kn of wind mean. GLASS STILL FALLING FAST: down a tenth in three hours, 7 hundredths in the last hour. That's the wake-up condition — watching it closely now. New standing order entered: 'tend the sheets on the watch' at watch change. Watching: glass rate and wind.

06:01. The captain's standing instruction: DO NOT shorten canvas without his word unless she begins straining at the bolt-ropes — he wants this speed all he can get. I will hold all plain sail until straining shows, and if it comes to that I can shorten on my own word as an immediate danger measure per my authority. Glass noted falling again (30.20, down 9 hundredths in 3 hrs) — front passing. Wind 9 kn WSW on the bow, making 4.5 kn. Watching: bolt-ropes and leeches, glass, horizon.

Handover note (handing over the deck): Handing the deck, sir — much obliged for the relief, I'm spent. She's in good order: wind NW by N light on the starboard bow, head WSW 248° on the shaping line, glass 30.15 steady and rising a hundredth an hour since the 30.09 trough, clear night coming on, smooth sea, no sail, 2-3 knots through the water. Standing orders all live: Hourly Shaping (5 miles north of Ribeira Grande), trim on the course, tend the sheets every glass, Lead Warning. Full allowance restored at 23:32, water 2.4 tons / 20 days foul, provisions 25 days — people cheerful. Watching for: the glass (it's mending, so less urgent), any wind shift west of NW (would fetch us off the line), and the horizon. Goodnight, sir.

We hove to for the fog and filled away at 19:43 on the starboard tack, NW by W 302° with fore-and-aft sail, the topsail in the gear. The wind is N 6 and falling and the glass 30.60 steady. 12:18 Anchored Ponta Delgada Road, best bower in 35 fathoms (deep; 176 fathoms veered, 131 out per readings), Mr Pacheco pilot aboard. Passage lessons: the dead-reckoning longitude was ~17 leagues out (west) until the landfall cross-bearings of St Mary's/St Michael's at 05:53 on the 28th; fog twice, hove to for an unidentified black topsail schooner (French, out of Bayonne per pilot, stays off Vila Franca/Santa Maria, will not come into the road under São Brás guns). I wrongly said I'd borne away when I had not the deck, and corrected it at once: without the deck I give no helm orders, say so plainly. Heaving to/tacking/anchoring need the captain's word or danger='...'. Pilot says water from the spring under the fort is sweet, Senhor Medeiros sells water and fresh meat; ours is foul (1.9 t). High water here about 18:45, 18 ft rise. Captain asked me to stand down for his rest; business ashore and the sealed letter for Bettencourt (Horta) later.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, 12:18 afternoon watch. Mr Bowen has brought her to anchor in Ponta Delgada Road with the best bower in 35 fathoms; the pilot Mr Pacheco is aboard. We came in from the east. Our dead reckoning was about 17 leagues out in longitude until the landfall bearings of St Mary's and St Michael's on the 28th, so trust the fixes over the account. A black topsail schooner showed no colours on the 28th and the fog hid us from her. The pilot says she is a French schooner out of Bayonne that stays off Vila Franca and Santa Maria and won't come into the road under the São Brás guns. Water is 1.9 tons and foul, provisions 21 days. Senhor Medeiros at the quay sells water and fresh meat, and the spring under the fort is sweet. High water is about 18:45 with an 18-foot rise. The road is open from east round south to west, so put to sea if it blows from there. The sealed letter for Senhor Bettencourt of Horta is still in the cabin. Standing orders: Hourly Shaping and trim-the-yards are belayed, and tend-the-sheets-on-the-watch is live. Lesson for whoever sits here: without the deck, give no helm or sail orders, and say so plainly. Mr Bowen is resting; keep watch on the cable, the weather and any sail.

Handover note (handing over the deck): 06:03 morning watch, 1 July. Handing the deck to Mr Bowen so I may rest. Under way from Ponta Delgada, pilot off. Steering WNW (295°) full and by, wind N, light, about 3 knots, for 38°29'N 27°58'W (first mark; then 38°41'N 28°28'W). 2 July 09:43 forenoon watch. Fayal approach: pilot Mr Terra aboard 08:49; ship repeatedly lost way and made sternway under reefed main and headsails in a 22-26 kn SW by W wind (veered from N during the night); boxed off at 09:22; best bower let go 09:32 in 46 fathoms, dragged, veered to 232-240 fathoms, then ship took the ground forward at 09:43 on sand and shell on the Praia by the old fort, 1½ fathoms, drawing 9 ft, heel 9°, tide falling; carpenter reports her strained and making water. Master reckons she floats at the flood about 16:30 (HW Fayal ~20:30). I ordered the kedge laid astern (to the E into deep water). Pilot Terra says sand, soft, wind off land blows her off, stays until the flood; port captain would send lighters (port's business: needs the captain's word). Lessons: (1) tell the captain at once when readings show sternway, (2) don't order sails mid-evolution, (3) anchor in 35-40 fathoms on sand needs full scope; 46 fathoms with wind 24 kn dragged. Captain asked me to journal and stand down; hands tired. Sealed letter for Bettencourt still in the cabin; Ruiz and Bettencourt ashore at Fayal; supercargo Mr Josiah Hale ashore in the tavern.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, 09:43 forenoon watch, 2 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter is aground forward in Fayal Road on the sand and small shell of the Praia by the old fort, 1½ fathoms by the chart, she draws 9 feet, heeling about 8-9°, tide falling, wind SW by W 24 kn off the land, glass 29.81 falling fast. The carpenter reports her strained and making water; the ship has no well to sound yet. The master reckons she floats at the flood, about half past four this afternoon (HW Fayal ~20:30). Best bower is down with all 240 fathoms, bar-taut; the kedge is being laid astern to the E into deep water by the boat, on the pilot's advice. All sail is being furled. Pilot Mr Terra of Fayal is aboard and says it is soft ground, she will not break, the wind blows her off, and the port captain would send lighters if asked (port's business: the captain's word). Watch on the pumps and the leak. Lessons for whoever sits here: tell the captain at once when the readings show 'making sternway'; never order sails or yards while an evolution is in hand; take the full scope in deep water; and without the deck give no helm or sail orders. The captain has the deck. Ashore at Fayal are Mr Ruiz the clerk, Senhor Bettencourt the merchant (the sealed letter for him is in the cabin), and Mr Josiah Hale the supercargo. The French schooner (12 guns, black) was last reported off Santa Maria; the Conceição brigantine from Funchal is overdue. The purse is £928 8s; water 5.7 tons, provisions 33 days. The captain asked for the stand-down because he needs a break.
Stood down by the officer of the watch: its own word.

Sherbourne cutter lies moored in Fayal Road on two bowers (best 240 fathoms, small 120, both full out) in 22 fathoms, kedge catted at the bows, holding all night within a cable of the account (fixes each glass: Guia SW by S, town W, Espalamaca N by E). Ashore: Bettencourt has the letter and wants forty pipes (20 tons) of Pico wine consigned to his son in Falmouth at £4 a ton, £40 on signing the bill of lading tomorrow and £40 on delivery; he'll sell the captain wine at £32 the ton for his own account; lighters from Madalena come out after dark tomorrow night, sail on the land breeze before dawn, keep it quiet because of the Basque (Etcheverry's black schooner). Mr Hale, supercargo of Salem, has agreed a £5 passage to Madeira, hammock with the hands; chest to the beach when the boat is sent. I advised: heave in the small bower at first light (twilight 05:36), ride by the best bower alone, then shift to a berth in 10 to 15 fathoms on the flood with Mr Terra's help and a rested watch. The captain has the deck and sends me ashore in the morning to fetch Hale and give Bettencourt the word on the lighters. Lessons: no anchor left to let go with both cables out; keep a stream/kedge ready; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'.

Noon observation: latitude 37° 54' N; the account moved a mile and a half NNW; account now 37° 51' N, 28° 01' W, good to two miles; Pico NNW 13 leagues, St George N 17, Caldeira NW by N 18, Santa Barbara NE by N 20; 1018 fathoms. Well an inch at the last sounding (not sounded since 02:00 by my orders; you can order it if wanted). Purse £842 15s; manifest 24 tons of Pico wine (20 for Bettencourt's son at Falmouth, 4 on your own account, marked C), room for 18; provisions 39 days, water 6.5 tons (54 days). Passenger: Mr Hale, £5 paid. Course plan agreed with you: hold SE to about 36° 30' N, 26° 40' W so we pass well south of Santa Maria and São Miguel and clear of the Basque's grounds, then haul to ESE (114°) for the point 10 miles south of Funchal road, Madeira 650 miles ESE. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch; 'heave the lead' is belayed (deep water). Watch: the masthead lookout reports every sail; none yet. Wake the captain for a sail, an easterly shift or the wind coming ahead, a strain warning, or land. Eaten and drunk at 12:01 (biscuit, cheese, scuttle-butt); going below to rest until called.
Handed over the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Turned in below, in the gunroom, asleep until called.

06:44 5 July 1806. Stand-down at the captain's word (he is taking a break; the game is saved). State: Sherbourne cutter under way for Funchal (shaped by the captain's word), steering SE by E (119°) since 00:03, making good SE (132°) at 5-6 knots by the log, wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant set; account 36° 54' N, 27° 44' W (really 26° 44' W by account), Ponta Delgada NE 23½ leagues, 1365 fathoms, glass 30.24 falling slightly, no sail sighted. Course plan: pencil line from the captain to a point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing São Lourenço by 20 miles; Madeira about 450 miles ESE. Purse £842 15s; 24 tons of Pico wine aboard (20 for Bettencourt's son in Falmouth, 4 for the captain on his own account, marked C); sealed letter for Falmouth in the captain's keeping; Mr Hale (supercargo, Salem) aboard for Madeira; provisions 39 days, water 6.4 tons. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch, trim the yards on the watch; 'heave the lead' (mate's) belayed. The French schooner (Etcheverry, Basque) was last said to be off Santa Maria; we are well south of her grounds. Lessons carried: no 'ring the bell' order exists; 'shape a course for' needs the captain's word by name for a new destination; 'how am I' shows hunger and thirst, so eat and drink ('Eat something', 'Drink some water') every watch; tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'; keep the lead going near land; never weigh the last anchor in fog without the captain's word.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, 06:44 morning watch, 5 July 1806. Sherbourne cutter is under way for Funchal, steering SE by E (119°) and making good SE (132°) at 5-6 knots, the wind NNW 11 kn on the larboard quarter, plain sail with square sail and topgallant set, glass 30.24 falling slightly, fair weather, no sail in sight. Account 36° 54' N, 26° 44' W, 1365 fathoms, Ponta Delgada NE 23½ leagues; we are well south of the Basque's reported grounds off Santa Maria. The captain's pencil line leads to a point 10 miles south of Funchal road, clearing São Lourenço by 20 miles; Madeira about 450 miles ESE. Aboard: 24 tons of Pico wine (20 for Bettencourt's son at Falmouth, 4 for the captain's own account, marked C), the sealed letter for Falmouth in the captain's keeping, Mr Hale (supercargo of Salem, passage paid £5), purse £842 15s, provisions 39 days, water 6.4 tons. Standing orders: Lead Warning, tend the sheets on the watch, trim the yards on the watch; 'heave the lead' belayed in deep water (turn it on near land). The captain has the deck and is taking a break; he asked me to journal and stand down. For whoever sits here next: no 'ring the bell' order exists; a new destination needs the captain's word by name; eat and drink with 'Eat something' and 'Drink some water' each watch (check with 'how am I'); tell the captain at once when 'making sternway'; keep the lead going in uncertain water; never weigh the last anchor in fog without the captain's word.

world_orders.order: message: at Falmouth from Messrs Rogers and Son, the owners: "Captain Bowen, a line before you sail. The letter you carry is for Senhor Bettencourt's own hand and no other's. His house has always taken our sailcloth at a fair price, and if the vintage is as good as they write, bring home as much of the Pico wine as she will stow and the purse will buy. Mind the season: the underwriters will not hold the policy on the cutter past the first of August, and we would have her home before it. Your obedient servants, Rogers and Son."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Been round with the lantern, sir. Sail room's dry and the spare canvas sound. The spare spars on the booms are all there and lashed. The well's making no more than she ought in this sea. The cooper's caulked the chimes on the leaguers, and they'll hold if we don't work her too hard. Nothing else amiss below that I can find."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Here, sir. On deck."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Hands to dinner, sir, pease and pork. Cook says the bread bags in the after locker are damp to the hand since that blow; I've had them turned and stowed higher, but I'd not swear to the bottom ones."

world_orders.order: aboard: the bread found mouldy

world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Luck or no, sir, the sun'll do the rest good. Thirty-odd days of bread yet, and the Fayal bakers'll sell us more. Glass is coming up a touch, too."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Begging your pardon, Mr Pearce, I heard 'a third' said. It weren't so bad: three bags out of the after locker, near forty in the bread room all told, and the rest sound once it's dried."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "She's backing her main topsail, sir, and there's a weft in her ensign! She means to speak us. A bit of sail and we'd be up with her in ten minutes."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Captain Tregarthen: "The Two Brothers of Falmouth, Tregarthen master, eleven days from Fayal with wine! What cutter is that? Come down within easy hail, if you'll have the news of the islands. I'll lie to for you."
world_orders.words: Captain Tregarthen spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Captain Tregarthen: "Bound for Falmouth, please God! Fair weather out of Fayal, and a word for you if you're for the islands: don't go west yet. We had the northerly steady from the islands up to forty-two, then nothing but these westerlies. Stand south first and you'll find it. Horta's quiet. Senhor Bettencourt's well and asking every boat after a packet from England. There's a young Spanish clerk on the quay asking after a cutter, the Sherbourne. And mind, there's a French privateer schooner, a black one, been seen off São Jorge, eight or ten guns. The Portuguese say she took a Guernseyman. What's the news of home? Is the Channel clear?"
world_orders.words: Captain Tregarthen spoke on the quarterdeck

world_orders.order: say as Captain Tregarthen: "Glad to hear it! A good passage to you, and my respects to Senhor Bettencourt. Tell him the Two Brothers is home with his wine. Keep a sharp eye off São Jorge!"
world_orders.words: Captain Tregarthen spoke on the quarterdeck

world_orders.order: aboard: the water found foul
world_orders.words: found aboard: the water found foul

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Sir, the new leaguer we started this morning stinks like a ditch. The ground tier's gone ropy in this warm weather. The hands'll drink it if they must, but they're turning from it. A fortnight's sweetening in the sun may mend some of it. If you'll let me, I'll have it aired with the windsail and boiled for the coppers."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye aye, sir, windsail and coppers it is. Three-quarters water I'll pass to the cook and the scuttlebutt, once you've given it as your order. The hands'll grumble, but they'll take it from you sooner than from me."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Sullen, sir, I'll not hide it. Half water in this sun is hard, and the forecastle's quiet the way it is when they're chewing on a thing. Nobody's spoke out of turn. The windsail's taken the worst of the stink off the leaguer, and boiled in the coppers it goes down well enough with the burgoo and the tea. But it's foul still, sir, and it'll stay so till we fill fresh. If you've a mind to ease them a little now the wind's come fair, a word that we're making our westing would do as much as a pint."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: weather: waypoint for "the Azores high" at 1805-06-19T18:00 -1900 -1550 1018
world_orders.words: a waypoint appended to the Azores high

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Southing, sir, if it was mine to say. The Fayal men get down into the latitude of the islands first and run their westing down on it after. Tregarthen said as much: the northerly's to the south'ard. Every mile north we make on this board we must pay back, and some easting on the other is cheaper. That's an old boatswain's notion, sir. Mr Bowen'll have the right of it by his figures."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye aye, sir! That'll go down better than the water itself. I'll tell the forecastle now, while the watch is on deck to hear it, and say it was your word. There'll be a few easier faces at the scuttlebutt in the morning."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Turtle asleep on the water, sir, two cables on the lee bow, and Portugee men-o'-war sailing all about her. Sure sign of the warm water. If you'd heave her to for a quarter-hour, the jolly boat could have him, and the cook says turtle soup would set the people up wonderful."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye aye, sir! Jolly boat's crew, lay aft! Softly with the oars, lads, he's asleep. I'll go myself, sir, if you'll give the word for the boat."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Boat's alongside, sir, and we have him! A fine hawksbill, the best part of a hundredweight. He woke as Tom Bray got the bowline round his flipper, and near had the boat over, but we have him. Turtle soup for all hands at dinner, and the shell for whoever wants it. Hook on and hoist away, lads!"
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: aboard: a hawksbill turtle of near a hundredweight, in the galley
world_orders.words: a hawksbill turtle of near a hundredweight made, in the galley

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Thank 'ee, sir. Bray's grinning like a dog with two tails. Boat's in and griped; you may fill away when you please."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as the cook: "Morning, sir. The turtle's on his back by the coppers with a wet swab over him, to keep him sweet. He'll go in the pot this forenoon for the people's dinner. There's fins and calipee enough for the cabin too, if you'll have it."
world_orders.words: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Spencer: "That I will, sir! The calipee for the cabin, with a glass of something to it, and the soup for the people at eight bells in the forenoon. Your steward shall have it hot. They're sniffing at the galley door already, sir."
world_orders.words: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Dinner's piped, sir, and you never heard such a quiet forecastle. Every man's head in his kid. The turtle soup's gone down handsome, and there's a cheer for the cabin if you'll go forward to hear it."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck

world_orders.order: say as Mr Spencer: "Your calipee, sir, hot from the coppers, and the steward's drawn a glass of the Madeira to it. Mind, not the owners' case! The hands sent word aft by Bray: 'Our respects to the captain, and three cheers for the turtle.'"
world_orders.words: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley

world_orders.order: say as Mr Spencer: "Your health, sir, and the turtle's! I'll not say no. Thirty year at the coppers and that's the first captain's glass I've had since the Bellerophon."
world_orders.words: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley

world_orders.order: say as Mr Spencer: "Aye, sir, a bowl kept hot at the back of the coppers for Mr Pearce, and a bit of the fin besides. He'll wake to it, never fear."
world_orders.words: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Hark at her, sir, six knots and the water talking under the forefoot! That's the Portugee trade, as Tregarthen promised. The forecastle's singing again for the first time since the Bay."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "There's one bottle left whole, sir, and a heel in another. I kept 'em back on purpose against your asking. I'll have Spencer carry them aft directly. The people had their two gills and blessed you for 'em."

world_orders.order: aboard: the small case of the owners' Madeira, in the cabin
world_orders.words: the small case of the owners' Madeira moved: it was in the galley, and is in the cabin

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Morning, Mr Pearce, and welcome back to the land of the living! All's well forward. The jib sheet's chafing a touch at the fairlead, and I've a hand serving it now. Nothing else amiss, and she's going like a witch."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye, Mr Pearce. I'll send Jem Hosking aloft with the glass at every bell, with a dollar for the man that first sights the land, if the captain'll stand it. Santa Maria's a high one in the middle, they say. You'll see her peak long before the shore."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye aye, Mr Pearce. Two hands in the fore-top and one on the bowsprit end, the lead coiled down in the starboard chains, and young Oliver to run aft. The land hereabouts is high and steep-to, by all accounts, so you'll smell it and hear the surf before the lead finds ground."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: person: make "Senhor Medeiros", a ship-chandler of Ponta Delgada, ashore at Ponta Delgada, at the quay, who speaks a sailor's English, has water boats and fresh beef to sell, and knows every vessel in the islands
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros, ship-chandler of Ponta Delgada, who speaks a sailor's English, has water boats and fresh beef to sell, and knows every vessel in the islands; made from words, ashore at Ponta Delgada, on the quay

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Fog's lifting, sir, and the masthead says the horizon's bare all round, not a sail in it! She's lost us, the black devil. That was well done, if I may say so."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Hark, sir, hear that? Bells, faint, away on the starboard bow, about NW by W. It's Sunday morning, and that'll be the churches of Ponta Delgada ringing for Mass. Sound carries a long way in a fog on still water. That gives you a bearing for the town, if not the distance."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pacheco: "Bem-vindo, senhor capitão. You come from the east? Then you were lucky in the fog. There is a black schooner, French, out of Bayonne, that lies off Vila Franca and Santa Maria these ten days, stopping the fishing boats for fresh fish and news. Our boats saw her yesterday evening to the south. Here in the road she will not come: the castle of São Brás has guns, and the Governor will not have it. You are safe at anchor."
world_orders.words: Mr Pacheco spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pacheco: "Três semanas! Then you will want water and fresh meat, and Senhor Medeiros at the quay will sell you both, with water boats to save your people the labour. The spring under the fort is good water, sweet. And this evening, if you go ashore, the procession of the Senhor Santo Cristo is past, but the taverns are not. Steer a little more to the north now, senhor, toward the tower."
world_orders.words: Mr Pacheco spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: mark: the place of the island that rose out of the sea in 1720 and was gone by 1722, where the water is discoloured green and milky, bubbles of gas rise, and there is a smell of sulphur on the wind, at 38 13 N 26 38 W
world_orders.words: a mark put in the world, the place of the island that rose out of the sea in 1720 and was gone by 1722, where the water is discoloured green and milky, bubbles of gas rise, and there is a smell of sulphur on the wind,, at 38 13 N 26 38 W

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye aye, sir. A hand on the cable and an eye on the glass, and if the wind comes round into the south I'll fire a musket and hoist the ensign at the masthead, so you'll know to come off quick. Mind the landing at the mole, sir. The surf's a sly one even on a calm day, by the look of the beach."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Bom dia, senhor capitão! Medeiros, ship-chandler, at your service. I saw your cutter come in with Pacheco this morning out of the fog, a fine little ship. English, yes? Welcome to São Miguel. You smell the oranges? The whole island smells of them in winter. Now it is the lupins and the tar, and the bread from the convent ovens, it being Sunday. You will want water, I think, after a long passage? I have two water boats and good casks, sweet water from the fountain under São Brás. Fresh beef, eggs, onions, wine of the island. And news, senhor, if you like news. Come, sit in the shade of my store, and we talk prices like Christians."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Fouled before Finisterre, and you come all this way? Coitados, your poor men! Come, this way, mind the fish baskets. Here is my store: cordage, canvas, pitch, beef in the barrel and on the hoof, biscuit from the convent bakery. You give me the word for the water and the provisions, senhor, and my boats are alongside your cutter within the hour. And now the news, since you are for Horta: a French schooner, a black one, has been all this fortnight between here and Santa Maria. She took the catch of two of our boats off Vila Franca on Friday, and paid in French paper, which is to say she paid nothing. The Governor has written to Lisbon. Nobody here thinks Lisbon will answer."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Nossa Senhora! Then the fog was your friend, and you should light a candle at São Sebastião before you sail. She will be watching the road from outside, I think. She knows a ship that waters here must sail again. If you go west for Fayal, go by night, and keep north of the island, under the land. The French do not like the north side: there is no shelter there for them, and our fishermen of Rabo de Peixe would see her and send word. That is advice from a chandler, senhor, not a sailor. You will judge."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "The market is shut, it being Sunday, but I know the prices as I know my children. Linen of the island eighty-five pounds the ton; barley eight; wine of the island forty, poor stuff beside the Pico; brandy ninety-five; sugar sixty and tobacco ninety, from Brazil by way of Lisbon; salt beef fifty, salt fish twenty-eight; timber seven. Canvas, senhor, sixty-five the ton, and dear, because the war stops the Russian hemp coming. You carry canvas? Then you would do as well here as at Horta, but no better. My boy Joaquim will write it fair for you."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Of course, of course. Talk with your mate. Meanwhile my boats go off with your water and the beef. Senhor, if you are for Horta, give my respects to Senhor Bettencourt. We do a little business, he and I, in wine and in news."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "No imposition at all, senhor. Furtado! — Furtado takes the water off now; he will say it to your mate word for word. 'Please try go ashore, despite your reservation.' A strange message, eh, but he will say it exactly so."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Furtado: "Senhor mate! Senhor Pearce! From your captain, by Senhor Medeiros — he says to me, say it exactly: 'Please try go ashore, despite your reservation.' The water is alongside, senhor, and my boat goes back to the quay when she is empty. There is room for you."
world_orders.words: Furtado spoke in the cabin

world_orders.order: person: "Furtado" goes ashore
world_orders.words: Furtado went ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Myself? Ah. Senhor, I am a chandler; I buy canvas to cut and sell again to every brig that comes in with her sails blown to rags, and they come in all summer. Furtado will look at it — if it is good English canvas, number one or two, dry, not mildewed from the passage — I give sixty-six the ton for the twelve tons, a pound over the market, in Spanish dollars at the counting house, and my lighter fetches it so your men do not sweat. Not more; I must live. And the wine, senhor — you ask Horta? Horta is where the Pico wine comes across the channel, the 'Fayal' wine the Americans take. It is cheaper there at the source than here, a few pounds the ton; here you pay my carriage. If you go to Bettencourt, buy your wine at Horta."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: aboard: twelve tons of canvas sold from the hold to Senhor Medeiros at the quay, at £66 the ton, £792 paid into the purse by Senhor Medeiros
world_orders.words: not carried out: 'twelve tons of canvas sold from the hold to Senhor Medeiros at the quay, at £66 the ton, £792' is no sum the purse reads: say '£30', '£6 10s', 'twenty guineas', 'thirty pounds'

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Furtado has seen it already, senhor — he looked in your hold while the casks went down: good number-one English duck, dry, he says, only a little smell of the bilge on the bottom bolts, nothing. So, we strike it. Go into the market and sell it there, all twelve tons — the clerk enters it at the market's sixty-five for the alfândega, the customs, it is simpler so; and the pound a ton over, the twelve pounds, I put into your hand myself in dollars, here, when my lighter has it. A handshake, senhor?"
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Bom. Done, senhor. The market is up the Rua dos Mercadores, two minutes; tell the clerk 'twelve tons of canvas, Medeiros buys', and my lighter goes off for it at once. I wait for you here with the dollars."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: aboard: £12 paid into the purse by Senhor Medeiros
world_orders.words: £12 paid into the purse by Senhor Medeiros; the purse £929 10s

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Medeiros: "Here, senhor — twelve pounds, in dollars, count them; my word is good. And I write you a little note of it in my own hand, for your owners' book, so your mate sleeps easy — he has an honest face, that one, he looked at me like a customs man. Boa viagem to Horta. My respects to Bettencourt; tell him Medeiros has his canvas and he must buy his sails from me now."
world_orders.words: Senhor Medeiros spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: person: make "Dona Rosa Cabral", keeper of the tavern on the quay, a widow of fifty, ashore at Ponta Delgada, in the tavern, whose late husband was lost with a Lisbon brig in the year two
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral, widow, fifty years of age, keeper of the tavern on the quay, whose late husband was lost with a Lisbon brig in the year two; made from words, ashore at Ponta Delgada, in the tavern

world_orders.order: person: make "Zé Botelho", a fisherman of Vila Franca do Campo, aged forty, ashore at Ponta Delgada, in the tavern, who knows the waters between St Michael's and Santa Maria
world_orders.words: Zé Botelho, fisherman of Vila Franca do Campo, forty years of age, who knows the waters between St Michael's and Santa Maria; made from words, ashore at Ponta Delgada, in the tavern

world_orders.order: say as Dona Rosa Cabral: "Boa tarde, senhores! Ingleses — from the little cutter in the road, yes? Sit, sit, out of the sun. I have the wine of the house, verdelho from Pico, and fish fresh this morning from Zé there. Zé! These are the English from the cutter."
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Zé Botelho: "Ingleses. Hm. You came in round the east end yesterday, in the fog? Then God loves you. There is a schooner, black, low, a Biscayan by the cut of her, very many men, stands off and on under Santa Maria since three, four days — I saw her this morning off the Ponta do Castelo when we hauled the lines, hove to, watching the channel. She does not fish, senhor. Nobody has seen her colours. The governor's people say she is a Frenchman and that is the Spaniard's business, or the Englishman's, not ours."
world_orders.words: Zé Botelho spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Zé Botelho: "Guns? I keep my boat far from her, senhor, I count from two miles. Six ports a side, painted, I think — and swivels on the rail, and the men, many, like a slaver. Always on the west side of Santa Maria, between the Ponta do Castelo and the Ilhéu da Vila, looking across the channel at us — never on the north side, never close in to Vila do Porto; the fort there has guns. In the morning she stands in, in the afternoon she stands off. Waiting for something from here or from Madeira, I think."
world_orders.words: Zé Botelho spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Dona Rosa Cabral: "*sets down two cups of the Pico verdelho and a plate of fried chicharros, lemon on the side, and leaves the senhor captain to his pipe* — Nothing to pay for the first cup. My husband was a seaman; I know the face of a man come in from the sea."
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Dona Rosa Cabral: "From Madeira? Not many, senhor; Madeira looks to Lisbon and to the English. The brigantine of Senhor Gomes, the Conceição, comes twice in the summer from Funchal with sugar and the Madeira wine for the governor's table and the friars, and takes back our wheat and oranges — and the money, they say, for the Funchal houses' bills. She comes about the feast of São Pedro, the end of June. This year she is late. *she crosses herself* Everybody says it, nobody says it to the governor."
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Dona Rosa Cabral: "*laughs* No, senhor — Zé's fish never suffer, only Zé. Eat. And if you sail tonight, go with God — and go by the north side."
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: say as Dona Rosa Cabral: "The first cup was mine, senhor. The rest — the fish, the bread, three cups more between you — call it half a crown in your money, a tostão and a half in ours. Medeiros's dollars will do very well."
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: aboard: 2s 6d paid from the purse to Dona Rosa Cabral

world_orders.order: say as Dona Rosa Cabral: "Obrigada, senhor capitão. Go with God."
world_orders.words: Dona Rosa Cabral spoke ashore at Ponta Delgada

world_orders.order: aboard: £0 2s 6d paid from the purse to Dona Rosa Cabral
world_orders.words: £0 2s 6d paid from the purse to Dona Rosa Cabral; the purse £929 8s

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pacheco: "Muito bem, capitão. My cutter follows under the land, there, astern. When we have the point of the Ponta Delgada abeam and a mile of water outside it, I go — heave to for me then and she runs alongside. Keep a cable's length off the reef under the fort; it runs out further than the chart says."
world_orders.words: Mr Pacheco spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pacheco: "*waves his hat twice over the taffrail; astern, under the land, a lugsail fills and the pilot cutter stands out toward us* — She comes, capitão. Heave to when you like and put me off; ten minutes, no more. Boa viagem — and keep well off the Ferraria at night, the sea breaks on it in any swell."
world_orders.words: Mr Pacheco spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pacheco: "She saw, capitão — but she has lost the breeze under the land, see, her lug hangs. My fault; I asked too soon. Don't wait for her hove to: fill away and stand on slowly, a mile more to sea, and she will find the wind outside and come up with us. When she is close I will ask you to shorten sail."
world_orders.words: Mr Pacheco spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Mr Pearce, sir — blows, there, broad on the larboard bow, two mile off! Sperm whales, sir, four or five of 'em, see the spout go forrard and slantwise. The Fayal men'll be out after them in their boats if they come in under the land."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye, sir — follow my arm: there, broad on the larboard bow, a point abaft it, two mile. Watch the water low down — there! A bushy spout, leaning forrard. And another. They're lying on the top, blowing, sir; they'll sound directly and show their flukes. That's their feeding ground, deep water off the islands; the Nantucket men cruise for 'em hereabouts."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: mark: a sperm whales' feeding ground over the deep water, where a pod is spouting, at 37 55 N 26 32 W
world_orders.words: a mark put in the world, a sperm whales' feeding ground over the deep water, where a pod is spouting,, at 37 55 N 26 32 W

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "There she goes, sir — see the flukes come up, square as a barn door, and down. She'll be twenty minutes under, maybe more. The rest are lying on the top yet, blowing slow. Fine sight, sir."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "Bom dia, capitão. Do not be afraid of the bank for a little cutter like this — twenty-two feet on the shoalest part at low water, and the ebb is half done; you draw, what, nine, ten feet? The sea breaks on it only in a great swell. Let her fall off, senhor, a point or two, fill everything and give her way — she is starving for drive with the wind so far forward. Then we stand in on this tack toward the Guia, and when the college opens of the Carmen we come up for the road. Thirty-five brazas, sand, a mile and a quarter off the town."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "She comes, she comes, capitão — see, three knots now. It is the Pico wind; it comes down off the mountain in puffs and holes, every ship loses her way here the first time. Keep her a little full, let the topsail draw, and she will walk."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.words: a waypoint appended to the Terceira trough

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "Not yet, capitão — here is still sixty, seventy brazas, too deep, the cable will not hold her. Five, six cables more, toward the town: when the college shows a little south of the Carmen and João Dias opens of Espalamaca, there is forty brazas, good sand. I will call it. Begin to shorten now — take in the topsail, keep only main and staysail — so at the mark you round her up and she stops in her own length. With this wind off the land, she will lie quiet."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "Calma, capitão — she paid off too far, she runs for Pico now. No matter: we have room, all the channel. Let her run a little, then wear her round, set the main sail again, two reefs, and come back on the larboard tack with the wind on the beam — not closer, the beam, she likes the beam — heading W by N for the town. Eight cables. When I say, let go."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "Capitão — my boat comes for me, the port captain signals from the mole; there is another ship off the Guia wants me. I am sorry. Listen: you are nearly there. Hold her W by N, the wind on the beam; in three cables the college opens south of the Carmen — there, forty brazas, sand. Round her up and let go. You do not need me for the rest."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "Nossa Senhora — she has walked her anchor right up onto the Praia, the sand by the old fort. Capitão, listen: this is sand and shell, soft, not rock; she will not break. The wind is off the land, it blows her off, it is good. Get the sails off her, pump, and send your boat with the kedge out astern, to the east, into deep water — heave it taut. At the flood this afternoon she floats like a duck. I stay with you until then; my boat can carry the kedge with yours. The whole town is watching — the port captain will send the lighters if you ask."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Terra: "Capitão, half the masters who come in here touch the Praia once — the wind comes down off the Guia in gusts and the ground there does not hold an anchor dragged across it. You did right to get the sail off her. She lies easy on soft sand, and the carpenter says she is dry; she is not hurt. Send your boat with the kedge out to the east, into the deep water, and heave it taut; my boat will go with yours. The flood serves from a quarter past two. By the half-tide she will feel it, and with the kedge's strain on her she comes off a little before the tide alone would lift her."
world_orders.words: Mr Terra spoke on the quarterdeck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Three inches an' gaining slow, sir — that's her seams forrard, strained where she took it. Nothing to fear on sand. Three things, sir. Man the pump, a spell each glass, and she'll suck in ten minutes at this rate — keeps the water from getting at the bread. Then shift what we can aft — the cable tier, the shot, the spare spars off the forecastle — to ease her bow on the ground, an' she'll come off the easier. And when she's afloat the carpenter can get at the seams from inboard with oakum an' a mallet, or we fother a sail under her bow if she's bad; though I'd sooner have the Horta caulkers look at her bottom in the road. Say the word an' I'll have the watch at the pump directly."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Aye aye, sir. Starboard watch, man the pump! Spell an' spell about, till she sucks."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: aboard: the well pumped out
world_orders.words: found aboard: the well pumped dry (0.07 m of water pumped out)

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "It's been done, sir — laying the topsail aback to drive her off astern. But not now: she's hard on, an' all it'll do at low water is put a strain on the topmast an' drive the kedge home. At the half-flood, when she starts to feel the water under her forefoot, a backed topsail with a strain on the kedge hawser might start her a few minutes early. I'd not try it before then, sir, and I'd have the hands ready to clew it up the moment she moves, or she'll go astern onto her own kedge."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

I'd say avast, sir: hold the strain where it is, pawl the capstan, and let the flood do its share first."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "Not hard, sir, no — she went on at a quarter to ten, an' the ebb had hours yet to run then; she's sat on her forefoot ever since an' the water left her. The lead gives four an' a half here, in the chains, but forrard she's on the sand. She'll not lift till the flood's given back all the water she had under her when she struck, an' a foot over — and that's not afore seven bells, by my reckoning of it, maybe eight. The master's table's for Gibraltar, sir, an' it's not much use here. She'll come; the topsail aback won't hurt so long as it don't blow up again."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Pascoe: "She's off, sir! She's off — felt her lift under me an' the hawser come home easy. Clew up that topsail afore she gathers sternway, an' we'll have the kedge in an' the best bower hove short."
world_orders.words: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

world_orders.order: say as Mr Josiah Hale: "*a glass of the Pico wine in his hand* Your pardon, sir — you'll be the master of the English cutter? The whole island watched you take the Praia this morning and come off it this evening. Josiah Hale, of Salem; supercargo, late of the brig Lydia, Coffin master. She sailed and left me here with a fever three weeks since, and I've waited on a passage ever since. Will you take a glass? They say your cutter goes on to Madeira."

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: "*a glass of the Pico wine in his hand* Your pardon, sir — you'll be the master of the English cutter? The whole island watched you take the Praia this morning and come off it this evening. Josiah Hale, of Salem; supercargo, late of the brig Lydia, Coffin master. She sailed and left me here with a fever three weeks since, and I've waited on a passage ever since. Will you take a glass? They say your cutter goes on to Madeira."
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: "*laughs, and pours the captain a glass from the jug* Slim, sir? They're bare to the bone. The whalers come in for water and go out again for the ground, the Lisbon packet won't call till August, and the Funchal brigantine is a week overdue and nobody will say why. A cutter that floats off the Praia under her own kedge in a gale of wind looks a good deal better to me than the wall of this tavern. I can pay — Spanish dollars, my owners' credit good at any house in Funchal — and I eat little and sleep anywhere. When do you sail, sir, and is Madeira truly your road?"
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: "*sets his glass down slowly* The black schooner? The Biscayan? Then she's the one. She took a Guernsey brig off Pico three weeks back, right under the eyes of this town — the brig's mate came ashore here in her boat with nothing but his shirt. I'd sooner take my chance in a Falmouth cutter that knows she's there than in a fat merchantman that doesn't. And mark this, sir: if she's waiting on Gomes's brigantine from Funchal, she's waiting south of St Michael's, not on your road from here to Madeira. Name your fare."
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: "*holds out his hand* Five pounds, a hammock with the hands and a turn at the lines — done, Captain, and gladly. I hauled on a brace or two in the Lydia; I'll not shame you. I'll pay it in dollars when I come aboard, and bring my sea-chest down to the beach at whatever hour you send the boat. And you'll want Bettencourt, I think — the old gentleman keeps his counting house open till all hours; his clerk was on the quay all the evening watching your cutter. Two streets up, the house with the green shutters."
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: "*catches the look, and smiles* No mystery in it, Captain — Horta's a small town. Every master who has come in these ten days has been asked by old Bettencourt himself whether he brought anything from Falmouth, and the Two Brothers' people said his Falmouth cutter was on the way before they sailed. When the island saw English colours on the Praia this morning, half of them said 'Bettencourt's cutter' before they said 'aground'. As for a bed — the widow Silveira lets the rooms above, clean, and her fish stew is the best thing on Fayal. Till the morning, then."
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "Captain of the Sherbourne? Come in, come in, out of the wind. Manuel Bettencourt. I have watched your cutter through my glass all this long day, on the Praia and off it, and I confess I prayed more than I have since my wife died. You have something for me from Falmouth, I think? Sit, sit. Ruiz is still on the quay, the fool; I sent him at noon to wait for your boat."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*he holds out a hand that is not quite steady, and looks long at the seal before he speaks* My own house's seal, and my son's hand on the cover. Unopened. You are an honest man, Captain, and I thank God for it, for there are men in these islands who would have given a great deal to read what is under that wax."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*he reads it through twice, slowly, and for a long moment says nothing; then he folds it and puts it inside his coat* Forgive me, Captain. It is family business, and the house's, and it is no small thing. I must answer it tonight, and my answer must go back by the hand that brought this — yours, if you will carry it, whether you go home by Funchal or straight. We will speak of freights and of what I owe you in the morning, when my head is clearer. Tonight you will not sleep in Silveira's garret; you will eat at my table and sleep under my roof. Come, sir."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*for the first time this evening the old man laughs, a short dry sound* The Madeira? The owners' Madeira, the case my son sends every year in the Falmouth ships to grease the wheels of my good opinion? Drunk in a calm, by thirsty Englishmen, when the water stank. Captain, that is the best use it was ever put to. Bring me the last bottle tomorrow and we will finish it together over the freights, and I will tell my son his wine saved a ship's company from the flux. Come — the table is laid."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*wipes his eyes, and refills the captain's glass from a dusty bottle of old Pico verdelho* Ah, Captain, I have not laughed so since my son sailed for Falmouth. My wife, God rest her, would have put us both out into the street for that one. Another — and then tell me of this calm of yours, and how an English cutter comes to lose her bread and her Madeira on the way to Fayal in June."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*the laughter goes out of his face* The Basque. Etcheverry, of Bayonne — yes, we know him here. Three weeks ago he took a Guernsey brig off the Pico shore in plain sight of this town, and the governor did nothing; a neutral port, he said. He keeps the sea between the islands and Madeira as a cat keeps a mouse-hole, and he has friends ashore who tell him what ships are expected and what they carry. That is why I gave thanks to see your seal unbroken, Captain. *he is quiet a moment* You hove to in the fog and let him go by. Good. You will do as well on your road home, I think, if you keep your own counsel about when you sail."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: "Thirty hours! Then not another word of business. *he takes up the candle* The room over the counting house looks on the bay — you may see your cutter's riding light from the window if you cannot sleep for thinking of her, though I think you will sleep. Maria will bring hot water. I shall be at my desk late; I have a letter to write. Good night, Captain, and God bless you for this day."
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he looks up from his letter, and turns it face down* You cannot sleep either. Sit, Captain. Wine, yes. My Pico wine lies in the lodge at Madalena across the channel, forty pipes, waiting for a ship. Your cutter cannot take forty, but she might take ten, and I will pay you freight to Falmouth at thirty-six pounds the ton, half here and half on delivery to my son. The Basque? *a small shrug* Etcheverry watches what is loaded on the quay at Horta. He does not watch the Pico boats; they cross every day with wine and nobody counts them. If the lighters come out to you after dark and you sail on the morning breeze, the town will know you are gone only when they see the empty water. Say nothing in the taverns, and tell your people the same.
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he laughs softly and holds up a hand* Forgive an old man at midnight, Captain. Thirty-six pounds the ton is what the wine fetches at the lodge, not the freight; no merchant on God's earth pays that to carry it. The freight to Falmouth is four pounds the ton, and that is a fair Western Islands rate. Twenty tons, then: all forty pipes, consigned to my son, eighty pounds the freight, forty paid tomorrow when the bill of lading is signed and forty by him in Falmouth. And if you will carry wine on your own account, I will sell it you at the lodge price less a friend's discount, thirty-two pounds the ton, for as many tons as your purse will stand; it fetches fifty and more in England, if the duty does not eat it. Tomorrow I send to Madalena for the lighters. They come out to you after dark tomorrow night, and you sail with the land breeze before dawn. Now go to bed. *he turns his letter over again*
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Ruiz: Good morning, Mr Pearce. *he folds his ledger under his arm* Nothing strange in the Road this morning: two American whalers, the Pico boats, and your cutter. No schooner. The word from São Miguel is that the black schooner was off Santa Maria last week and robbed a fishing boat of her catch, so she is far to the east of us, God be thanked. But there was a man in the tavern last night, a Frenchman who calls himself a wine buyer, asking the watermen which English vessel came in with her bottom scraped and what she carried. Nobody told him much. Senhor Bettencourt is at his desk already; he has hardly slept. Go up, he expects you.
world_orders.words: Mr Ruiz spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: aboard: a sealed letter for Falmouth, in the keeping of Senhor Bettencourt
world_orders.words: a sealed letter for Falmouth made, in Senhor Bettencourt's keeping

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: Good morning, Mr Pearce. *he waves the Madeira away with a smile* Let the captain bring it himself; it will taste better from his hand. Two lighters from Madalena, twenty pipes in each, six men and the patrão in each with their own tackle. They will leave Madalena at dusk and be alongside two hours after dark, about ten o'clock. Let her lie where she is: out there nobody on the quay can see what goes into her. Show no lights but one lantern hooded low at the gangway, and have your fall and slings rigged before they come; a pipe is half a ton and must go into the hold gently. Ruiz goes out in the first lighter with the bill of lading for the captain to sign, and forty pounds in gold for the freight. *he takes a sealed letter from the desk and holds it out* And this, for my son in Falmouth, into the captain's own hand, please. One more thing: Ruiz tells me a Frenchman was asking questions on the quay last night. Say nothing of wine or the hour of sailing to anyone, and if you go to the tavern for Mr Hale, drink little and listen much.
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: aboard: the sealed letter for Falmouth, on the desk, ashore at Fayal, at the counting house
world_orders.words: the sealed letter for Falmouth moved: it was in Senhor Bettencourt's keeping, and is ashore at Fayal, at the counting house

world_orders.order: say as Senhor Bettencourt: The same, written by candle and sealed at three this morning. *he lays it on the desk before you* Take it up, Mr Pearce; my hand shakes too much at this hour to put it in yours. Keep it inside your coat until the captain has it.
world_orders.words: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: *a lean New Englander rises from a corner bench, his coat buttoned to the throat in spite of the warmth* Mr Pearce. Josiah Hale, of Salem. The fever has left me, thank God, though it has left me thin. My chest is corded and lies behind the bar; the landlord keeps it for me. I am ready whenever the boat is. *lower* A word before we go, since you are her mate. A fellow sat at that table last night, a Frenchman by his speech, in a brown coat, though he called himself a buyer of wine. He stood the watermen drinks and asked what the English cutter carried and when she sailed. He asked me too, being a stranger here myself. I told him I was waiting for the Boston packet and knew nothing of any cutter. He went out an hour before midnight, toward the beach at Porto Pim, not toward the town.
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal

world_orders.order: say as Mr Hale: Nothing of any cutter, Mr Pearce. *he calls to the landlord in careful Portuguese, and a boy shoulders the corded chest* I'll follow you down directly.
world_orders.words: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal
